              CLAUSE - 8

8. Clause 8 seeks to amend Section 32 of the Limited Liability Partnership
Act, 2008.

8.1 Provisions proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

         In section 32 of the principal Act, in sub-section (2), the following provisos
shall be inserted, namely: --

         "Provided that the monetary value of contribution of each partner of a
Specified International Financial Services Centre LLP shall be accounted for
and disclosed in a permitted foreign currency in its accounts:

         Provided further that a limited liability partnership set up in an
International Financial Services Centre prior to the commencement of the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026 may convert monetary value of
contribution of each of its partners from Indian rupee to a permitted foreign
currency within such period and in such manner, as may be specified by the
International Financial Services Centres Authority, in consultation with the
Central Government:

         Provided also that a limited liability partnership referred to in the first
proviso shall not be permitted after such commencement, to receive or accept
monetary contribution from any partner, without converting its monetary
contribution into a permitted foreign currency.".

8.2 Relevant provisions of the Principal Act (The Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008):

32. (1) *  *  *           *  *

(2) The monetary value of contribution of each partner shall be accounted
for and disclosed in the accounts of the limited liability partnership in the
manner as may be prescribed.

8.3 Reasons/justification furnished by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for
the proposed provisions:

         "The amendment is intended to align the accounting treatment of contributions
by Specified IFSC LLPs with the foreign currency-based framework applicable in

                                                       45
International Financial Services Centres. It enables such LLPs to account for and
disclose partner contributions in a permitted foreign currency, while also providing a
transition mechanism for existing IFSC LLPs and ensuring that future contributions
are converted into the permitted foreign currency."

8.4 Important views/suggestions given by experts/stakeholders:

8.4.1 Allowing LLPs in IFSCs to use foreign currency in their capital and accounts
will make it easier for these entities to integrate with global financial systems and
attract offshore investors. It eliminates the constant conversion of capital and
financial statements into rupees, which can simplify compliance and reduce currency
risk for international operations. This reform is a logical extension of the changes
made for companies and will further enhance the competitiveness of Indian IFSCs.
However, the introduction of multiple currencies in financial records can add
complexity to regulatory oversight and compliance. Providing explicit standards (e.g.,
requiring disclosure of conversion rates used, periodic submission of rupee-
equivalent financial information, etc.) can help both businesses and regulators
manage multi-currency accounting in a consistent and transparent way. Clarity is
especially important for tax calculations and any reporting to Indian authorities that
still need INR figures. By addressing these details through clear rules and guidance,
the reform will allow IFSC-based LLPs to smoothly operate in foreign currency, while
maintaining transparency and compliance with the Indian legal framework;

8.4.2 The substantive reform - dollar-denominated capital in GIFT-IFSC - is strongly
supported as it aligns Indian IFSC vehicles with competing jurisdictions. It is
recommended that the clause be retained, subject to the clarification that the
conversion period to be specified by the IFSCA shall not be less than twelve months
from commencement, and that the conversion shall be affected at a reference
exchange rate specified by the IFSCA. A statutory floor for the transition window and
a prescribed reference rate will avoid valuation and audit disputes on conversion and
give existing IFSC LLPs certainty;

8.4.3 Auditing, scrutiny, investigation etc. would become difficult for Income-tax and
all other regulatory agencies as the freedom to prepare books in foreign currency
may be misused. For Income-tax Returns, reporting has to be made in Indian
currency. ICDS VI requires foreign currency transaction to be recorded in Indian
rupee at the time of initial recognition as well as at last day of each tax year. Further
any gain or loss on foreign exchange fluctuation will be recognized in profit and loss
account as per section 43 of the IT Act, 2025. Therefore, the books may be required
to be maintained in permitted foreign currency as well as in Indian rupee;

8.4.4 Explicitly permit contributions through regulated tokenised securities or
tokenised fund units approved by IFSCA. It would support tokenised fundraising and
RWA ecosystems;

                                                       46
8.4.5 Expressly include Category I and Category II Alternative Investment Funds
within the "prescribed class" of LLPs eligible for annual reporting and foreign-
currency-capital relief. Without an express inclusion, the relief intended for VC/PE
funds structured as LLPs remains contingent on future notification rather than
automatic;

8.4.6 Since the concept of "permitted foreign currency" and related procedural
matters are to be specified by IFSCA in consultation with the Central Government, it
is suggested that such subordinate frameworks be evolved in close inter-ministerial
coordination so as to remain aligned with India's broader trade, investment and
external sector policy objectives.

8.5 Examination by the Committee:

8.5.1 In response to a suggestion for providing explicit standards (e.g., requiring
disclosure of conversion rates used, periodic submission of rupee-equivalent
financial information, etc.) to help both businesses and regulators manage multi-
currency accounting in a consistent and transparent way, the Ministry of Corporate
Affairs furnished the following:

                  "Detailed consultations will be held before notification of the
         subordinate legislation in this matter and the necessary clarifications will be
         issued at the time of framing of the rules."

8.5.2 Pursuant to the request that the conversion period to be specified by the
IFSCA should not be less than twelve months from commencement, and that the
conversion shall be affected at a reference exchange rate, the Ministry submitted as
under:

                  "A transition period will be provided to facilitate conversion of
         contribution of the partners after due consultation. The time period for
         conversion will be specified by IFSCA."

8.5.3 Regarding a suggestion that the books may be required to be maintained in
permitted foreign currency as well as in Indian rupee for income tax returns, the
Ministry stated that Income Tax Act may provide its own requirement for the purpose
of taxation.

                                                       47
8.5.4 About a request to permit contributions through regulated tokenised securities
or tokenised fund units approved by IFSCA, the Ministry placed on record that:

                  "Section 32 covers all forms of contributions. It states that, a
         contribution of a partner may consist of tangible, movable or immovable or
         intangible property or other benefit to the limited liability partnership, including
         money, promissory notes, other agreements to contribute cash or property,
         and contracts for services performed or to be performed. Thus, all forms of
         contributions are already recognised."

8.5.5 On the subject of inclusion of Category I and Category II Alternative
Investment Funds within the "prescribed class" of LLPs eligible for annual reporting
and foreign-currency-capital relief, the Ministry stated that the necessary inclusion
will take place through the rules, after due consultation with SEBI, IFSCA and all
other stakeholders.

8.5.6 With respect to the suggestion that subordinate framework may be evolved in
close inter-ministerial coordination, the Ministry submitted the following:

                  "This would be appropriately dealt with during framing of subordinate
         legislation. The suggestion pertains to the manner in which the regulatory
         framework governing permitted foreign currency and related procedural
         requirements is to be operationalised. Since these matters are proposed to be
         prescribed through subordinate legislation and regulations, the issue of inter-
         ministerial consultation and coordination would be addressed at the stage of
         formulation of the relevant Rules."

8.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

8.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 8 of the Bill seeks to insert three new
provisos in sub-section (2) of section 32 of the Limited Liability Partnership
Act, 2008. The proposed amendments provide that the monetary value of
contribution of each partner in a Specified IFSC LLP shall be accounted for
and disclosed in a permitted foreign currency. The Clause further provides a
transitional framework for the Specified IFSC LLPs established before the
commencement of the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026, to convert the

                                                       48
monetary value of the partners' contributions from Indian Rupees to a
permitted foreign currency within the period and in the manner as specified by
the International Financial Services Centres Authority, in consultation with the
Central Government. It also provides that, after the commencement of the
proposed legislation, such LLPs shall not receive or accept any monetary
contribution from a partner unless the monetary value of such contributions
has first been converted into a permitted foreign currency.

         The Committee are of the opinion that the proposed amendments are
intended to bring uniformity and consistency in the accounting and reporting
practices of Specified IFSC LLPs by ensuring that the monetary value of
partner contributions is maintained and disclosed in a permitted foreign
currency. Further, the transitional provisions provided for existing IFSC LLPs
would facilitate a smooth transition to the proposed regulatory framework
without causing any disruption to their operations.

         Accordingly, having considered the justification furnished by the
Ministry, the views and suggestions received from stakeholders and experts,
and the deliberations held thereon, the Committee accept the Clause 8 of the
Bill as proposed.

                                                       49
                                                CLAUSE - 9

9. Clause 9 seeks to insert new Section 33A in the Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008.

9.1 Provisions proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

         After section 33 of the principal Act, the following section shall be inserted,
namely: --

                  "33A. The provisions of section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013 shall
         mutatis mutandis apply for the valuation, required to be made in respect of
         contribution of a partner of a limited liability partnership, or of any property or
         assets or net worth of such limited liability partnership, or its liabilities under
         the provisions of this Act or rules made thereunder.".

9.2 Relevant provisions of the Principal Act (The Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008):

         There are no corresponding provisions in the Principal Act. New Section 33A
has been inserted to provide those provisions of section 247 of the Companies Act,
2013 shall apply for valuation in respect of Limited Liability Partnerships.

9.3 Reasons/justification furnished by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for
the proposed provisions:

         "This amendment seeks to clarify that where valuation is required in relation to
an LLP's contribution, property, assets, net worth, or liabilities; section 247 of the
Companies Act, 2013 will apply mutatis mutandis."

9.4 Important views/suggestions given by experts/stakeholders:

9.4.1 Separate carved out provisions may be made for IFSC units. Applying rigid
domestic valuation standards to entities in the IFSC could hinder cross-border capital
structuring. Valuation mechanisms must dynamically account for permitted foreign
currency transactions and global pricing benchmarks unique to the IFSC;

9.4.2 While introducing a valuation standard for LLPs is a positive step for
governance, the implementation should be proportionate. It is recommended that
Section 33A (or its rules) allow appropriate exemptions so that very small LLPs or
minor transactions are not unduly burdened with having to engage a licensed valuer.

                                                       50
In addition, the rules should clearly specify the triggers and scope of the valuation
requirement. For example, identifying which transactions or situations in an LLP
(such as major asset sales, mergers or significant related-party transactions) must
be valued by a registered valuer. This clarity will help avoid over-burdening small
firms with unnecessary requirements;

9.4.3 There is no clarity on how the "Premium" on the stake of partnership shall be
recorded. In case of Companies, there is a concept of Securities Premium Account,
wherein excess amount over Face Value is accounted for at the time of issuance of
fresh capital, however, there is no such provision for LLPs. A better clarity on this
would produce a meaningful effect & usage of the Valuation norms in the event an
existing LLP brings in money at a premium & fresh stake is infused by new partner.
Lastly, any such change should be aligned with the provisions of Section 45(4) of the
erstwhile Income Tax Act, 1961 which deals with such scenarios;

9.4.4 For LLPs operating in IFSCs (International Financial Services Centres), it be
explicitly stipulated that any required valuation must be done by an IBBI-registered
valuer. Ensuring that even IFSC-based LLPs use Indian registered valuers (as
opposed to potentially unregulated foreign professionals) will maintain consistent
standards and oversight. These refinements will build trust in the reliability of LLP
valuations while keeping compliance obligations proportional to the size and scale of
the business;

9.4.5 Insert a Grandfathering Clause as under:

"Notwithstanding anything contained in Section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013 or
the Rules made thereunder, every person who was registered as a Valuer under
Section 34AB of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957 and who continues as a Registered Valuer
under Section 514 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 read with Rule 246 of the Income-tax
Rules, 2026 shall be deemed eligible to undertake valuation assignments under the
Companies Act, 2013 and the LLP Act, 2008, subject to such conditions, as may be
prescribed by the Central Government."

9.4.6 Parliament itself has recognized continuity of registration of Wealth-tax Act
Valuers under Section 514 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The Companies Act should
adopt the same legislative policy to maintain consistency across Central laws and
protect vested rights of experienced valuers;

9.4.7 Clarify that valuation under the LLP Act may be carried out by Registered
Valuers under the Companies Act and Grandfathered Valuers recognized under
Section 514 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. It would ensure uniformity between Central
legislations, avoid contradictory regulatory frameworks and preserve availability of
experienced valuation professionals;

                                                       51
9.4.8 The valuation reports issued by Grandfathered Valuers should have the same
legal validity and evidentiary value as those issued by Registered Valuers under the
Companies Act. It would prevent discrimination between professionals recognized
under different Central legislations and provide certainty to companies, banks, courts
and regulatory authorities;

9.4.9 Existing valuers covered under Section 514 of the Income-tax Act may be
provided a simplified migration mechanism to the Registered Valuer framework
without duplication of educational qualifications, examinations or lengthy procedural
requirements, giving due recognition to their professional experience. It would
recognize decades of professional experience and facilitate smooth transition without
adversely affecting senior valuers;

9.4.10 Appointment of Valuer should be approved by the Board of Directors/ Partners
through a formal resolution and removal before completion of assignment should be
permitted only by recording reasons in writing, after giving reasonable opportunity of
being heard. It would protect independence of valuation professionals and prevents
undue influence or pressure from management;

9.4.11 Liability of a Valuer should arise only in cases involving fraud, wilful
misconduct or gross negligence. Mere difference in professional opinion or variation
in valuation should not attract civil or criminal liability. Valuation is an opinion based
upon accepted methodologies, assumptions and market conditions and cannot be
treated as an exact science;

9.4.12 Before initiating disciplinary, penal or criminal proceedings against a Valuer,
the matter should first be examined by an independent Technical Valuation Review
Committee comprising experienced valuation professionals, representing
Government Registered Valuer Organisations. It would ensure technical scrutiny
before legal action and minimize frivolous litigation arising from differences in
valuation methodology;

9.4.13 Company/LLP management should remain solely responsible for the
correctness, completeness and authenticity of financial, legal and technical
information supplied to the Valuer. The Valuer should not be held responsible for
incorrect or concealed information unless knowingly relied upon. It would clearly
allocate responsibility and protect valuers acting in good faith on information supplied
by management;

9.4.14 Introduce statutory protection for Valuers acting in good faith. No legal
proceeding should be initiated after three years from submission of valuation report
except in cases involving fraud or wilful misconduct. It would protect professionals
from perpetual litigation, while ensuring accountability in genuine cases of fraud;

                                                       52
9.4.15 Every valuation report should contain a declaration regarding independence,
conflict of interest, professional standards followed and category of registration of the
Valuer. MCA may prescribe standardized reporting formats based upon Indian
Valuation Standards and International Valuation Standards. It would improve
transparency, consistency and quality of valuation reports across the country;

9.4.16 IBBI as designated valuation authority should have a minimum of 05 duly
elected valuation professional representatives from all five proposed zones of India
(viz. north, south, east, west & central). These representatives may be from the
active/practicing eminent valuation professionals having requisite statutory
qualification as registered valuers and having long standing professional, academic
experience and reputation;

9.4.17 The clause be retained as drafted, with commencement synchronised with
Clause 73 (restructured section 247), so that LLP valuations are performed under the
new Valuation Authority framework from inception. A single valuation discipline
across companies and LLPs removes arbitrage and professionalises LLP valuations
(relevant to conversions under Clauses 12-13 and to contribution in kind).
Synchronised commencement under clause 1(2) avoids a transitional vacuum;

9.4.18 Notify valuation standards for crypto assets, tokenised assets, utility tokens,
stablecoins and blockchain protocols as traditional valuation frameworks do not
adequately cover digital assets;

9.4.19 Before framing or amending Rules relating to valuation under the Companies
Act or LLP Act, the Central Government should consult Registered Valuer
Organisations and recognized national professional valuation bodies including
Practising Valuers Association of India (PVAI) and All India Valuers Association
(AIVA). Stakeholder participation would result in practical, balanced and effective
legislation and reflect the experience of practising professionals;

9.4.20 The rule-making and regulation-making powers under this clause should be
exercised with due regard to compliance costs, proportionality of fees and penalties,
and availability of adequate professional capacity, especially where business
sentiment and cost of compliance may be indirectly affected.

9.5 Examination by the Committee:

9.5.1 Justifying the proposed insertion of Section 33A in the Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs placed on record the
following:

                                                       53
                  "The absence of a statutory valuation framework under the LLP Act,
         2008 has remained a significant legislative gap. While the Income-tax Act
         increasingly relies upon fair market valuation for taxing partner retirements
         and LLP reconstitutions, the LLP Act has not prescribed a corresponding
         mechanism. The proposed insertion of Section 33A through the Corporate
         Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, is therefore, a significant reform expected to
         ensure consistency, transparency, legal certainty and better coordination
         between corporate law and income-tax law, while reducing valuation-related
         litigation and protection of the government revenue interest."

9.5.2 In response to a suggestion that separate carved out provisions may be made
for IFSC units in order to account for permitted foreign currency transactions and
global pricing benchmarks unique to IFSC, the Ministry submitted as under:

                  "Section 33A has been inserted specifically to recognise the powers of
         the registering authority (viz. The Insolvency & Bankruptcy Board of India) with
         regard to recognition of valuers, organisations and registration of valuers. In
         tandem, provisions are being introduced to grant power to the Insolvency and
         Bankruptcy Board of India to specify regulatory and procedural requirements
         by way of regulations.

                  This amendment has been brought about to maintain uniformity
         between companies and limited liability partnerships, as well to enable
         Insolvency & Bankruptcy Board to have authority to regulate.

                  Further, requiring valuations to be carried out by registered valuers is
         expected to improve the quality of reliability and consistency in valuations,
         particularly in cases involving non-monetary or in-kind contributions,
         valuations of assets or net-worth, or other specific transactions. Given the
         varying nature and complexity of such valuations, a uniform framework
         administered by qualified valuers may be beneficial."

9.5.3 Concerning the issue that Section 33A (or its rules) should allow appropriate
exemptions, so that very small LLPs or minor transactions are not unduly burdened
with having to engage a licensed valuer, the Ministry placed on record that:

                  "Valuation would be required at different stages, like where the
         contribution is for other than cash, mergers, etc. There are clear provisions for
         this in the LLP Act. Valuation is not applicable on the day-to-day business of
         the LLPs. Exemptions would not be applicable to small LLPs in cases, where
         valuation would be required under the Act."

                                                       54
9.5.4 On being asked about the instances where valuation would be mandatorily
required in case of limited liability partnership, the Ministry replied that:

                  "The proposed amendment provides a framework for carrying out
         valuations which are required under the provisions of the Act or rules. This is
         not an ongoing compliance, but it would only be required in specific cases
         under the Act and the rules. The proposal is to align the valuation framework
         of the LLPs with the existing provisions under the Companies Act, 2013.

         Instances where valuation is required

         · Contributions held in kind: Section 32(1) of the LLP Act, 2008 outlines
         that contribution may consist of tangible, movable, immovable, or intangible
         property. Rule 23(1) of the LLP Rules, 2009 explicitly mandates that the
         monetary value of such non-monetary contributions must be accounted for
         and certified. Contribution is a criterion to determine as to whether an LLP is a
         small LLP or not. This will bring in transparency for those cases, where
         contribution is in kind.

         · Mergers: Rule 35(3)(a)(v) of the LLP Rules, 2009 states that when the
         NCLT orders meetings for compromises or arrangements, it provides
         directions for determining the values of the creditors and/or the partners, as
         the case may be, whose meetings have to be held.

         · Winding up related provisions: Valuation of assets requirement in case
         of voluntary winding up under rule 7(2)(d) of the Limited Liability Partnership
         (Winding up and Dissolution) Rules, 2012. For other liquidations too, valuation
         is required to be done as per rule 34."

9.5.5 Concerning the demands that valuation under the LLP Act may be carried out
by Registered Valuers under the Companies Act and Grandfathered Valuers
recognized under Section 514 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 and the valuation reports
issued by Grandfathered Valuers should have the same legal validity and evidentiary
value as those issued by Registered Valuers, the Ministry clarified that the provisions
relating to valuation in the LLP Act are aligned with the Companies Act, which does
not recognize valuers under the Wealth Tax Act.

                                                       55
9.5.6 Regarding a suggestion that existing valuers covered under Section 514 of
the Income-tax Act may be provided a simplified migration mechanism to the
Registered Valuer framework, the Ministry furnished as follows:

                  "The provisions relating to valuation in LLP Act are aligned with the
         Section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013. Clause 73 proposes to amend
         Section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013 which is in force since Oct, 2017.
         The IBBI was already given statutory powers u/s section 247 through
         notification issued under section 458 of the Companies Act, 2013. The
         proposed amendment recognizes IBBI as Valuation Authority."

9.5.7 About a request that appointment of Valuer should be approved by the Board
of Directors/ Partners through a formal resolution and removal before completion of
assignment should be permitted only by recording reasons in writing after giving
reasonable opportunity of being heard, the Ministry explained as under:

                  "The provisions relating to valuation in LLP Act are aligned with Section
         247 of the Companies Act, 2013. Section 247 of the Act requires appointment
         of valuer by the Board of Directors. Sub section (2) of Section 247 prescribes
         for independence of the Valuer. Valuer is appointed for a specific transaction,
         as such there is no tenure. Introducing a detailed statutory procedure for
         removal may delay corporate transactions that depend upon timely valuation."

9.5.8 With respect to a suggestion that liability of a Valuer should arise only in cases
involving fraud, wilful misconduct or gross negligence, the Ministry placed on record
the following:

                  "The Bill provides a multi-layered accountability framework, ensuring
         that valuers incur civil or criminal liability depending on the nature of breach.
         Acts of fraud will lead to criminal liability."

9.5.9 For the suggestions that before initiating disciplinary, penal or criminal
proceedings against a Valuer, the matter should first be examined by an independent
Technical Valuation Review Committee; company/LLP management should remain
solely responsible for the correctness, completeness and authenticity of financial,
legal and technical information supplied to the Valuer; statutory protection should be
introduced for Valuers acting in good faith; and that every valuation report should

                                                       56
contain a declaration regarding independence, conflict of interest, professional
standards followed and category of registration of the Valuer, the Ministry stated that
these suggestions would be considered while framing of the regulations by Valuation
Authority and valuation standards by the Central Government.

9.5.10 Following a suggestion that IBBI as designated valuation authority should
have a minimum of 05 duly elected valuation professional representatives from all
five proposed zones of India, the Ministry submitted that:

                  "IBBI is established under section 188 of the IBC, 2016 which shall be
         Valuation Authority for the purpose of Section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013
         and Section 33A of the LLP Act. A statutory regulator must function as an
         objective, independent supervisor. Elections may interfere with strict market
         oversight, and undermine objective enforcement."

9.5.11 Further, responding to the demand to include 05 duly elected valuation
professional in IBBI, the representative of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs deposed
before the Committee that:

                  "This cannot be done through Companies Act; it is governed by IBC
         Act. Valuation professionals being in the Board of IBBI will be a conflict of
         interest, because the IBBI will be basically handling the disciplinary actions
         related to valuers."

9.5.12 On the request for notifying valuation standards for crypto assets, tokenised
assets, utility tokens, stablecoins and blockchain protocols as traditional valuation
frameworks do not adequately cover digital assets, the Ministry clarified that:

                  "Valuation Standards will be notified in consultation with IBBI. As such,
         this suggestion is not relevant for the purposes of this amendment, as the
         amendment only provides an enabling framework."

9.5.13 While accepting the suggestion that before framing or amending Rules
relating to valuation under the Companies Act or LLP Act, the Central Government

                                                       57
should consult Registered Valuer Organisations and recognized national professional
valuation bodies, the Ministry furnished as under:

                  "The provisions relating to valuation in LLP Act are aligned with the
         Section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013. Section 247(9) of the Act provides
         for regulation making power of Valuation Authority which may include
         provision for prior public consultation."

9.5.14 In pursuance of a suggestion that the rule-making and regulation-making
powers under this clause should be exercised with due regard to compliance costs,
proportionality of fees and penalties, and availability of adequate professional
capacity, the Ministry submitted as under:

                  "This would be appropriately dealt with during framing of subordinate
         legislation. The suggestion pertains to the manner in which the rule-making
         and regulation-making powers are to be exercised."

9.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

9.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 9 of the Bill seeks to insert a new
section 33A in the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, to provide that the
provisions of section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013, relating to valuation by
registered valuers, shall apply mutatis mutandis to the valuation of a partner's
contribution in an LLP, or valuation of any property, assets, net worth or
liabilities of such LLP, or wherever such valuation is required under the
provisions of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 or the rules made
thereunder.

         The Committee observe that while the Income-tax Act increasingly relies
upon fair market valuation principles for determining tax implications in cases
such as, partner retirement and reconstitution of LLPs, the Limited Liability
Partnership Act does not presently provide for a corresponding mechanism to
ensure uniformity and transparency in valuation. The Committee agree with
the contention of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs that, in the absence of a

                                                       58
specific statutory valuation framework under the Limited Liability Partnership
Act, 2008, there has been a legislative gap in relation to valuation requirements
concerning partner contributions, assets, liabilities and other financial aspects
of LLPs. Therefore, the Committee believe that the proposed amendment
would address the absence of a specific statutory valuation framework under
the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, by providing a consistent and
legally recognized valuation mechanism for LLPs.

         The Committee are of the view that by adopting the established
framework under section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013, the proposed
amendment would enhance transparency, ensure greater certainty in
valuation-related matters, facilitate better coordination between corporate law
and taxation provisions, and help in reducing disputes and litigation arising
from valuation issues, while safeguarding the revenue interests of the
Government. Accordingly, the Committee recommend that Clause 9 of the Bill
be accepted without any amendment.

9.6.2 Further, the Committee note the submissions made by the Ministry of
Corporate Affairs that certain suggestions relating to Clause 9, which were
raised during the deliberations of the Committee, would be duly considered at
the time of formulation of Regulations by the Valuation Authority and the
Valuation Standards by the Central Government. These suggestions, inter alia,
include mandating consultation with Registered Valuer Organizations and
recognized professional bodies before framing or amending valuation rules;
ensuring that the exercise of rule-making and regulation-making powers under
the proposed provision takes into account compliance costs, proportionality
of fees and penalties, and the availability of adequate professional capacity;
examination of matters by an independent Technical Valuation Review
Committee before initiation of any disciplinary, penal or criminal proceedings
against a Valuer; ensuring that the management of a company or LLP remains
responsible for the correctness, completeness and authenticity of the
financial, legal and technical information provided to the Valuer; providing
statutory protection to Valuers acting in good faith; and requiring every

                                                       59
valuation report to contain a declaration regarding the independence of the
Valuer, absence of conflict of interest, professional standards followed, and
the category of registration of the Valuer, etc.

         The Committee are of the opinion that these issues and suggestions are
important for ensuring a robust, transparent and balanced valuation
framework and should be appropriately addressed while framing the relevant
rules, regulations and valuation standards. The Committee, therefore,
recommend that due consideration should be given to the above suggestions
at the time of formulation of the rules and regulations under the proposed
provisions by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs and the Insolvency and
Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI).
9.6.3 The Committee have examined in detail the relevant provisions of
Section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013, relating to valuation by registered
valuers, under Clause 73, and have given their observations/
recommendations in paragraph nos. 73.6.1, 73.6.2, 73.6.3 and 73.6.4 of this
Report.

                                                       60
         CLAUSE - 10

10. Clause 10 seeks to amend Section 34 of the Limited Liability Partnership
Act, 2008.

10.1 Provisions proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

In section 34 of the principal Act, --

(a) in sub-section (1), the following provisos shall be inserted, namely:--

         "Provided that a Specified International Financial Services Centre LLP,
maintaining its contribution in a permitted foreign currency, shall prepare and
maintain its books of account, books and papers, financial statement and all
other records in the permitted foreign currency:

         Provided further that a Specified International Financial Services
Centre LLP may be permitted to prepare its books of account, books and
papers, financial statement and other records in Indian rupee, if so allowed by
the International Financial Services Centres Authority.";

(b) in sub-section (5), for the word, brackets and figure "sub-section (3)",
the words, brackets and figures "sub-sections (1), (2) and (3)" shall be
substituted;

(c) in sub-section (6), the words, brackets and figures "sub-section (1),
sub-section (2) and" shall be omitted.

10.2 Relevant provisions of the Principal Act (The Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008):

34. (1) The limited liability partnership shall maintain such proper books
of account as may be prescribed relating to its affairs for each year of its
existence on cash basis or accrual basis and according to double entry
system of accounting and shall maintain the same at its registered office for
such period as may be prescribed.

*  *  *                                 *  *  *.

         61
         (5) Any limited liability partnership which fails to comply with the provisions
         of sub-section (3), such limited liability partnership and its designated partners
         shall be liable to a penalty of one hundred rupees for each day during which
         such failure continues, subject to a maximum of one lakh rupees for the
         limited liability partnership and fifty thousand rupees for every designated
         partner.

         (6) Any limited liability partnership which fails to comply with the provisions
         of sub-section (1), sub-section (2) and sub-section (4), such limited liability
         partnership shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than twenty-
         five thousand rupees, but may extend to five lakh rupees and every
         designated partner of such limited liability partnership shall be punishable with
         fine which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees, but may extend to one
         lakh rupees.

10.3 Reasons/justification furnished by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for
the proposed provisions:

         "This amendment seeks to align the maintenance of books of account for
Specified IFSC LLPs with the foreign currency-based framework applicable in
International Financial Services Centres by permitting such LLPs to prepare and
maintain their records in a permitted foreign currency, while allowing the IFSCA to
permit Indian rupee presentation, where appropriate.

         Further, the amendment rationalises the penalty structure under section 34 by
extending the penalty under sub-section (5) to non-compliance with sub-sections (1)
and (2), while limiting sub-section (6) to non-compliance with sub-section (4) only.
This avoids overlap in penal consequences and simplifies the compliance
framework, thereby decriminalising the provision to that extent."

10.4 Important views/suggestions given by experts/stakeholders:

10.4.1 Auditing, scrutiny, investigation etc. would become difficult for Income-tax and
all other regulatory agencies as the freedom to prepare books in foreign currency
may be misused. For Income-tax Returns, reporting has to be made in Indian
currency. ICDS VI requires foreign currency transaction to be recorded in Indian
rupee at the time of initial recognition as well as at last day of each tax year. Further
any gain or loss on foreign exchange fluctuation will be recognized in profit and loss
account as per section 43 of the IT Act, 2025. Therefore, the books may be required
to be maintained in permitted foreign currency as well as in Indian rupee;

10.4.2 Permitting LLPs in IFSCs to denominate their capital and maintain accounts in
an approved foreign currency will streamline their operations and reporting, making
them more attractive and competitive in an international context. To implement this

                                                       62
effectively, the regulatory framework should include clear guidance on practical
aspects. For instance, rules or notifications should detail the acceptable foreign
currencies, how to perform currency conversion for statutory filings (e.g., at what
reference rates to convert any rupee-based thresholds or fees), and how to handle
exchange rate fluctuations in accounts and reports. Additionally, any necessary
adjustments under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) or tax laws
should be clarified to ensure that maintaining books in a foreign currency does not
conflict with other legal requirements;

10.4.3 Permit digital ledgers, blockchain-native accounting records and cryptographic
audit trails as supporting books of account. Blockchain records improve auditability
and transparency;

10.4.4 The Committee may consider creating a distinction for the quantum of penalty
on reasonable grounds. For instance, companies may be divided into tiers based on
their share-capital and penalised accordingly, instead of a uniform amount being
prescribed for all companies. This would ensure a more equitable approach while
penalising companies for non-compliance. The justification for incorporating a tiered
approach stems from the recognition that standard or uniform penalties for non-
compliance would affect different LLPs disproportionately. A uniform amount may be
too small for a large-scale partnership and significant for a smaller LLP. The rationale
for incorporating total partner contribution as a basis for the tiered approach is
threefold. Firstly, this is an objective indicator of the size of an LLP and its' ability to
pay penalties. Secondly, an LLP's total partnership contribution may be easily
identified by the review of the partnership agreement. Thirdly, an LLP's total partner
contribution is less likely to undergo volatile changes as compared to turnover or
profit;

10.4.5 The Committee may consider keeping aggravated penalties for Specified
International Financial Services Centre LLPs considering the nature of the services
and products such LLPs are dealing with. For instance, a proviso could be added to
subsections (5) and (6) specifying the additional quantum of payment that needs to
be paid by the Specified International Financial Services Centre LLP. The justification
for seeking separate and aggravated penalties for Specified International Financial
Services Centre LLPs is due to the products such LLPs deal with. All Specified
International Financial Services Centre LLPs will be dealing with financial products
and it is in the best interest of the stakeholders to keep proper books of accounts,
statement of accounts and insolvency, and regular audit of such statements. While a
potential concern could be raised regarding the ease of doing business, it is pertinent
to mention that the maximum penalty of one lakh for violation under subsection (5)
and a maximum penalty of five lakhs under subsection (6) is a miniscule amount
compared to the corpus of the fund. Given the nature of Specified International
Financial Services Centre LLPs, to ensure a meaningful deterrent, the penalty
imposed on such LLP should exceed the quantum of penalty charged against any
other LLP;

                                                       63
10.4.6 Since the concept of "permitted foreign currency" and related procedural
matters are to be specified by IFSCA in consultation with the Central Government, it
is suggested that such subordinate frameworks be evolved in close inter-ministerial
coordination so as to remain aligned with India's broader trade, investment and
external sector policy objectives.

10.5 Examination by the Committee:

10.5.1 Regarding the suggestion that the books may be required to be maintained in
permitted foreign currency as well as in Indian rupee, the Ministry of Corporate
Affairs stated that Income Tax Act may provide its own requirement for the purpose of
taxation.

10.5.2 Clarifying about the requirement for a specified IFSC LLP to prepare and
maintain its books of account, financial statement and all other records in the
permitted foreign currency, the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs deposed
before the Committee that:

                  "     ,  particular    
              they have to be compliant.      
                       
           ,               
             purposes      It is not for the tax
         purposes........IFSCA is a foreign territory area, where all the enterprises that
         are coming in, or that are being established, they are coming with a very
         different mindset of getting investment into the country and are being very
         compliant."

10.5.3 In response to a view that rules or notifications should detail the acceptable
foreign currencies, how to perform currency conversion for statutory filings and how
to handle exchange rate fluctuations in accounts and reports, the Ministry furnished
the following:

                  "Detailed consultations will be held before notification of the
         subordinate legislation in this matter and the necessary clarifications will be
         issued at the time of framing of the rules."

                                                       64
10.5.4 With respect to a request to permit digital ledgers, blockchain-native
accounting records and cryptographic audit trails as supporting books of account, the
Ministry clarified that:

                  "There is no need of a specific provision in this regard. The LLP has
         flexibility in terms of the manner of maintaining its books of account.
         Necessary cybersecurity measures may be kept in place for such situations."

10.5.5 Concerning the suggestions that companies may be divided into tiers based
on their share-capital and penalised accordingly, and aggravated penalties may be
prescribed for specified IFSC LLPs considering the nature of the services and
products such LLPs are dealing with, the Ministry placed on record the following:

                  "The second proviso to Section 76A(3)(a) of the LLP Act, 2008
         mandates that when an Adjudicating Officer imposes a penalty on a Small LLP
         or a Start-up LLP (or its partners/designated partners), the penalty shall be
         one-half of the amount specified in the respective provision. Furthermore, it
         caps the maximum penalty liability at Rs. 1,00,000 for the LLP and Rs. 50,000
         for each partner or designated partner. Thus, the penalties are already
         calibrated based on the types of LLPs."

10.5.6 About the suggestion that subordinate framework may be evolved in close
inter-ministerial coordination, the Ministry submitted as under:

                  "This would be appropriately dealt with during framing of subordinate
         legislation. The suggestion pertains to the manner in which the regulatory
         framework governing permitted foreign currency and related procedural
         requirements is to be operationalised. Since these matters are proposed to be
         prescribed through subordinate legislation and regulations, the issue of inter-
         ministerial consultation and coordination would be addressed at the stage of
         formulation of the relevant Rules."

10.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

10.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 10 of the Bill seeks to insert two new
provisos in sub-section (1) of section 34 of the Limited Liability Partnership
Act, 2008, to provide that a Specified IFSC LLP maintaining its partners'

                                                       65
contributions in a permitted foreign currency, shall also prepare and maintain
its books of account, financial statements and other records in permitted
foreign currency. The Clause further provides that such LLP may prepare and
maintain the aforesaid records in Indian Rupees, if permitted by the
International Financial Services Centres Authority. The Clause also seeks to
decriminalize the offences under sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 34 by
rationalizing the applicable penalty provisions.

         The Committee observe that the proposed amendments intend to align
the accounting and record-keeping requirements of Specified IFSC LLPs with
the foreign currency-based framework applicable to entities operating within
International Financial Services Centres, thereby ensuring consistency
between their financial reporting practices and the nature of their operations.
At the same time, the provision enabling IFSCA to permit preparation of
accounts and records in Indian Rupees, provides the necessary flexibility and
facilitates ease of compliance. The Committee further observe that the
proposed rationalization of penalty provisions under section 34 aims to
simplify the compliance framework by avoiding duplication and overlap in
penal consequences, which is in line with the objective of decriminalizing
procedural offences, while ensuring effective regulatory compliance.

         In view of the above, the Committee are satisfied that the proposed
amendments would provide greater regulatory clarity, facilitate ease of doing
business for Specified IFSC LLPs and ensure consistency with the regulatory
framework applicable to entities operating in International Financial Services
Centres. Therefore, the Committee accept the Clause 10 of the Bill as
proposed.

* * * * *

11.3. Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry for the proposed provisions:

"The amendment distinguishes between non-compliance with summons and
requisitions by removing requisitions from sub-section (3) and introducing a separate
penalty provision. It subjects failure to comply with requisitions to a fixed monetary
penalty, thereby decriminalising the provision."

11.4. Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:
                                                       67
11.4.1 "Monetary penalties under rules and amended provisions be calibrated

11.5. Examination by the Committee:

11.5.1 In response to the suggestion regarding calibration of penalties, the Ministry in
its written reply submitted as under:

"The monetary penalties under the Amendment Bill have been proposed after
considering the nature and gravity of the defaults and the aspect of proportionality.

The Amendment Bill already incorporates a calibrated penalty framework based on
the seriousness of the default.

The proviso to Section 76A of the LLP Act already provides for if penalty is payable
for non-compliance of any of the provisions of this Act by a small limited liability
partnership or a startup limited liability partnership or by its partner or designated
partner or any other person in respect of such limited liability partnership, then such
limited liability partnership or its partner or designated partner or any other person,
shall be liable to a penalty which shall be one-half of the penalty specified in such

11.6. Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

The Committee find that the amendment proposed under Clause 11 pertains to
Section 38 of the LLP Act,2008. The Committee note the suggestion that

The Committee also note the reply of the Ministry that the monetary penalties
under the Amendment Bill have been proposed after considering the nature

                                                       68
and gravity of the defaults and the aspect of proportionality. The Ministry has
also stated that the Amendment Bill already incorporates a calibrated penalty
framework based on the seriousness of the default.
Thus, after considering the replies of the Ministry and noting that the proposed
provision is aligned with the stated object of ease of doing business and is
likely to reduce avoidable risk perception for investors, boards and
entrepreneurs in relation to non- substantive compliance lapses, the
Committee are of the view that the amendment under Clause 11 is appropriate.
Accordingly, the Committee accept the amendment in its present form.

12. Clause 12 amends Section 57 of the Principal Act (LLP Act, 2008) by
proposing to insert new-subsection 57 A:

12.1. Provision proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

12. After section 57 of the principal Act, the following section shall be inserted,
namely:--

"57A. A specified trust may convert into a limited liability partnership in accordance
with the provisions of this Chapter and the Fifth Schedule.

Explanation.--For the purposes of this section, the term "specified trust" means a
trust established under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 or under a Central Act or State
Act, and registered by the Securities and Exchange Board of India, or by the
International Financial Services Centres Authority, as the case may be, having such
activities as may be prescribed.".

12.2. Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (Companies Act, 2013):

Sub-section newly inserted

12.3. Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry for the proposed provisions:

"This amendment introduces a statutory framework to enable specified trusts,
registered by SEBI or IFSCA having prescribed activities to convert into LLPs. It
facilitates the adoption of the LLP structure by investment vehicles with provisions on
eligibility and the conversion process, thereby promoting flexibility in fund structuring
and improving ease of doing business. This is part of the Amendment Bill's broader
regulatory framework for such entities through amendments to section 23, 25, 58,
and insertion of Schedule V of the LLP Act."

12.4. Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

12.4.1.  "Section 57A and the Fifth Schedule (Refer: Section 57A read with Fifth

Schedule - Para 2) introduce a framework enabling conversion of SEBI/IFSC

                            70
regulated trusts into Limited Liability Partnerships. It is suggested that the Ministry of
Corporate Affairs (MCA), in consultation with SEBI, should provide the framework to
streamline the conversion process and ensure that mandatory investor protection
clauses are preserved."

"NOC should be mandatory from SEBI or IFSC as may be applicable for purpose of
conversion. The tax implication if any on such conversion should also be addressed
in consultation with CBDT. To avoid potential stamp duty implications under
applicable state laws on conversion, all references to "transfer" should be replaced
with "vesting," as the conversion results in vesting rather than a transfer."

12.4.2.        "The new Section 57A inter alia proposes that a 'specified trust'

registered with SEBI or IFSCA may convert into LLP in accordance with the new Fifth

Schedule. Suggestion: In Paragraph 3 of the Proposed Fifth Schedule, the word

"trustees" may be replaced with "investors" and also "Managers" may be permitted to

become "Partners". Proposed revised draft clause: Para 3 of the proposed Fifth

Schedule: "Eligibility for conversion. --A specified trust may apply to convert into a

limited liability partnership in accordance with this Schedule, only if the partners of

the limited liability partnership into which the specified trust is to be converted, are

trustees investors in such specified trust and the manager of such specified trust and

no one else."

12.4.3.        "SEBI's registration is granted to AIF which may operate like an

umbrella structure. i.e., under one Registration, an AIF may launch more than one

scheme. Each scheme is independently recognised by the regulator. Further, each

such "scheme" constitutes a distinct and separately identifiable pool of investor

capital, with its own investment objective, commitment amounts, fee terms, and

vintage. Each scheme holds a separate Permanent Account Number (PAN) under

the Income Tax Act, maintains its own bank account, dematerialised securities

account with the depository, and files its own tax return. The pass-through taxation

mechanism under Section 115UB of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (now Section 224 of

the Income Tax Act, 2025) operates at the level of the individual scheme, not the

umbrella trust. Having the reference of Schemes in proposed section 57A will bring

more clarity of tax neutrality benefit at the time of transfer of assets of the Scheme. If

the definition of "specified trust" does not expressly extend to schemes, only the trust

layer would be eligible for conversion. The underlying schemes, where all investor

capital is actually pooled, where portfolio investments are held, and where regulatory

compliance obligations are discharged, would remain as trust structures. This would

render the conversion incomplete and may not achieve the stated legislative

purpose. Under multiple scheme structure, Portfolio companies have issued

securities (equity, debt instruments, units) to specific schemes, not to the umbrella

               71
AIF trust. Continuity of title over these investments, requires that the entity in whose
name securities are registered (i.e., the scheme) is the entity that converts rather
than to umbrella AIF trust."

12.4.4.      "Recommend that the law or accompanying rules explicitly address

how existing rights and obligations will be preserved through such conversions. In

particular, guidance is needed on how to handle security interests and fiduciary

duties when, say, an investment trust or securitization trust converts to an LLP. For

example, if a trust held assets on behalf of investors (as in Alternative Investment

Funds or securitization vehicles), upon conversion to an LLP: How are the beneficial

ownership and trustee obligations preserved? Will liens or guarantees remain

enforceable without interruption? We suggest incorporating provisions to ensure

continuity of contracts, transfer of licenses/approvals without fresh registrations/

creditor rights, and fiduciary responsibilities post-conversion, perhaps via a deemed

vesting of all assets/liabilities and continuation of trust arrangements in the new LLP

form. For regulated trusts, prior approval or no objection requirements from sectoral

regulators such as SEBI or IFSCA may be clearly prescribed to avoid procedural

ambiguity."

12.4.5.      "The draft bill does not seem to restrict that trusts registered with SEBI

are not converted to LLPs registered by IFSCA. If this is allowed, this may lead to

circumvention of capital controls under FEMA, 1999."

12.4.6.      "The definition of `specified trust' must expressly include Schemes of

the trust recognised by SEBI/IFSCA"

"Conversion of specified trusts to LLPs is a welcome step for flexibility. In particular,
guidance is needed on how to handle fiduciary duties when, say, an investment trust
or securitization trust converts to an LLP. For example, if a trust held assets on
behalf of investors (as in Alternative Investment Funds or securitization vehicles),
upon conversion to an LLP: How are the beneficial ownership and trustee obligations
preserved?"

12.5. Examination by the Committee:

12.5.1 With regard to the conversion process of a Trust to LLP, the Ministry in its
reply stated as follows:

                                     72
"Suggestion from stakeholders to expressly define the specified trust as a trust
regulated by SEBI and IFSCA in order to bring more clarity."

12.5.2 The representatives of DGFT with regard to conversion of specified Trust into

"Clause 12, 13 and 17 talks about convergence of specified trust into LLP. We would
like to highlight that these provisions are particularly relevant for regulated
infrastructure such as AI type vehicles and they can actually facilitate commercially
efficient restructuring into LLP form without unnecessary disruption. We suggest that
the implementation guidance in these cases should clearly address continuity of

Also, please refer Examination of the Committee for Clause 17.

12.6. Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

The Committee note that Clause 12 of the Bill seeks to insert a new subsection
ie. 57A after Section 57 of the Principal Act. This amendment introduces a
statutory framework to enable specified trusts, registered by SEBI or IFSCA
having prescribed activities to convert into LLPs. It facilitates the adoption of
the LLP structure by investment vehicles with provisions on eligibility and the
conversion process, thereby promoting flexibility in fund structuring and
improving ease of doing business.

The Committee note that various suggestions received with respect to Clause
12 pertain to Schedule V being introduced under Clause 17 of the Bill.
However, the Ministry, based on stakeholder suggestions received on other
associated Clauses, has accepted the need to bring greater clarity with regard
to the conversion process from Trust to LLP.

In this regard, as a step towards introducing clarity in Clause 12, the
Committee recommend that the Explanation under Clause 12 be reframed to
include in the meaning of `Specified Trusts' those Trusts which are not only
registered but also regulated by Securities and Exchange Board of India, or by
the International Financial Services Centres Authority. Thus, Clause 12 may be
redrafted as under:

                                                       73
"After section 57 of the principal Act, the following section shall be inserted,
namely: -- 57A. A specified trust may convert into a limited liability partnership
in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter and the Fifth Schedule.
Explanation. --For the purposes of this section, the term "specified trust"
means a trust established under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 or under a Central
Act or State Act, and registered and regulated by the Securities and Exchange
Board of India, or by the International Financial Services Centres Authority, as
the case may be, having such activities as may be prescribed.".

13. Clause 13 substitutes Section 58 of the Principal Act

13.1. Provision proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

For section 58 of the principal Act, the following section shall be substituted,
namely:-- (1) The Registrar, on satisfying that a firm, private company, unlisted
public company or a specified trust, as the case may be, has complied with the
provisions of the Second Schedule, the Third Schedule, Fourth Schedule or the Fifth
Schedule, as the case may be, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and the
rules made thereunder, register the documents submitted under such Schedule and
issue a certificate of registration in such form as the Registrar may determine stating
that the limited liability partnership is, on and from the date specified in the certificate,
registered under this Act:

Provided that the limited liability partnership shall, within fifteen days of the date of
registration, inform the concerned Registrar of Firms or Registrar of Companies or
any other authority, as the case may be, with which it was registered or established
under the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 (9 of 1932) or the
Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013), or any other law, as the case may be, about the
conversion and of the particulars of the limited liability partnership in such form and
manner as may be prescribed.

(2) Upon such conversion, the partners of the firm, the shareholders of private
company or unlisted public company, or the trustees of the specified trust, as the
case may be, the limited liability partnership to which such firm or such company or
such specified trust has converted, and the partners of the limited liability partnership
shall be bound by the provisions of the Second Schedule, the Third Schedule, the
Fourth Schedule or the Fifth Schedule, as the case may be, applicable to them.

(3) Upon such conversion, on and from the date of certificate of registration, the
effects of the conversion shall be such as specified in the Second Schedule, the
Third Schedule, the Fourth Schedule or the Fifth Schedule, as the case may be.

(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force,
on and from the date of registration specified in the certificate of registration issued
under the Second Schedule, the Third Schedule, the Fourth Schedule or the Fifth
Schedule, as the case may be,--

                                                       75
(a) there shall be a limited liability partnership by the name specified in the certificate
of registration registered under this Act;

(b) all tangible (movable or immovable) and intangible property vested in the firm, the
company or the specified trust, as the case may be, all assets, interests, rights,
privileges, liabilities, obligations relating to the firm, the company or the specified
trust, as the case may be, and the whole of the undertaking of firm, the company or
the specified trust, as the case may be, shall be transferred to and shall vest in the
limited liability partnership without further assurance, act or deed; and

(c) the firm, the company or the specified trust, as the case may be, shall be deemed
to be dissolved and removed from the records of the Registrar of Firms or Registrar
of Companies or such other authority, as the case may be.".

13.2. Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (LLP Act, 2008):

58. (1) The Registrar, on satisfying that a firm, private company or an unlisted public
company, as the case may be, has complied with the provisions of the Second
Schedule, the Third Schedule or the Fourth Schedule, as the case may be, shall,
subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, register the
documents submitted under such Schedule and issue a certificate of registration in
such form as the Registrar may determine stating that the limited liability partnership
is, on and from the date specified in the certificate, registered under this Act:

Provided that the limited liability partnership shall, within fifteen days of the date of
registration, inform the concerned Registrar of Firms or Registrar of Companies, as
the case may be, with which it was registered under the provisions of the Indian
Partnership Act, 1932 or the Companies Act, 2013 as the case may be, about the
conversion and of the particulars of the limited liability partnership in such form and
manner as may be prescribed.

(2) Upon such conversion, the partners of the firm, the shareholders of private
company or unlisted public company, as the case may be, the limited liability
partnership to which such firm or such company has converted, and the partners of
the limited liability partnership shall be bound by the provisions of the Second
Schedule, the Third Schedule or the Fourth Schedule, as the case may be,
applicable to them.

                                                       76
(3) Upon such conversion, on and from the date of certificate of registration, the
effects of the conversion shall be such as specified in the Second Schedule, the
Third Schedule or the Fourth Schedule, as the case may be.

(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force,

         (a) there shall be a limited liability partnership by the name specified in the

         (b) all tangible (movable or immovable) and intangible property vested in the
firm or the company, as the case may be, all assets, interests, rights, privileges,

         (c) the firm or the company, as the case may be, shall be deemed to be

13.3. Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry for the proposed provisions:

"This amendment expands the scope of conversion into LLPs to include specified
trusts by incorporating a new Schedule V and aligning section 58(1) accordingly. It
facilitates the use of the LLP structure for Alternative Investment Funds by providing
a clear statutory pathway for their conversion, while also streamlining post-
registration intimation requirements."

13.4. Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

Suggestions were received regarding the process of conversion from Trust to LLP
including:

         77
13.4.1.  "Lower the 75% investor-consent threshold, coupled with a dissenter

exit right; tighten the indemnity provision in Fifth Schedule para 16 to limit residual

trustee liability; and (for onward reference to the Ministry of Finance/States) confirm

tax and stamp-duty neutrality on conversion."

13.4.2.  "Introduce a similar simplified statutory pathway for converting an OPC

to an LLP and vice versa with automatic continuity of PAN and registrations."

13.4.3.  "This conversion framework introduced includes detailed provisions on

vesting of property, continuity of proceedings, and personal liability of former trustees

for pre-conversion obligations. (i) Tax liability on conversion of Company to LLP:

Conversion of companies into LLPs remains highly restrictive. The turnover limit of

60 lakh and asset limit of 5 crore for conversion have remained unchanged since

2009 and are now unrealistically low, limiting wider adoption of the LLP model. (ii):

Economic Double Taxation: Arises when the same corporate profits are taxed

twice--first at the company level and again when distributed as dividends to

shareholders. While the taxes are levied on different entities, the underlying income

is effectively taxed twice before reaching the ultimate beneficiary. (iii) LLP

Compliance: Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs) are highly favored by small

entrepreneurs for their flexibility, but sudden changes in partner composition or small

delays in filing Form 8/11 still attract disproportionate daily late fees."

13.4.4.  "Specified trusts definition to include any private trusts (not only

SEBI/IFSCA trusts); and permit conversion of such trusts into LLPs and/or

companies (including Section 8 companies) Proposed Section 57A to be revised to

state: ' ..the term "specified trust" means a trust established under the Indian Trusts

Act, 1882 or under a Central Act or State Act including such trusts registered with

Securities and Exchange Board of India, or by the International Financia Services

Centres Authority) introduce similar provision in the Companies Act, 2013. [Note: The

enabling regime must be trust- appropriate including permitting. scheme- level [not

whole-trust) conversion.] Section 58(2): "Upon such conversion, the partners of the

firm, the shareholders of private company or unlisted public company, or the trustees

Investors of the specified trust and the authorised representatives of the Manager of

the Alternative Investment Fund, as the case may be, the limited liability partnership

to which such firm or such company or such specified trust has converted, and the

partners of the limited liability partnership, shall be bound by the provisions of the

Second Schedule, the Third Schedule, the Fourth Schedule or the Fifth Schedule, as

the case may be, applicable to them."

13.4.5.  "In a trust-structured AIF, the "trustees" are custodial and fiduciary

intermediaries. They are not the economic stakeholders of the fund. The investors

                                       78
(Limited Partners) are the beneficial owners who have committed and contributed
capital. Upon conversion to an LLP, these investors must become the partners of the
LLP - they are the persons with the economic interest, and the LLP Act's partnership
framework presupposes that partners are the persons with capital at risk".

13.4.6.  "The AIF Manager, as defined under Regulation 2(1)(q) of the SEBI AIF

Regulations, 2012, is the entity responsible for all investment decisions, regulatory

compliance, portfolio management, and reporting. Under the LLP Act, a "Designated

Partner" (Section 7) is the partner responsible for the compliance and management

obligations of the LLP. The Manager is the natural, and the only suitable, entity for

this role. Without the Manager as a Designated Partner, the LLP would lack a

managing partner and SEBI's entire regulatory and supervisory architecture would

become incompatible with the converted entity."

13.4.7.  "If "trustees" are retained as the persons who become partners, a

fundamental legal contradiction arises: once the trust converts to an LLP, the trust

ceases to exist, and there are no more "trustees." The persons who need legal

continuity in the LLP are the investors (as partners with capital contributions) and the

Manager (as the Designated Partner responsible for management). The current

drafting would create a structural vacuum immediately upon conversion."

13.4.8.  "Provision should be made to the effect that on issuance of Certificate

of Registration to LLP, further compliance with respect to filing of charge etc. can be

dispensed with/ waived and the LLP will be liable for the liabilities of the Pvt.

Company/ Unlisted Co/ Specified Trust"

13.4.9.  "It is proposed that, to the effects of conversion (Section 58(4)) or by

Note on Clauses, a clarification to the following effect: securities held in

dematerialised form by a specified trust shall, upon conversion, transition to the

demat account of the resultant LLP by way of statutory succession and shall not be

treated as a transfer or change of beneficial ownership; and depositories may give

effect to such transition without mandatory account closure and fresh opening."

"It is submitted that a trust and an LLP are distinct legal persons and demat accounts
are entity specific. Existing depository frameworks do not expressly provide for
conversion-based transition. Treating conversion as statutory succession (consistent
with the vesting language already in the Bill) ensures continuity and uniform DP
practice and avoids disruption to investor holdings."

                                        79
13.4.10. "Suggested modification as underlined: (2) Upon such conversion, the
partners of the firm, the shareholders of private company or unlisted public company,
or the trustees or investors of the specified trust, as the case may be, the limited
liability partnership to which such firm or such company or such specified trust has
converted, and the partners of the limited liability partnership, shall be bound by the
provisions of the Second Schedule, the Third Schedule, the Fourth Schedule or the
Fifth Schedule, as the case may be, applicable to them."

"The investors (beneficiaries/unit holders) of a specified trust have the substantive
economic interest in the trust, whereas trustees generally act in a fiduciary or
professional capacity. Accordingly, it is appropriate that investors, in addition to
trustees, are expressly bound by the applicable provisions governing the conversion.
This amendment also provides greater legal clarity regarding the persons who
continue to be subject to the applicable schedules following conversion"

13.4.11. "Replace `Trustees' with `Investors' and `Manager' Trustees are
custodial/fiduciary intermediaries, not economic stakeholders. Investors (LPs) are the
beneficial owners and capital contributors - they must become LLP partners."

"The AIF Manager (Reg 2(1)(t), SEBI AIF Regs 2024) is responsible for all
investment decisions, compliance and reporting; they are the natural Designated
Partner under Section 7, LLP Act. Once the trust converts, it ceases to exist and
there are no more `trustees.' The persons who need legal continuity are the Investors
(as partners) and the Manager (as Designated Partner). Aligns with international
precedent: Singapore VCC, UK LP (1907), Luxembourg SCSp: the fund manager
assumes the GP/managing partner role in all comparator jurisdictions. SEBI's
enforcement and supervisory apparatus runs through the Manager. If the Manager
has no legal status in the converted LLP, SEBI and IFSCA loses their primary
regulatory locus."

13.5. Examination by the Committee:

13.5.1 On the suggestion asking for a simplified statutory pathway for converting an
OPC to an LLP, the Ministry in their written reply stated as under:

"An OPC cannot be converted into an LLP, as an OPC has only 1 member, whereas
an LLP must have at least 2 partners."

                                                       80
13.5.2 With regard to the effect on liabilities on conversion, the Ministry submitted as
follows:

"There is adequate clarity in the Schedule that ongoing liabilities are not affected due
to conversion. "

13.5.3 On the suggestion that securities held in dematerialised form by a specified
trust shall, upon conversion, transition to the demat account of the resultant LLP, the
Ministry in its written reply submitted as under:

"There is adequate clarity in the provision that the entire entity is being converted into
LLP and the trust would also be dissolved after that. No further clarification is
