17(14).2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008):

A new provision has been proposed in the Bill by inserting the Fifth Schedule under
Section 57A of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, to regulate the conversion
of specified trusts into limited liability partnerships.

17(14).3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
for the proposed provision:

"This is the corresponding schedule to the amendments proposed in section 23, 25,
and 58."

                                                      132
17(14).4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

In regard to Clause 17(14), this clause should be for the designated partner of the
LLP and not the trustee of the specified trust. The current formulation referring to the
trustee is inappropriate post-conversion, as the trustee's role ceases upon transition
from a trust to an LLP structure. Under the LLP framework, designated partners are
the persons responsible for management, representation, and regulatory
compliance, and therefore must be the appropriate counterpart for continuity of
appointments, rights, and powers. Retaining references to trustees would create a
legal inconsistency and ambiguity regarding who is authorised to act on behalf of the
converted entity. Aligning the provision with designated partners ensures structural
coherence, preserves continuity of legal relationships, and reflects the governance
framework applicable to LLPs.

17(14).5 Examination by the Committee:

When the Committee sought the comments of the Ministry on the above suggestion,
the Ministry stated as follows:

"This clause may not be required for the purposes of the AIF LLP. Authority or power
in the LLP is governed by the LLP agreement. This clause is being omitted."

17(14).6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

The Committee note that para 14 seeks to provide for continuation of the
existing appointments, authorities and powers of the specified trust or its
trustee upon conversion into a limited liability partnership. The Committee note
that a suggestion was made to omit the proposed provision relating to
continuation of existing appointments, authorities and powers upon
conversion, as the governance and authority of the converted LLP would be
governed by the LLP Agreement. The Committee also note that the Ministry has
also accepted the suggestion for omission of the said paragraph. Therefore,
the Committee recommend omission of para 14 of the proposed Fifth Schedule.

17(15) Para 15 of Clause 17 seeks to provide for the continuation of
approvals, permits and licences after conversion.

                                                      133
17(15).1 Provision proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

15. Application of paragraphs 7 to 14.--The provisions of paragraphs 7 to 14 (both
inclusive) shall apply to any approval, permit or licence issued to the specified trust
under any other Act, which is in force immediately before the date of registration of
the limited liability partnership, subject to the provisions of such other Act under
which such approval, permit or licence has been issued.

17(15).2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008):

A new provision has been proposed in the Bill by inserting the Fifth Schedule under
Section 57A of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, to regulate the conversion
of specified trusts into limited liability partnerships.

17(15).3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
for the proposed provision:

"This is the corresponding schedule to the amendments proposed in section 23, 25,
and 58."

17(15).4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

The Stakeholder has stated to specifically include approvals and authorisations
issued under FT(D&R) Act, Customs Act and FTP among approvals that continue
after conversion. Provides legal certainty regarding validity of Advance Authorisation,
EPCG, Status Certificate and other DGFT permissions.

17(15).5 Examination by the Committee:

In response to the above suggestion of the stakeholder, the Ministry has stated that
"Specific provision is not required."

17(15).6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

17(15).6.1 The Committee note that para 15 of the proposed Fifth Schedule
provides that the provisions relating to the effect of conversion shall apply to

                                                      134
any approval, permit or licence issued to the specified trust under any other
Act, which is in force immediately before the date of registration of the limited
liability partnership, subject to the provisions of such Act under which such
approval, permit or licence has been issued.

The Committee are of the view that the proposed provision would ensure
continuity of statutory approvals, permits and licences notwithstanding the
conversion of the specified trust into a limited liability partnership. The
Committee accept the para 15 of the proposed Fifth Schedule, however, with
the following amendments. The word "Act" be substituted with the word "law"
so as to provide greater clarity and avoid any ambiguity in the application of
the proposed provision.

17(15).6.2 Consequent upon the omission of the existing para 14, the words
"paragraphs 7 to 14" be substituted with "paragraphs 7 to 13".

17(16) Para 16 of Clause 17 seeks to provide that trustees remain liable for
pre-conversion obligations with indemnity from the LLP.

17(16).1 Provision proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

16. Partner liable for liabilities and obligations of specified trust before conversion.--
(1) Notwithstanding anything in paragraphs 7 to 14, every trustee of a specified trust
that has converted into a limited liability partnership, shall continue to be personally
liable (jointly and severally with the limited liability partnership) for the liabilities and
obligations of the specified trust which were incurred prior to the conversion or which
arose from any contract entered into prior to the conversion.

(2) If any such trustee discharges any liability or obligation referred to in sub-
paragraph (1), he shall be entitled (subject to any agreement with the limited liability
partnership to the contrary) to be fully indemnified by the limited liability partnership
in respect of such liability or obligation.

17(16).2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008):

                                                      135
A new provision has been proposed in the Bill by inserting the Fifth Schedule under
Section 57A of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, to regulate the conversion
of specified trusts into limited liability partnerships.

17(16).3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
for the proposed provision:

"This is the corresponding schedule to the amendments proposed in section 23, 25,
and 58."

17(16).4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

In regard to Clause 17(16), the current provision imposing personal liability on
trustees is inconsistent with the fundamental nature of trust structures, where
trustees act in a fiduciary and representative capacity and are not intended to bear
economic risk, except in cases of misconduct. In commercial trust structures--
particularly those regulated by SEBI and IFSCA--the economic risk is borne by the
trust assets and, where applicable, investor commitments, not by trustees
individually. Extending personal liability to trustees post-conversion would be
commercially untenable, deter professional trusteeship, and misalign with global
standards. Accordingly, liability should appropriately rest with the resulting LLP and
its underlying asset pool, with recourse limited to trustees only in cases of fraud,
wilful misconduct, or breach of trust, thereby ensuring a balanced framework that
protects creditors while preserving the fiduciary nature of trusteeship.

17(16).5 Examination by the Committee:

When comments were sought on the above suggestion of the stakeholder, the
Ministry stated:

"This provision does not create any new liability or obligations. It only refers to the
ongoing liabilities, if any, on account of actions prior to the conversion of the trust. It
may be noted that post-conversion, the liability in any case is joint and several with
the LLP and there are also safeguards for indemnity. Such a provision is required to
be created considering the fact that the trust did not enjoy limited liability prior to its
conversion. Considering the unique position of the AIF trusts, the liability for past
actions is also being extended to managers besides trustees."

17(16).6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

17(16).6.1 The Committee note that para 16 of the proposed Fifth Schedule
provides that every trustee of a specified trust shall continue to remain

                                                      136
personally liable, jointly and severally with the resulting limited liability
partnership, for liabilities and obligations incurred prior to conversion, while
retaining the statutory right of indemnity from the limited liability partnership.
The Committee are of the view that the proposed provision appropriately
safeguards the interests of creditors while ensuring continuity of liabilities
arising prior to conversion. The Committee accept para 16 of the proposed
Fifth Schedule, however, with the following amendments:

In order to ensure that managers, who are also recognized under the proposed
conversion framework, are subject to the same liability as trustees in respect of
obligations incurred prior to conversion, in sub-para (1), after "every trustee",
the words "and manager" be inserted.

17(16).6.2 Further, due to the inclusion of managers in sub-para (1), and so
as to extend the statutory right of indemnity to managers who discharge such
liabilities, in sub-para (2), after the words "such trustee", the words "or
manager" be inserted.

17(16).6.3 Also, consequent upon the omission of the existing para 14, the
words "paragraphs 7 to 14" be substituted with "paragraphs 7 to 13".

17(17)  Para 17 of Clause 17 seeks to require the LLP to disclose its

conversion in correspondence for a set period.

17(17).1 Provision proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

17. Notice of conversion in correspondence.--

(1) The limited liability partnership shall ensure that for a period of twelve months
commencing not later than fourteen days after the date of registration, every official
correspondence of the limited liability partnership bears the following, namely:--

(a) a statement that it was, as from the date of registration, converted from a
specified trust into a limited liability partnership; and

                                                      137
(b) the name and registration number, if applicable, of the specified trust, from which
it was converted.

(2) Any limited liability partnership which contravenes the provisions of sub-
paragraph (1) shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than ten thousand
rupees but which may extend to one lakh rupees and with a further fine which shall
not be less than fifty rupees but which may extend to five hundred rupees for every
day after the first day after which the default continues.

17(17).2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008):

A new provision has been proposed in the Bill by inserting the Fifth Schedule under
Section 57A of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, to regulate the conversion
of specified trusts into limited liability partnerships.

17(17).3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
for the proposed provision:

"This is the corresponding schedule to the amendments proposed in section 23, 25,
and 58."

17(17).4 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

The Committee note that para 17 of the proposed Fifth Schedule seeks to
require every limited liability partnership converted from a specified trust to
disclose, for a period of twelve months, in all its official correspondence, that it
was converted from a specified trust together with the particulars of the
specified trust from which it was converted.

The Committee are of the view that the proposed provision would promote
transparency and ensure that persons dealing with the converted limited
liability partnership are duly informed of its legal status and origin during the
transitional period. The Committee, therefore, recommend that para 17 of the
proposed Fifth Schedule be adopted without any amendment.

18.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the

"The amendment seeks to align the definition with the correct statutory terminology,
replacing the earlier reference to "Cost and Works Accountants" with "Cost
Accountants" without altering the substance of the provision.

The proposed proviso seeks to provide greater flexibility in financial year alignment.
It enables companies and body corporates to realign their financial year to 31 March
in certain cases, subject to Central Government approval.

This is intended to include the definition of term "Regional Director" in the definition
clause i.e. section 2 of the Act.

The new Clause (74A) is being inserted to provide an express definition of
"registered valuer". This is for clarity and consistency to valuation-related provisions
by linking the term to the certificate of registration under section 247.

This amendment enhances the upper thresholds for paid-up share capital and
turnover for a "small company" to 20 crore rupees and 200 crore rupees,
respectively. This is intended to widen the scope of such companies so that more
companies are covered therein. The revision also seeks to provide flexibility to align
these thresholds with the classification limits prescribed by the Ministry of Micro,
Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) from time to time"

                                                      141
18.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

Some of the important suggestions of the stakeholders in this regard are furnished
below:

18.4.1.  "Definition of "Cost Accountant" needs to be modified in the LLP Act,

2008 as proposed in the Companies Act, 2008. The definition of "Cost Accountant"

should be aligned across the Companies Act, 2013 and the LLP Act, 2008 to ensure

consistency in statutory terminology. Since the Companies Act proposes to update

the definition to reflect the current legal name of the professional institute, a

corresponding amendment should also be made in Section 2(h) of the LLP Act, 2008.

This will maintain uniformity between the two Acts, avoid interpretational

inconsistencies, and ensure that references to the profession remain aligned with the

governing legislation."

18.4.2.  "An objective criterion should prescribe and process the application.

The eligibility criteria should be determined in light of global reporting requirements,

sectoral regulations, and business integration. Further, applications should be

disposed of within 30-45 days from the receipt of a complete application. In cases

where the authority seeks additional information or clarification, the applicant may be

provided an opportunity to resubmit or rectify the application. The acceptance of such

resubmission may be considered by the authority on a case-to-case basis,

depending on the facts and circumstances of each case and introduce a statutory

Compliance Window structure Further MCA portal be linked with PAN, GSTIN,

EPFO, IEC, ESIC, LEI portal and other statutory authority portal and create

databases to eliminate duplicate information and enable pre-filled forms if any. Time-

bound approvals reduce regulatory uncertainty, enhance transparency, boost

confidence in applicants and Investors and strengthen India's attractiveness as a

preferred destination for global businesses by promoting ease of doing business."

18.4.3.  "On an application made by a company or body corporate, the Central

Government may, for reasons to be recorded in writing and having regard to the

need for consolidation of accounts, the financial year followed by its ultimate holding

entity, applicable law in a foreign jurisdiction, or such other prescribed business

necessity, allow to adopt such financial year or such period as may be prescribed,

subject to such conditions and maximum duration as may be specified in the Rules.

Provided, further that such application shall be disposed of within 60 days from the
date of submission of a complete application.

                         142
Provided also that the order shall specify the transitional financial period and shall
not affect any liability relating to taxation, audit, filing or disclosure for any period
preceding such order"

Greater flexibility is commercially justified for multinational groups and other
legitimate cross-border structures. However, an open-ended discretion may result in
inconsistent decisions, administrative delays and uncertainty concerning annual
accounts, annual returns audit, AGM timelines and statutory filings. Objective criteria,
a disposal period and express transitional treatment would improve predictability
while preventing the flexibility from being used to defer compliance or obscure
financial reporting. A blanket deemed- approval mechanism is not recommended
because a change of financial year has consequences across tax, accounting and
regulatory regimes."

18.4.4.  "In the Companies Act, 2013 (hereafter in this Chapter referred to as

the principal Act), in section 2,--

(ii) in clause (41), after the third proviso, the following proviso shall be inserted,
namely:--

"Provided also that the Central Government may, on an application made in such
form and manner as may be prescribed, by a company or body corporate referred to
in the first proviso or, on commercial considerations, by any other company or body
corporate, allow the company or body corporate to realign its financial year as the
period ending on the 31st day of March of the following year;"

The Bill should either define the term 'commercial considerations' or include the
proposed clause:

"For the purposes of this proviso, commercial considerations shall include such
circumstances as may be prescribed." The expression "commercial considerations"
is not defined anywhere in either the Companies Act or the Bill. This will create
uncertainty because: a. Lack of Uniform Standards- different Regional Directors may
adopt different standards; b. Absence of Objective Criteria- no objective parameters
exist for approval; c. Difficulty in Judicial Review- judicial review will become difficult
due to absence of legislative guidance."

18.4.5.  "Enhancement of the threshold limits from 10 crore to 20 crore and

from 100 crore to 200 should not be implemented. Increasing the limits of paid-up

capital and turnover to 20 crore and 200 crore would be excessive, as companies

of such scale reasonably be classified within a less stringent regulatory framework

from a governance perspective. The proposed enhancement would result in a

substantial number of comparatively large entities being brought under relaxed

compliance requirements, thereby diluting the intent of regulatory oversight. The

                                     143
MSME classification under the MSMED Act, 2006 uses investment and turnover-
based caps which are significantly lower, as provided below:

i. Micro: Investment in Plant and Machinery or Equipment: Rs. 2.5 crore and Annual
Turnover not more than Rs. 10 crores.

ii. Small: Investment in Plant and Machinery or Equipment: Rs. 25 crore and Annual
Turnover not more than Rs. 100 crores.

iii. Medium: Investment in Plant and Machinery or Equipment: Rs. 125 crore and
Annual Turnover not more than Rs. 500 crores.

A "small company" under the Companies Act post-amendment may not qualify as a
"small enterprise" under MSME law.

A company having turnover of 100 crore or 200 crore cannot be regarded as
"small" in practical or economic terms, considering its operational scale, stakeholder
base, and market impact. In the event the plethora of exemptions/privileges are
made available to various small companies (on the basis of revised increased
thresholds, if implemented), the same is likely to result in unintended consequences
by virtue of losing regulatory oversight over the affairs of such companies (which
would otherwise be having sizable operations)."

18.4.6.  "The proposed amendment may be viewed in conjunction with the

MSME classification framework. The current proposal further expands the scope of

coverage by also including medium enterprises. The concept of small company may

be aligned with the definition of Small Enterprise under MSMED Act, for determining

the threshold limit so that there is clarity in the minds of the stakeholders. The

definition of "Small Company" may be aligned, to the extent practicable, with the

classification criteria of Small Enterprise prescribed under the MSMED Act. The

Companies Act can simply refer to the Small Enterprise as defined under MSMED

Act. Such alignment would promote regulatory consistency, reduce compliance

burden, and provide greater clarity to businesses regarding their statutory obligations

and eligibility for various benefits under different laws."

18.4.7.  "Remove clause (b) of the proviso to section 2(85) relating to Section 8

companies, so that such companies may also qualify as small companies based on

the prescribed thresholds. This would promote ease of compliance for smaller

Section 8 companies while retaining the existing exclusions for holding/subsidiary

companies and entities governed by special Acts. Accordingly, the proviso to Section

2(85) may be revised as follows:

"Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to-
                                                      144
(A) a holding company or a subsidiary company; or

(B) a company or body corporate governed by any special Act."

Section 8 companies are essentially not-for-profit entities prohibited from distributing
dividends. A significant number of such entities function as educational institutions,
charitable organisations, or trust-like structures, many of which are also registered
under the Income Tax Act. Imposing the same level of compliance burden applicable
to commercial and profit-oriented companies may therefore not be commensurate
with their nature and operations. Accordingly, extending the benefit of small company
classification to Section 8 companies meeting the prescribed thresholds would be
aligned with the broader objective of promoting ease of doing business and
rationalising compliance requirements."

18.4.8.  "Definition of Small Company should be modified for the purpose of

ease of doing business, there are implications of excluding these companies from

dematerialisation. Thus, dematerialisation of securities should be made applicable to

all companies. The words "other than a small company" should be deleted from Sub

rule 1 of Rule 9B under section 29. Further, the companies should provide a

confirmation for compliance with Rule 9B to MCA through online filing. The expanded

definition of a small company under the Corporate Laws ( Bill, 2026 has important

consequences for the monitoring of share transfers by promoters and other

shareholders When companies are excluded from the depository system, their

securities remain outside the purview of electronic record keeping and regulatory

oversight This creates significant risks Lack of Transparency in Share Transfers

Unlisted companies whose shares are not admitted into the depository system can

transfer ownership privately, without standardized valuation or disclosure Since the

value of such shares is not publicly known, promoters and shareholders may

transact at arbitrary prices, opening avenues for manipulation Risk of Money

Laundering and Tax Evasion In the absence of depository monitoring, promoters can

engage in circular transactions to artificially inflate or deflate share values for

example, Shareholder A transfers shares to Shareholder B at 20 per share, and B

later transfers them back to A at 10 per share, creating a notional loss that can be

misused for tax avoidance or laundering illicit funds Weak Safeguards for

Shareholders Physical share certificates are vulnerable to theft, forgery, and loss

Without depository admission, shareholders lack the protection of secure electronic

ownership records, leaving them exposed to disputes and fraud Benefits of

Admission into the Depository System Admitting companies even small and unlisted

ones into the depository framework ensures Transparency (all transfers recorded

electronically), Accurate Ownership Records (tamper proof, reducing disputes),

Regulatory Supervision (monitoring by SEBI and other authorities), and Investor

Protection (secure dematerialised holdings, free of risks tied to physical certificates)."

18.4.9.  "The turnover Cap should be increased above INR 200 crores relatively

and also Paid up cap. The Company Law Committee Report of 2022 (CLC Report) is

already 4 years old now and the new corporate laws (Amendment Bill) 2026 will take

some more time to come into force, and when it does come into force, the INR 200

         145
Crores Turnover cap will look significantly a small number considering the way
businesses are growing in India. A turnover cap of >350 crores would be preferred if
implemented and paid-up capital cap be raised to INR 50 crores instead of only INR
20 crores."

18.4.10. "Committee should recommend that the thresholds be revised
periodically through notifications linked to inflation and economic growth, technical
viability, business and market conditions and after considering other factors, instead
of requiring legislative amendments. Vibrant thresholds will ensure that the law
remains responsive to economic and business conditions including technical factors
and reduce the need for frequent statutory amendments."

18.4.11. "Categorization of companies should be based on their listing status as
the Companies Act, 2013, is designed to promote corporate transparency and
governance; therefore, the categorization of companies should be determined based
on their listing status. Approximately 97% of enterprises are categorized as `firms,'
while only 3% fall under `companies.' The Companies Act applies exclusively to
these 3%, largely because the high compliance costs deter firms from registering as
companies."

18.4.12. "Clarity should be brought in respect of companies crossing thresholds mid
year. While the Bill raises the threshold limits for "small companies" under section 2
(85) it fails to specify how to transition companies that cross these thresholds mid-
year or at the start of the next compliance cycle Explicit transition rules are needed to
prevent compliance ambiguity."

18.4.13. "Words "or subsidiary company" should be deleted from the proviso to
Section 2(85). Consequently, a subsidiary company satisfying the prescribed paid-up
capital and turnover thresholds should also be eligible to qualify as a small company.

Draft Revised Provision:

"Small Company" means a company, other than a public company,--

(i) paid-up share capital of which does not exceed fifty lakh rupees or such higher
amount as may be prescribed which shall not be more than ten crore rupees; and

(ii) turnover of which as per profit and loss account for the immediately preceding
financial year does not exceed two crore rupees or such higher amount as may be
prescribed which shall not be more than one hundred crore rupees Provided that
nothing in this clause shall apply to-- (A) a holding company; (B) a company
registered under section 8; or (C) a company or body corporate governed by any
special Act.

                                                      146
The regulatory concessions available to a small company are intended to be based
on the size and scale of its operations, as reflected by objective financial thresholds
such as paid-up capital and turnover, rather than its ownership structure. A
subsidiary company that independently satisfies the prescribed thresholds does not
cease to be "small" merely because it is controlled by another body corporate. The
blanket exclusion of all subsidiary companies denies genuine MSMEs, startups,
special purpose vehicles, and wholly-owned subsidiaries the benefit of simplified
compliance, despite presenting no greater regulatory risk than similarly placed
standalone companies. Since the Companies Act, 2013 already provides adequate
safeguards through consolidated financial statements, audit requirements, related-
party transaction provisions, and regulatory oversight, retaining this exclusion is not
necessary for investor protection. Deleting the words "or subsidiary company" would
better align the provision with the Government's objective of promoting ease of doing
business while preserving appropriate governance standards."

18.4.14. "The maximum permissible limits for a small company (paid-up share
capital to 20 crore and turnover to 200 crore) should not be increased, noting that
these limits were already increased on 1 December 2025 (from 4 to 10 crore and
40 to 100 crore respectively); a further increase may lead to a larger number of
entities qualifying for exemption from compliance requirements. The JJ Irani
Committee report, which introduced small company provisions to align Indian law
with English law, used a key criterion of number of employees that is not covered in
the Indian definition and could also be considered for Indian companies."

18.4.15. "Retain the relief provisions, and it should reach eligible companies
automatically from their existing MCA21 filings, without a separate application. The
Bill raises the small-company thresholds in section 2(85) to 20 crore of paid-up
capital and 200 crore of turnover (clause 18), raises the Corporate Social
Responsibility (CSR) trigger in section 135 to 10 crore (clause 43), allows
prescribed companies to forgo appointing an auditor (section 139, clause 44), caps
additional fees (section 403, clause 93), and reduces penalties for the smallest
companies (section 446B, clause 98). Eligibility for most of this relief can be read
from filings a company has already made, including its annual return, financial
statements, paid-up capital, turnover, and recognised start-up status. The Ministry of
Corporate Affairs (MCA) should apply the relief from those filings on the MCA21
system, pre-filling the relevant forms and charging lower fees and reduced penalties
by default, so that an eligible company receives the relief without making a fresh
application for a benefit it already qualifies for. For the auditor exemption, It is
suggested that the exempt class be small, low-risk companies, and that a small
company with public borrowing, a regulated activity, or material related-party
transactions should still be audited, because its lenders, regulators, and related
parties rely on those accounts. A first procedural default made in good faith, with no
fraud and no harm, should be curable before penalties escalate, so that an honest
oversight can be put right without a penalty."

18.4.16. "A sub-clause (d) may be added to the proviso to Section 2(85):

                                                      147
Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to:

"(D) a company in which any individual, whether by himself or together with one or
more relatives, holds significant beneficial ownership, within the meaning of section
90, in more than one company availing the benefit of this clause, where the
aggregate paid-up share capital or aggregate turnover of such companies exceeds
the limits specified in sub-clause (i) or (ii), as the case may be.

"The increased thresholds are defensible given the evolving markets, but it may need
a caveat. This is because while the proviso to section 2(85) excludes holding and
subsidiary companies; it only covers vertical structures. It does not cover horizontal
structures where an individual directly or indirectly holds a significant beneficial
ownership across multiple standalone companies qualifying under the new increased
thresholds. The incentive to fragment businesses across companies increases to
exercise the exemptions given to small companies while indirect control may be
retained. Hence, a cross referencing with Section 90 may be beneficial."

18.5 Examination by the Committee:

18.5.1 While accepting the suggestion for corresponding amendment of the Limited
Liability of Partnership Act, 2008 by incorporating definition of "Cost Accountant" in
line with the proposed definition amendment of clause 18(v), the Ministry submitted
that:

"The Amendment Bill proposes to update the definition of "Cost Accountant" under
the Companies Act, 2013 to reflect the current nomenclature of the governing
legislation. A corresponding amendment in the LLP Act, 2008 may also be
considered, as appropriate, to maintain consistency in statutory terminology across
the two Acts."

18.5.2 With respect to eligibility criteria for realignment of Financial year u/sec 2(41)
as mentioned in suggestions at serial number (ii), and (iii) above, the Ministry
submitted as stated below:

"Clause 2(41) itself only inserts the enabling proviso empowering the Central
Government to allow realignment of financial year "in such form and manner as may
be prescribed." Matters like eligibility criteria for realignment, timelines for disposal of
applications, a resubmission/rectification process, and portal integration with other
statutory databases are all administrative and procedural in nature. Such matters
may be addressed through delegated legislation, without requiring an amendment to

                                                      148
the Act. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be
retained without any change."

18.5.3 Regarding the inclusion of additional proviso after third proviso in section
2(41) of the Bill, the Ministry submitted: -

"(i) The expression "commercial considerations" has been intentionally under in
broad terms to enable the Central Government to consider a range of legitimate
business circumstances that may warrant realigned of a company's financial year.

(ii). The manner of making applications and other procedural aspects are proposed
to be prescribed through delegated legislation. Therefore, the suggestion will be
considered appropriately during framing of subordinate legislation."

18.5.4 In respect of not agreeing with the revised threshold for small company and
alignment of the statutory ceiling for small company under Bill with the MSMED Act,
2006, as mentioned in suggestion v & vi, the Ministry furnished following reply:

"The Amendment Bill seeks to increase the statutory ceiling for a small company
from 10 crore to 20 crore paid-up share capital and from 100 crore to 200 crore
turnover. The actual thresholds will be prescribed separately and can be revised as
required without further amendment to the Act. Since thresholds under the MSMED
Act, 2006 are periodically revised, retaining flexibility in the Companies Act provides
that the prescribed threshold may be updated, if needed. Further, the objective of the
Amendment Bill is to reduce compliance burdens and promote ease of doing
business in India. This proposed amendment may enable a larger number of
companies to qualify as small companies and avail the associated compliance
relaxations. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may
be retained without any change."

18.5.5 As regards the removal of "Not for Profit" entities under Section 8 from
section 2(85), the Ministry stated the following:

"Section 8 companies have been incorporated for a specific purpose of promoting
arts, commerce etc and do not pay dividends to their shareholders. Companies
constituted under Section 8 already enjoy relaxed compliance requirements under
the Companies Act, 2013 in terms of board meeting and annual general meetings,
appointment of independent directors, Nomination and Remuneration Committee
etc., Many Section 8 companies receive donations, CSR funds under section 135,
grants from Governments and hold assets dedicated to charitable purposes.
Turnover and paid-up capital thresholds would not be the appropriate or sufficient

                                                      149
criteria in the case of Section 8 companies as some section8 companies manage big
assets and receive substantial quantum of funds. Further, Small companies and
companies licensed under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 constitute 2
different classes of companies and are subject to separate compliance requirements.
Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained
without any change."

18.5.6 The Ministry in respect of requested deletion of the words "other than a
small company from Sub rule 1 of Rule 9B under section 29 provided that:

"The suggestions pertain to the scope of applicability of Rule 9B of the Companies
(Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 and the prescription of
additional compliance requirements. Accordingly, these suggestions may be
considered, as appropriate, while framing or amending the relevant Rules. Hence,
the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without
any change."

18.5.7 Regarding the proposal recommending further increase in the statutory
ceiling, for a small company u/sec 2(85), the Ministry submitted following written
reply:

"The Amendment Bill seeks to increase the statutory ceiling for a small company
from 10 crore to 20 crore paid-up share capital and from 100 crore to 200 crore
turnover. The actual thresholds will be prescribed separately and can be revised as
required without further amendment to the Act. Since thresholds under the MSMED
Act, 2006 are periodically revised, retaining flexibility in the Companies Act provides
that the prescribed threshold may be updated, if needed. The objective of the
Amendment Bill is to reduce compliance burdens and promote ease of doing
business in India. The proposed increase in thresholds seeks to ease compliance for
a larger number of small businesses. The proposed increase in thresholds seeks to
balances ease of doing business with preserving the intended scope of the small
company framework. Increasing the statutory ceilings further, as suggested, may
significantly expand the scope of the category beyond the intended objective. Hence,
the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without
any change."

18.5.8 As regards the prescription of thresholds for turnover and paid-up share
capital through notifications instead of Act, the Ministry gave following reply:

"The suggestion proposes that the thresholds for turnover and paid-up share capital
be prescribed through notifications instead of within the Companies Act, 2013 as part
of the definitions. The Amendment Bill expressly proposes a change in the definition

                                                      150
of small companies to ensure legislative clarity, certainty and maintain ease of
interpretation. The issuance of periodic notifications to amend the thresholds for
small companies may prove cumbersome for the industry from a regulatory
compliance standpoint. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment)
Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

18.5.9 The Ministry on suggestion regarding the categorization of companies based
on their listing status, submitted that:

"The Companies Act, 2013 classifies companies based on different criteria
depending on the regulatory objective sought to be achieved. While listing status is
relevant for requirements relating to securities markets, investor protection and
corporate governance applicable to listed companies, other classifications based on
factors such as size, ownership, control and nature of business facilitate a
proportionate regulatory framework under the Act. Listing status is therefore one of
several attributes relevant for specific regulatory purposes and is not intended to
serve as the sole basis for the categorisation of companies. Hence, the provision in
the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

18.5.10 In respect of treatment of companies crossing the prescribed thresholds
during a financial year, the Ministry in their written response submitted:

"This suggestion pertains to treatment of companies crossing the prescribed
thresholds during a financial year. The provision is amply clear that the company
loses small company status once its paid up capital or turnover crosses prescribed
limits and accordingly applicable compliance requirements will change. Hence, the
provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change."

18.5.11 The Ministry in respect of exclusion of `Subsidiary Companies' from the
definition of a "small company" submitted that:

"The exclusion of subsidiary companies from the definition of a "small company" is a
conscious legislative policy intended to ensure that compliance relaxations are
available only to genuinely independent privately held small companies. A subsidiary
company forms part of a larger corporate group and may have access to greater
financial, managerial and operational resources than is reflected by its standalone
paid-up share capital or turnover. Further, if subsidiary company is included in
definition of small company, it may create tendency to fragment or divide the
business into multiple subsidiaries just to avail relaxations of exempting them from
auditor rotation, cash flow statement preparation etc. which otherwise are applicable

                                                      151
to such businesses. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,
2026 may be retained without any change."

18.5.12 On the suggestion, disapproving further increase of the maximum
permissible threshold for a small company, the Ministry submitted:

"The Amendment Bill seeks to increase the statutory ceiling for a small company
from 10 crore to 20 crore paid-up share capital and from 100 crore to 200 crore
turnover. The actual thresholds will be prescribed separately and can be revised as
required without further amendment to the Act. Since thresholds under the MSMED
Act, 2006 are periodically revised, retaining flexibility in the Companies Act provides
that the prescribed threshold may be updated, if needed. Further, the objective of the
Amendment Bill is to reduce compliance burdens and promote ease of doing
business in India. This proposed amendment may enable a larger number of
companies to qualify as small companies and avail the associated compliance
relaxations. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may
be retained without any change."

18.5.13  About the manner of implementation of the proposed compliance

relaxations and the operationalisation of the MCA21 system, the Ministry submitted

the following response:

"Suggestion will be considered appropriately during framing of subordinate
legislation.

1. The suggestion relates to the manner of implementation of the proposed
compliance relaxations and the operationalisation of the MCA21 system. It may be
considered during drafting of relevant subordinate legislation regarding the same.

2. The Amendment Bill empowers the Central Government to prescribe the class
or classes of companies and the conditions subject to which the exemption from
appointment of auditors may be available. Accordingly, the suggestion regarding the
eligibility criteria for such exemption may be considered, as appropriate, while
framing the relevant Rules.

3. The Amendment Bill already rationalises the enforcement framework by
decriminalising several procedural defaults and providing for adjudication and
settlement mechanisms. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment)
Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

18.5.14 In response to the suggestion for increasing thresholds for `small company,
the Ministry responded:

"The objective of the proposed amendment is to reduce compliance burdens and
promote ease of doing business in India. This proposed amendment may enable a
larger number of companies to qualify as small companies and avail the associated
compliance relaxations. The fragmentation of business in multiple companies is
linked to commercial considerations and consequent control of such companies is
subject to provisions related to number of directorships, beneficial interest and other
compliance requirements. Suggested exclusion based on significant beneficial

section 90 serves a distinct purpose of ensuring transparency of beneficial ownership
and is not intended to determine eligibility for classification as a small company.
Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained
without any change."

18.5.23 The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 confers rule-making powers
under certain provisions which are proposed to be amended or inserted by the
Central Government. This Rule making proposed in the Bill are mainly in those
provisions which are procedural or process related. As regards the rule making
powers enshrined under clause 18 of the Bill, the Ministry submitted following details:

"It proposes to prescribe form and manner of an application to be made to the
Central Government by a company or body corporate. These kinds of delegations
are procedural in nature. They do not affect the substantive conditions for
compliance, which are exhaustively set out in the parent statute. Instead, they enable
administrative standardisation and technological adaptability."

                                                      157
18.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

18.6.1 The Committee, note that Clause 18 of the Corporate Laws (Amendment)
Bill, 2026 seeks to amend Section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013 (Companies
Act) which defines terms used in the said Act as mentioned below:

(i) To substitute in clause (28) in reference to the appropriate title of "The
Cost Accountants Act, 1959".

(ii) To insert new proviso to clause (41) for empowering the Central
Government to allow conversion of the financial year to the period ending on
31st March of the following year, on application by a company or a body
corporate, referred to under the first proviso, or on the basis of commercial
considerations, by any other company or body corporate, as the case may be.

(iii) To insert definition of "Regional Director" as a new clause (73A) to mean
a person appointed by the Central Government under section 396 as Regional
Director for the purposes of the Companies Act who shall include an
Additional Regional Director or Joint Regional Director, or Deputy Regional
Director.

(iv) To insert new clause (74A) to define the term "Registered Valuer" to
mean a person who holds a certificate of registration granted under section
247.

(v) To amend sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of clause (85) to expand the definition
of small companies by increasing the existing upper limit of paid-up share
capital to twenty crore rupees and existing upper limit of turnover to two
hundred crore rupees.

The Committee note that the proposed changes in clause (28), seeks to alter
foundational definition by replacing the title "Cost and Works Accountants"

                                                      158
with "Cost Accountants" in Section 2(28). As the existing text mentions
outdated legislative reference for financial professionals, the amendment
rectifies this by substituting the reference with the correct and appropriate
legal title which removes nomenclature ambiguities and ensures systemic
legal harmony.

The Committee note that the proposed proviso to clause (41) seeks to enable
companies and body corporates to realign their financial year to 31 March in
certain cases, subject to Central Government approval. Under the current
framework, shifting away from a uniform April-to-March financial cycle
involves complex legal hurdles. The proposed amendment empowers the
Central Government to permit corporate bodies to shift their financial year
closures based on applications citing legitimate corporate structures or
distinct "commercial considerations". This is a pro-business flexibility which
will greatly benefit Indian companies operating with foreign parent companies
or global joint ventures.

The Committee observe that while "Regional Directors" exercise significant
delegated enforcement and adjudicative authority under the Companies Act,
the insertion of the definition for "Regional Director" formally confirms the title
of "Regional Director" which would reduce institutional friction and provide
statutory backing, as the Ministry shifts from criminal trials to localized
monetary penalty structures.

The Committee also note the statutory formalisation of the "Registered Valuer"
by inserting a new clause (74A) defining the term "Registered Valuer". The
Committee agrees with views of the Ministry that this is for clarity and
consistency to valuation-related provisions for providing a single point of
reference that seamlessly aligns across valuation-related provisions by linking
the term to the certificate of registration under section 247.

Further, under Clause (85) the definition of "Small Company" doubles the paid-
up capital threshold from 10 crore to 20 crore and the turnover threshold

                                                      159
from 100 crore to 200 crore. The Committee underscores this as a vital
milestone for MSMEs. By expanding these boundaries, a vast cohort of mid-
sized firms automatically enters a reduced-compliance landscape, boosting
market liquidity and reducing operational overheads. A significantly larger
number of private companies will now qualify as "small companies" and gain
access to abridged compliance obligations facilitating ease of doing business
for small sized Companies.

After considering the suggestions of stakeholders, responses thereto, views of
experts, and deliberations held, the Committee recommend that Clause 18 be
accepted without any amendment. The Committee in this regard, however
note that under clause (28), the title "Cost and Works Accountants" has been
proposed to be replaced with legally correct title of "Cost Accountants" for
ensuring systemic legal harmony with "The Cost Accountants Act, 1959".
Acknowledging this, Committee recommend that in line with the proposed
amendment in clause (28) a corresponding amendment in the Limited Liability
Partnership Act, 2008, must also be brought to update the nomenclature of
"Cost Accountant'. Therefore, the Committee recommend the following
amendments in section 2, sub-section (1) of the Limited Liability Partnership
Act, 2008:

"in clause (h), for the words "the Cost and Works Accountants", the words
"the Cost Accountants" shall be substituted."

                                               CLAUSE - 19

19. Clause 19 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 4 of the Companies Act,
2013.

19.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

In section 4 of the principal Act, in sub-section (5), in clause (ii), in sub-clause (a), for
the words "which may extend to one lakh rupees", the words "of fifty thousand
rupees" shall be substituted.

19.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (the Companies Act, 2013)

4. (1) * * * * *

(5) (i) Upon receipt of an application under sub-section (4), the Registrar may, on the
basis of information and documents furnished along with the application, reserve the
name for a period of twenty days from the date of approval or such other period as
may be prescribed:

Provided that in case of an application for reservation of name or for change of its
name by an existing company, the Registrar may reserve the name for a period of
sixty days from the date of approval.

(ii) Where after reservation of name under clause (i), it is found that name was
applied by furnishing wrong or incorrect information, then,--

(a) if the company has not been incorporated, the reserved name shall be cancelled
and the person making application under sub-section (4) shall be liable to a penalty
which may extend to one lakh rupees;

* * * * *

19.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment seeks to change the penalty framework under section 4(5)(ii)(a) by
replacing the discretionary penalty (which may extend to one lakh rupees) with a
fixed penalty of fifty thousand, thereby removing adjudicatory discretion."

                                                      161
19.4 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:
19.4.1 The Committee note that Clause 19 of the Bill seeks to amend section
4(5)(ii)(a) of the Companies Act 2013 to provide for a fixed penalty amount of
fifty thousand rupees where companies default in compliance with such
provisions. The proposed provision Replaces the discretionary fine "which
may extend to one lakh rupees" with a fixed penalty "of fifty thousand rupees"
for improper use of a company name reserved under Section 4. This is a
broader shift from variable, court-adjudicated fines to fixed, in-house penalties
continuing the decriminalisation and rationalisation agenda. The fixed penalty
provided under Section 4 removes adjudicating discretion and litigation for
making enforcement faster and more predictable. Therefore, after having
examined the amended provision and justifications submitted by the Ministry,
the Committee are of the view that Clause 19 may be retained as proposed
without any modification.

                                                      162
                                               CLAUSE - 20

20. Clause 20 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 7 of the Companies Act,
2013.

20.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

In section 7 of the principal Act, in sub-section (1), for clause (b), the following
clauses shall be substituted, namely:-

"(b) a declaration in the prescribed form by a person named in the articles as a
director, manager or secretary of the company, that all the requirements of this Act
and the rules made thereunder in respect of registration and matters precedent or
incidental thereto have been complied with;

(ba) a declaration in the prescribed form by an advocate, a chartered accountant,
cost accountant or company secretary in practice, where a company engaged such
professionals in its formation or incorporation;".

20.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (the Companies Act, 2013)

7. Incorporation of Company.

(1) There shall be filed with the Registrar within whose jurisdiction the registered
office of a company is proposed to be situated, the following documents and
information for registration, namely:--

* * * * *

(b) a declaration in the prescribed form by an advocate, a chartered accountant, cost
accountant or company secretary in practice, who is engaged in the formation of the
company, and by a person named in the articles as a director, manager or secretary
of the company, that all the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder
in respect of registration and matters precedent or incidental thereto have been
complied with;

* * * * *

                                                      163
20.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment seeks to modify section 7(1) to make professional certification at
the time of incorporation optional rather than mandatory. This seeks to reduce
compliance burden and facilitate ease of doing business, by providing flexibility to
companies in the incorporation process."

20.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

(i) "Professional certification may continue to be mandatory for companies above a
prescribed paid-up capital or turnover threshold. Professional certification at the
incorporation stage serves as an important quality-control mechanism and promotes
compliance with statutory requirements. Retaining such certification for larger
companies would strengthen stakeholder confidence and ensure greater regulatory
discipline."

(ii) "Insert a new sub-section in s.7 requiring the Registrar to register a complete
incorporation application within 1 working day, with deemed approval if not disposed
of within that period. Optional certification removes a cost but gives no time certainty.
New Zealand and Singapore incorporate in under 1 day as standard; certainty of
timeline is what founders and investors price in."

(iii) "The requisite amendments to the relevant rules and applicable forms be carried
out simultaneously. At present, the provisions governing the incorporation of a
Company mandatorily requires a declaration from a practicing professional, namely
an Advocate, Chartered Accountant, Cost Accountant, or that all the requirements
of the Act and the rules made thereunder in respect of registration and matters
precedent or incidental thereto have been complied with. The aforesaid provision
implies that for formation or incorporation of a company engagement of a
professional is mandatory. The proposed amendment appears to make it optional for
the company to engage a professional for the formation or incorporation of the
company. The related rules and forms should be modified simultaneously so as to
ensure that a company can be incorporated without a declaration or certification by
the professional."

20.5 Examination by the Committee:

20.5.1.  The Ministry in respect of the suggestion pertaining to continuance of

professional certification as a mandatory practice for companies above a prescribed

paid-up capital or turnover threshold, the Ministry responded as mentioned below:

         164
"This amendment seeks to facilitate ease of living for corporates and other
stakeholders. This amendment is aimed at ease of doing business, as it removes the
mandatory requirement of engaging a professional for incorporation documents,
thereby reducing compliance burdens for companies, while still permitting such
certification where a company chooses to engage a professional. It is in light of
these goals, that the Amendment Bill has made the requirement of appointing a
professional optional at the time of incorporating a company. Hence, the amendment
under the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change".

20.5.2 Regarding the Insertion of a new sub-section in s.7 requiring the Registrar to
register a complete incorporation application within one working day, the Ministry
submitted that:

"Under the Companies Act, 2013, the Registrar is required to satisfy himself that the
requirements of the Act and the rules made thereunder have been duly complied with
before registering a company. Prescribing a mandatory one working day timeline
coupled with a deemed approval mechanism may not provide adequate opportunity
to examine the documents and information furnished, particularly in cases requiring
verification or where deficiencies are noticed. Incorporation under the Companies
Act, 2013 creates a separate legal entity with perpetual succession and limited
liability, and therefore requires appropriate statutory scrutiny before registration. The
existing framework appropriately balances ease of doing business with the need to
preserve the integrity of the corporate registry and prevent fraudulent or non-
compliant registrations. Accordingly, the existing provision may be retained. Hence,
the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without
any change."

20.5.3 Ministry in context of the suggestion for carrying out the requisite
amendments to the relevant rules and applicable forms simultaneously, submitted
that:

"This suggestion recommends that the Amendment Bill and all related rules be
carried out simultaneously. This would be appropriately considered while framing
Rules post enactment of the Bill. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

20.5.4. In respect of scope and ambit of rulemaking powers enshrined in the clause
20, the Ministry informed that;

                                                      165
"It proposes to prescribe form of the declarations at incorporation stage. These kinds
of delegations are procedural in nature. They do not affect the substantive conditions
for incorporation, which are exhaustively set out in the parent statute. Instead, they
enable administrative standardisation and technological adaptability."

20.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

20.6.1 The Committee note that the Clause 20 of the Bill seeks to amend
clause (b) and insert new clause (ba) in sub-section (1) of section 7 of the
Companies Act to provide that the requirement of declaration by an advocate,
chartered accountant, cost accountant or company secretary in practice
during formation or incorporation of a company shall be applicable only when
the company engages such professionals in its formation or incorporation and
thereby making professional certification at the time of incorporation optional
rather than mandatory. The Committee after going through the suggestions
and Ministry's response, acknowledges that this amendment seeks to reduce
compliance burden and facilitate ease of doing business, by providing
flexibility to companies in the incorporation process and confines professional
liability for false certification to situations where the professional was
genuinely retained. The proposed amendment makes it optional for the
company to engage a professional for the formation or incorporation of the
company, contrary to the earlier mandatory compliance. Accordingly, the
Committee accept Clause 20 as proposed and recommend no modification.

20.6.2  The Committee however, further note and recommend that in sub-

section (9), of section 8 of Company Law 2013, pertaining to `Formation of

companies with charitable objects, etc.' the words "and having similar objects"

shall be omitted. As residual assets on dissolution are typically fungible so

their charitable end use does not materially depend on whether recipient

Section 8 company has similar objects or not. The modified sub-section (9) of

Section 8 would read as under:

"In section 7 of the principal Act, in sub-section (1), for clause (b), the
following clauses shall be substituted, namely:--

                                                      166
"(b) a declaration in the prescribed form by a person named in the articles as a
director, manager or secretary of the company, that all the requirements of this
Act and the rules made thereunder in respect of registration and matters
precedent or incidental thereto have been complied with;
(ba) a declaration in the prescribed form by an advocate, a chartered
accountant, cost accountant or company secretary in practice, where a
company engaged such professionals in its formation or incorporation;".
20A. In section 8 of the principal Act, in sub-section (9), the words "and having
similar objects" shall be omitted."

                                               CLAUSE - 21

21. Clause 21 of the Bill seeks to insert Section 12A after Section 12 of the
Companies Act, 2013

21.1 Provision proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

After section 12 of the principal Act, the following section shall be inserted, namely:--

"12A. (1) The class or classes of companies, as may be prescribed, shall maintain a
website, an e-mail address and other modes of communication in such form and
manner, as may be prescribed.

(2) The details of website, e-mail address and other modes of communication
referred to in sub-section (1) and the changes, if any, therein, shall be intimated to
the Registrar in such form and within such period, as may be prescribed."

21.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (the Companies Act, 2013)

There are no corresponding provisions in the Principal Act as new clauses have
been inserted after section 12.

21.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision

"In order to have transparency and ease of communication, section 12(A) is
proposed to mandate that such class or classes of companies as may be prescribed
shall, at all times, maintain a functional website, email address and other modes of
communication in the prescribed manner."

21.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

(i) "Email address and other modes of electronic communication as may be
prescribed, should be applicable to all companies. The requirement of maintaining
website may be excluded for Small Companies and OPCs. Email and other modes
of electronic communication are now becoming the norm under various laws and for
legal proceedings as well, both for individuals and non-individuals. Although small
companies are voluntarily maintaining the website for business reasons. Website for
Small Companies and OPCs who operate with limited resources, can be made
optional, as it may result in additional cost and compliance burden without providing
significant practical."

                                                      168
(ii) "The "prescribed class of companies" required to maintain a website should
explicitly cover all companies meeting the CSR eligibility criteria under Section 135.
Companies subject to CSR obligations are expected to maintain a high degree of
transparency and stakeholder engagement. Mandatory digital communication
platforms would facilitate effective public disclosure and accountability."

(iii) "(a) Exempt wholly owned subsidiaries from this requirement and should not
be mandated to have a website merely because they fulfil certain threshold
requirements (generally linked to their share capital, net worth or turnover). However,
if the holding company is not an operating company, then no exemption should
be given to wholly owned subsidiaries of such companies. (b) Companies should be
given the option to provide landline number or mobile number as their telephone
numbers. Large unlisted companies generally have websites for business purposes.
However, mandating wholly owned subsidiaries to have a website, incur related
costs and comply with the related requirements seems unwarranted. In such cases,
the holding company's website already reflects the group's governance framework
and financial position, including financial statements of subsidiaries. Therefore,
exempting wholly owned subsidiaries would aid in reducing compliance burden and
administrative cost, and would also be in line with the approach adopted by MCA in
various other requirements of the Act such as constitution of Board Committees,
appointment of Independent Directors etc. Permitting companies to give mobile nos.
In today's context, most companies may not have a landline number. Hence, they
should be provided the flexibility to instead provide mobile numbers on the letterhead
etc. The related. e-forms would need to be amended in this connection.

(iv) Export and import-oriented entities, require maintenance of active email linked
to IEC and MCA records. This improves regulatory communication, grievance
handling and scheme administration.

(v) Website/e-mail (Section 12A) single-window with the Registrar filing, shared to
exchanges and depositories."

(vi) "Adopt an approach by promoting paperless governance and digital
communication while exempting small companies and start-ups from the proposed
requirement or making compliance voluntary or such entities. The requirement
should be made mandatory only for listed companies and other companies meeting
the prescribed net worth, shareholder threshold, or such other specified eligibility
criteria. Alternatively, the Committee may consider making digital communication
optional rather than mandatory for such members."

(vii) "Insert a proviso in Section 12A to the effect that for companies regulated by
SEBI, compliance with SEBI's LODR Regulations regarding maintenance and
disclosure of contact information, website details, and electronic communication
channels shall be deemed to constitute compliance with Section 12A, without
requiring a separate or duplicate intimation to the RoC. The MCA and SEBI should
establish a shared data interface so that updates made on SEBI-regulated portals

                                                      169
(SCORES, stock exchange platforms) are automatically reflected in MCA21. The Bill
aims to move towards a more agile, technology -driven compliance framework that
reflects contemporary business realities. However, listed companies already
maintain comprehensive digital infrastructure and disclose all contact/website
information under SEBI's LODR Requiring a separate intimation to the Registrar
every time there is a change creates a duplicative compliance obligation A "deemed
compliance" mechanism and shared data infrastructure between SEBI and MCA
would significantly reduce redundant regulatory filings, saving significant time and
cost for regulated entities."

(viii) "Many global organisations, where the Indian subsidiary is not permitted to
maintain an independent website due to global branding, cybersecurity, and
Information Technology governance policies. Instead, the Indian entity is featured on
the parent company's website with a dedicated webpage containing its corporate
information. The proposed Section 12A, if interpreted to require every company to
maintain its own standalone website, would impose an unnecessary compliance
burden without materially advancing transparency. Hence, insert a proviso to clarify
that "where a company does not maintain an independent website, compliance with
Section 12A shall be deemed to be satisfied if the company maintains a dedicated
webpage or profile on the website of its holding company or group company, clearly
displaying the particulars prescribed under the Act, together with a functional
company-specific email address". Numerous wholly-owned subsidiaries of
multinational groups operate under a centralised global digital governance policy and
are not permitted to maintain independent websites. Instead, their corporate
information is hosted on the global website of the holding company. Since the
objective of Section 12A is to ensure public accessibility of company information, this
objective is equally achieved through a dedicated webpage on the holding
company's website. Mandating a separate website would increase compliance costs
and administrative burden without providing any additional regulatory or stakeholder
benefit. The proposed clarification would preserve transparency while
accommodating widely adopted global corporate governance practices and further
the Government's ease of doing business objectives."

(ix) "(a) Wholly owned subsidiaries should be exempted from this requirement and
should not be mandated to maintain a website merely because they meet certain
threshold requirements (generally linked to share capital, net worth, or turnover). It
suggested further that Small Companies (as defined under Section 2(85)) be
expressly excluded from any mandatory requirement to maintain a website,
designated email address, or other prescribed digital communication modes under
Section 12A. It is also suggested that instead of prescribing the applicability based
on the category of companies, objective financial thresholds such as paid-up capital
or net worth may be considered for determining the requirement to maintain a
website. (b) In the present context, most companies may not have a landline number.
Accordingly, they should be provided the flexibility to furnish mobile numbers on
letterheads and other official documents. The related e-forms would need to be
amended in this regard. Large unlisted companies generally have websites for
business purposes. However, mandating wholly owned subsidiaries to maintain a
website, incur related costs, and comply with associated requirements appears

                                                      170
unwarranted. In such cases the holding company's website already reflects the
group's governance framework and financial position, including the financial
statements of subsidiaries. Accordingly, exempting wholly owned subsidiaries would
reduce compliance burden and administrative costs, and would also be consistent
with the approach adopted by the MCA in respect of various other requirements
under the Act, such as the constitution of Board Committees and the appointment of
Independent Directors. Small companies typically operate with limited resources and
lean administrative structures with geographically dispersed operations. Mandating
website maintenance and formal digital communication infrastructure would impose
disproportionate compliance and cost burden. Introduction of threshold would make
compliance obligation uniform and easier to monitor than requiring specific
referencing of separate sets of regulations for select companies. Given the
widespread shift towards mobile-based communication and the declining use of
landline telephones by businesses, many companies do not maintain a dedicated
landline number. Permitting the disclosure of mobile numbers on letterheads and
official documents would better reflect current business practices and facilitate
stakeholder communication."

(x) "Retain the clauses, subject to the following modifications: (i) small companies,
One Person Companies and dormant companies be expressly excluded from
prescription; and (ii) intimation of particulars be effected through the annual return
under section 92 rather than by a separate e-form, with only event-based changes
requiring separate intimation. Digital reachability of companies serves stakeholders
and regulators; however, a fresh standalone filing obligation, backed by penalty
under section 450/469 would be a new compliance layer contrary to the Bill's stated
object. Embedding the disclosure in the annual return achieves the regulatory
purpose at nil marginal burden."

(xii  "The proposal requiring prescribed classes of companies to maintain a

website, e-mail address and other modes of communication, and suggests

exemptions for closely-held companies with a limited number of stakeholders, and

for companies whose accounts are consolidated with a holding company that already

maintains a functional website, to promote ease of doing business and mitigate

compliance costs for smaller companies was partially disagreed."

(xii) "The `Email address' maintained under Section 12A be treated as the Primary
Legal venue for the service of DGFT notices for all export oriented entities thereby
preventing disruptions caused by physical Mail delays."

(xiii) "The tech-driven start-ups in the IFSC be permitted to maintain "Virtual
Registered Offices for the first 24 Months of operation. This Statutory recognition
would significantly reduce capital expenditure and entry barriers for global digital first
entrepreneurs."
