21.5.19 The representatives from Ministry added further explanation as under:

"Section 12A. Apart from the procedural aspects, there is a prescription which
classes of companies has to maintain website compulsorily. We received so many
suggestions to include companies for example, all those companies which are
having CSR mandate, they have to maintain a website compulsorily. We received
such kinds of suggestions. That is a reason we are keeping this provision to
prescribe classes of companies through rules. This is an economic clause. There will
be a lot of suggestions from stakeholders. For example, if we are going to freeze it
right now that only listed companies have to maintain website then we will not have
any flexibility to change it later."

21.5.20  In this regard, the Ministry submitted detailed explanatory note on

rational for proposed Section 12A:

"These provisions of proposed section 12A are sought to be made applicable to
listed companies or other unlisted public companies meeting relevant thresholds to
be provided by rules. This section seeks to provide an express statutory basis, in
respect of prescribed classes of companies, to maintain a website, an e-mail address
or other mode of communication. SEBI has already mandated similar requirement for
listed entities. The proposed Section 12A also seeks to require such prescribed
classes of companies to intimate the details of such website, an e-mail address or
other mode of communication or any change therein to the Registrar in the
prescribed e-form. The objective is to ensure that these modes of information-
sharing and communication for large companies are recognized in the Act itself."

21.5.21 The Ministry also submitted their views on the extent of rule framing

powers provided for under the provision 12A as under:

"It proposes to prescribe class or classes of companies which shall comply with the
requirements of this section. The use of "class or classes" is a well-established
legislative device in corporate law, enabling dynamic calibration without frequent
statutory amendments. The essential policy, i.e., that differential compliance may be

                                                      177
warranted, is determined by the legislature; only the identification and periodic
revision of such classes is delegated. It also proposes to prescribe form and manner
for maintaining website, an email address and other modes of communication. It also
proposes to prescribe form and period within which details of website, e-mail address
and other modes of communication and any changes therein, shall be intimated to
the Registrar. These kinds of delegations are procedural in nature which does not
affect substantive conditions of compliance."

21.5.22 When in this regard Committee pointed out the inconvenience caused due
to the uncertainty created by frequent changes in rules, which makes it difficult to
keep track of the everchanging rule position, the Secretary, MCA clarified:

"Sir, this may be true for general departments, but as far as MCA is concerned, our
rule-making process is very onerous. If you see our website, you will get the details
on how many rules we have changed in the past years. This is more for the
regulators, not for the Government."

21.5.23 The Ministry in respect of Rule framing powers enshrined in the clause 21
submitted the following information:

"It proposes to prescribe class or classes of companies which shall comply with the
requirements of this section. The use of "class or classes" is a well-established
legislative device incorporate law, enabling dynamic calibration without frequent
statutory amendments. The essential policy, i.e., that differential compliance may be
warranted, is determined by the legislature; only the identification and periodic
revision of such classes is delegated. It also proposes to prescribe form and manner
for maintaining website, an email address and other modes of communication. It also
proposes to prescribe form and period within which details of website, e-mail address
and other modes of communication and any changes therein, shall be intimated to
the Registrar. These kinds of delegations are procedural in nature which does not
affect substantive conditions of compliance."

21.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

21.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 21 of the Bill seeks to insert a new
section 12A in the Companies Act, 2013 to provide that the prescribed class or
classes of companies shall maintain a website, an email address and other
modes of communication in such form and manner as may be provided by
rules. It further provides that these details and the changes therein shall be
intimated to the Registrar in such form and within such period as may be

                                                      178
provided by rules. The Committee acknowledge that the proposed amendment
seeks to provide an express statutory basis, in respect of prescribed classes
of companies, to maintain a functional website, an e-mail address or other
mode of communication, in order to have transparency and ease of
communication. The provision covers a class of companies, and the specifics
of form/manner, are to be taken up while framing Rules. The Committee note
that this operationalises the Bill's broader push toward electronic governance.

In this regard, the Committee further note from the Ministry's submissions that
mentioning of "E-Mail" along with Website and other modes of communication
affirms the objective that these modes of information-sharing and
communication for large companies are recognized in the Act itself. The
Committee endorse the intent of the Ministry. However, it is also of the view
that the Ministry's proposal to prescribe only certain classes of companies for
compliance with this provision would exempt all other companies also from
the basic requirement of maintaining an email-ID. Since maintaining an email
ID is a standard and essential practice for carrying out day-to-day business
operations in an increasingly digital environment, the Committee are of the
opinion that this requirement should not be limited only to the prescribed
classes of companies. The Committee however, after having examined the
amended provision, justifications submitted by the Ministry and deliberations
held, accept Clause 21 as proposed without any modification.

                                                    CLAUSE - 22

22. Clause 22 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 20 of the Companies Act,
2013.

22.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

In section 20 of the principal Act, in sub-section (2), for the proviso, the following
provisos shall be substituted, namely:--

"Provided that the service of such class of documents by such class or classes of
companies, as may be prescribed, to its members, shall take place only through
electronic mode, in such manner as may be prescribed, and such service shall be
deemed to be sufficient compliance for the purposes of this Act:

Provided further that a member may request for delivery of any document through a
particular mode, for which he shall pay such fee as may be determined by the
company in its general meeting."

22.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (the Companies Act, 2013)

20. Service of documents

(1) * * * * *

(2) Save as provided in this Act or the rules made thereunder for filing of documents
with the Registrar in electronic mode, a document may be served on Registrar or any
member by sending it to him by post or by registered post or by speed post or by
courier or by delivering at his office or address, or by such electronic or other mode
as may be prescribed:

Provided that a member may request for delivery of any document through a
particular mode, for which he shall pay such fees as may be determined by the
company in its annual general meeting.

* * * * *

                                                      180
22.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"This clause proposes to permit service of documents through electronic mode for
such class or classes of companies and documents as may be prescribed as
electronic communication is cost effective and convenient mode for service of
documents."

22.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

(i) "Allow hybrid service; fee should not be mandatory for any other mode other
than electronic. Sole electronic mode excludes members without access; fee
penalises choice of physical mode."

(ii) " Retain the clause, subject to the modification that the fee for physical delivery
shall not exceed the actual cost of printing and dispatch, and that members who
have not registered an e-mail address shall be entitled to physical delivery of
statutory documents without fee. Electronic-only service generates real cost savings
and is environmentally sound; however, mandatory e-service must not
disenfranchise members lacking digital access, particularly retail and rural
shareholders. A cost-based fee ceiling prevents the fee from operating as a deterrent
to the exercise of statutory information rights."

(iii) "Keep the provision advisory in nature and not mandatory for small companies.
In other words, they may be permitted manual servicing of documents, if it is
convenient to them."

22.5 Examination by the Committee:

22.5.1 As regards the allowance of service of documents in hybrid mode, the Ministry
submitted following reply:

"The proposed amendment seeks to promote digital communication, reduce
compliance costs and facilitate timely service of documents by enabling prescribed
classes of companies to serve prescribed classes of documents through electronic
mode. At the same time, adequate safeguards have been provided by permitting a
member to request delivery of documents through a particular mode. The provision
also enables the company to recover the additional cost of providing such service
through a fee determined by the members in the general meeting. Accordingly, the
proposed framework appropriately balances ease of doing business with shareholder

                                                      181
convenience and does not require any modification. Hence, the provision in the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

22.5.2.  Regarding suggestion about fees for physical delivery, the Ministry

stated that same will be determined by the Company in AGM where members can

participate. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may

be retained without any change.

22.5.3 The Ministry in context of keeping the provision advisory in nature and not
mandatory for small companies submitted following response:

"This would be appropriately dealt with during framing of subordinate legislation. The
proposed amendment applies only to such class or classes of companies as may be
prescribed, and the specific categories and manner of compliance will be governed
by Rules. Proposed amendment is intended for listed and other public interest
entities. However, the prescribed classes of companies will be decided after having
detailed consultations with public as well as with all relevant stakeholders. The
suggestion will be examined at the rulemaking stage, if required. Hence, the
provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change."

22.5.4 The Ministry in respect of Rule framing powers enshrined in the clause 22

submitted following information:

"It proposes to prescribe the class or classes of companies, the class of documents
which may be serviced and the manner of service of such documents by such
companies. The use of "class or classes" is a well-established legislative device
incorporate law, enabling dynamic calibration without frequent statutory
amendments. The essential policy, i.e., that differential compliance may be
warranted, is determined by the legislature; only the identification and periodic
revision of such classes is delegated. The provision to prescribe manner of service of
documents is a delegation which is directed at procedural flexibility."

22.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

22.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 22 of the Bill seeks to insert a proviso
after sub-section (2) of section 20 of the Companies Act to provide that
service of prescribed class of documents by prescribed class or classes of
companies to their members shall take place only through electronic mode in
such manner as may be provided by rules. Since electronic communication is

                                                      182
cost-effective and convenient mode for dispatching and delivering documents,
the proposed amendments seek to allow communication in such form. The
manner in which members would be entitled to receive physical copies of the
prescribed classes of documents would be provided in the rules. In the second
proviso, it is proposed to replace the words "annual general meeting", with the
words "general meeting" to allow determination of fees for delivery of any
document to a member through a particular mode in the extraordinary general
meetings also. The Committee further note and agree with the justifications
submitted by the Ministry that the proposed amendment intends to promote
digital communication, reduce compliance costs and facilitate timely service of
documents by enabling prescribed classes of companies to serve prescribed
classes of documents through electronic mode. The Committee in this regard
take note of the Rule framing powers, enshrined in the clause, which
prescribes the class or classes of companies, to be decided by executive
authorities while formulating Rules and Guidelines under the provision. The
Committee, are of the strong view that the extensive discretionary powers
should not be delegated in name of procedural flexibility and must form an
integral part of the legislation. The Committee however, support the core
objective of the proposed Section 20 and considers the change crucial, as it
aligns with the objective of ease of doing business. Therefore, subject to the
concern raised, the Committee accept the proposed amendment without any
modification.

                                               CLAUSE - 23

23. Clause 23 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 24 of the Companies Act,
2013.

23.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

In section 24 of the principal Act, in sub-section (2), the words, brackets and figures
"and the matters delegated to it under proviso to sub-section (1) of section 458" shall
be omitted.

23.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013)

Section-24 Power of SEBI to regulate issue and transfer of securities, etc.:-

24. (1) * * * * *

(2) The Securities and Exchange Board shall, in respect of matters specified in sub-
section (1) and the matters delegated to it under proviso to sub-section (1) of section
458, exercise the powers conferred upon it under sub-sections (1), (2A), (3) and (4)
of section 11, sections 11A, 11B and 11D of the Securities and Exchange Board of
India Act, 1992.

* * * * *

23.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment removes the reference to matters delegated to SEBI under the
proviso to section 458(1) from section 24(2). This is a consequential change, as the
proviso to section 458(1) relating to such delegation was omitted in 2017. The
existing reference has therefore become redundant and is proposed to be deleted to
ensure statutory consistency and avoid ambiguity."

23.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

(i) "Clause 23 proposes that the phrase 'and the matters delegated to it under proviso
to sub-section (1) of section 458' is deleted from Section 24(2). It is suggested that

                                                      184
the reference to Section 458(1) within Section 24(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 may
be retained with a technical modification to delete the word "proviso".

Proposed revised draft clause:

23. In section 24 of the principal Act, in sub-section (2), the words, brackets and
figures "and the matters delegated to it under `proviso to' sub-section (1) of section
458" shall be omitted.

Section 24

Power of Securities and Exchange Board to regulate issue and transfer of securities,
etc.

(1) .................

(2) The Securities and Exchange Board shall, in respect of matters specified in sub-
section (1) and the matters delegated to it under proviso to sub-section (1) of section
458, exercise the powers conferred upon it under sub-sections (1), (2A), (3) and (4)
of section 11, sections 11A, 11B and 11D of the Securities and Exchange Board of
India Act, 1992.

Section 458 of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Central Government to, by
notification, delegate any of its powers or functions under this Act to such authority or
officer as may be specified in the notification. Such Authority may include SEBI.

(ii) Thus, if reference to Section 458 in Section 24 is omitted, SEBI would not be able
to exercise its powers under sub-sections (1), (2A), (3) and (4) of section 11,
sections 11A, 11B and 11D of the SEBI Act, if any matters are delegated to SEBI in
future.

(iii) In view of the above, it is suggested that the reference to Section 458(1) may be
retained in Section 24(2) of the Companies Act, 2013. (iv) Further, it may be noted
that the proviso to Section 458(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, was omitted vide the
Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017, effective from 9th February 2018. Accordingly,
it is suggested that the word "proviso" may be omitted from the relevant text of
Section 24(2) as shown in the adjacent column."

                                                      185
23.5 Examination by the Committee:

The Ministry in regard to the suggestion submitted that proviso to sub-section 1 of
Section 458 has been deleted via the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017, and
therefore the reference to such deleted proviso in Section 24(2) is redundant.
Additionally, Section 24(1)(a) explicitly states that the Securities Exchange Board of
India is tasked with administering regulations regarding `transfer and issue of
securities' in so far as they relate to listed companies or to be listed companies. This
language provides sufficient leeway to the central government, covering any future
delegations that it may undertake towards SEBI. Hence, the provision in the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change.

23.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

The Committee note that Clause 23 of the Bill seeks to amend sub-section (2)
of section 24 of the Companies Act, to omit the words "and the matters
delegated to it under proviso to sub-section (1) of section 458". As the
reference to such proviso to sub-section (1) of section 458 in sub-section (2)
of section 24, is redundant and accordingly being omitted. The Committee
observe that this is a consequential change, as the proviso to section 458(1)
relating to such delegation was omitted in 2017 and its purpose is to remove
interpretive overlap rather than to expand or contract any regulator's authority.
The Committee, after considering the justification given by the Ministry of
Corporate Affairs and examining the proposed provision, accept Clause 23 as
proposed without any modification.

24.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

(9) If a prospectus is issued in contravention of the provisions of this section, the
company and every person who is knowingly a party to the issue of such prospectus
shall be liable to a penalty of two lakh rupees.

24.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (the Companies Act, 2013)

Section-26 Matters to be stated in prospectus: -

26. (1) * * * * *

(9) If a prospectus is issued in contravention of the provisions of this section, the
company shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand
rupees but which may extend to three lakh rupees and every person who is
knowingly a party to the issue of such prospectus shall be punishable with fine which

* * * * *

24.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment seeks to decriminalise section 26(9) by replacing the existing fine-
based punishment with a fixed monetary penalty. The amendment is part of the
broader decriminalisation exercise under the Bill."

24.4 Examination by the Committee:

During the course of the examination of the Bill, the Committee came to know about
the amendment relating to proviso to sub section (1) of Section 26 that the "financial"

                                                      187
word in proviso is not in line with wording of rest of the clause and therefore needs
amendment.

24.5 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

24.5.1 The Committee note that Clause 24 of the Bill seeks to substitute sub-
section (9) of section 26 of the Companies Act, to provide that if a prospectus
is issued in contravention of such section, the company and every person who
is knowingly a party to the issue of such prospectus shall be liable to a penalty
of two lakh rupees. Accordingly, the offence is being decriminalised. The
Committee observes that the provision simplifies enforcement and removes
ambiguity about quantum, but the fixed amount applies uniformly. After
detailed examination of the proposal and consideration of the justification
provided by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, the Committee find the
amendment to sub-section (9) of section 26 to be appropriate and recommend
its acceptance as proposed without any modification.

24.5.2 While examining and deliberating upon Clause 24, the Committee also
came across a drafting error in the provision of the Company Law 2013, apart
from the proposed amendments, where the word "financial" in proviso to sub-
section (1) of section 26 of the principal Act, is not in line with the wording of
rest of the Clause. The Committee recommend that in place of the words" in
respect of such financial information", the words "in respect of such
information" shall be substituted. The modified clause would read as under:

"In section 26 of the principal Act,--

(a) in sub-section (1), in the proviso, for the words "in respect of such financial
 information", the words "in respect of such information" shall be substituted;

(b) for sub-section (9), the following sub-section shall be substituted, namely:-

                                                      188
"(9) If a prospectus is issued in contravention of the provisions of this section,
the company and every person who is knowingly a party to the issue of such
prospectus shall be liable to a penalty of two lakh rupees.".

                                               CLAUSE - 25

25. Clause 25 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 40 of the Companies Act,
2013.

25.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

In section 40 of the principal Act,--

(a) in sub-section (5), for the words "this section", the word, brackets and
figure "sub-section (3)" shall be substituted;

(b) after sub-section (5), the following sub-section shall be inserted, namely:--

"(5A) If a default is made in complying with the provisions of this section, other
than sub-section (3), the company shall be liable to a penalty of twenty-five
lakh rupees and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to
a penalty of two lakh rupees."

25.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013)

Section-40 Securities to be dealt with in stock exchanges: -

(1) * * * * *

(5) If a default is made in complying with the provisions of this section, the company
shall be punishable with a fine which shall not be less than five lakh rupees but which
may extend to fifty lakh rupees and every officer of the company who is in default
shall be punishable or with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but
which may extend to three lakh rupees.

* * * * *

25.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

                                                      190
"The amendment restructures the penalty framework under section 40 by limiting the
existing criminal punishment under sub-section (5) specifically to contraventions of
sub-section (3). For all other defaults under the section, a new sub-section (5A)
introduces a civil penalty regime with fixed monetary penalties for the company and
officers in default. The amendment is part of the broader decriminalisation exercise
under the Bill."

25.4 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

25.4.1 The Committee note that Clause 25 of the Bill seeks to amend sub-
section (5) of section 40 of the Companies Act, to provide that punishment
under such sub-section shall be applicable only for defaults under sub-section
(3) thereby decriminalising offences under sub-sections (1), (2) and (4) of
section 40. It further seeks to insert new sub-section (5A) to provide that in
case of defaults under sub-sections other than sub-section (3), penalty of
twenty-five lakh rupees for every company and two lakh rupees for every
officer of the company shall be leviable. The Committee observe that the Bill
differentiates between the specific default under sub-section (3) and broader
non-compliance with allowing a materially higher penalty of 25 lakh to
specifically target the latter reflecting the greater investor-protection. The
Committee, therefore, after examining the proposed provision and considering
the justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, accept Clause 25 as
proposed without any modification.

26. Clause 26 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 42 of the Companies Act,
2013.

26.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

In section 42 of the principal Act,--

(a) in the marginal heading, for the word "shares", the word "securities" shall be
substituted;

(b) in sub-section (2), after the words "employees stock option", the words "or such
other scheme linked to the value of the share capital of a company," shall be
inserted;

(c) in sub-section (10), for the words "which may extend to", the words "equivalent to"
shall be substituted.

26.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013)

Section-42 Issue of shares on Private Placement basis:

(1) * * * * *

(2) A private placement shall be made only to a select group of persons who have
been identified by the Board (herein referred to as "identified persons"), whose
number shall not exceed fifty or such higher number as may be prescribed excluding
the qualified institutional buyers and employees of the company being offered
securities under a scheme of employees stock option in terms of provisions of clause
(b) of sub-section (1) of section 62, in a financial year subject to such conditions as
may be prescribed.

* * * * *

(10) Subject to sub-section (11), if a company makes an offer or accepts monies in
contravention of this section, the company, its promoters and directors shall be liable
for a penalty which may extend to the amount raised through the private placement
or two crore rupees, whichever is lower, and the company shall also refund all

                                                      192
monies with interest as specified in sub-section (6) to subscribers within a period of
thirty days of the order imposing the penalty.

* * * * *

26.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment seeks to recognises schemes such as Restricted Stock Units
(RSUs) and Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs), in addition to Employee Stock Option
Plans (ESOPs). Further, the amendment to sub-section (10) replaces the
discretionary penalty with a fixed penalty."

26.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

(i) "(a)Since the existing heading of Section 42 already uses the term "securities," the
proposed modification appears unnecessary. The proposed term already exists in
section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013; (b) The existing penal provisions of Section
42 may not be amended as the proposed penalty is too strict considering the
technical defaults like non opening of separate bank account etc. The penalty
amount is not commensurate with the nature of defaults such as technical lapses
pertaining to non-opening of separate bank account or missing details in return of
allotment."

(ii) "The Committee should clarify the scope of such schemes through the relevant
rules and expressly provide that genuine employee incentive schemes, including
Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs) and phantom stock plans if any and are covered,
while incorporating appropriate safeguards to prevent their misuse as disguised
public offers. The proposed approach will strengthen employee incentive
frameworks, facilitate the adoption of modern value-based compensation structures,
and provide greater commercial flexibility to companies".

(iii) "Confirm that the RSU/SAR enabling provision is not limited to listed companies,
and codify that promoters and founder-directors of recognised startups are eligible to
participate in RSU/SAR schemes, mirroring the existing 10-year ESOP relaxation
under Rule 12 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules.
Delaware/US law imposes no promoter exclusion founders, directors and advisors
routinely hold options and RSUs. Indian law already permits founder participation in
ESOP schemes of startups for 10 years; RSU/SAR treatment should be aligned."

(iv) "The amended clauses should be retained, subject to the insertion of a
definition in section 2, as follows:

                                                      193
`"scheme linked to the value of the share capital" means a scheme, by whatever
name called, under which an employee or director is entitled to receive shares, or a
payment referable to the value or appreciation in value of shares, of the company, as
may be prescribed.'

Statutory recognition of SARs and value-linked instruments removes a long-standing
gap in executive compensation law and aligns the Act with the SEBI SBEB
Regulations for listed companies. An anchoring definition is necessary because the
phrase appears in at least four operative provisions with penal and buy-back
consequences; leaving its content wholly to inference invites disputes over cash-
settled versus equity-settled schemes."

(v) " Insert: "or under a scheme involving restricted stock units or equity-settled stock
appreciation rights in section 42(2) after employees' stock option.

"In section 62(1)(b), after employees' stock option, insert: "or restricted stock units or
equity-settled stock appreciation rights, subject to such conditions as may be
prescribed:

Provided that a cash-settled stock appreciation right, or other instrument linked to
the values of share capital not culminating in issue or transfer of shares, shall not be
treated as an issue of shares or securities under this Act."

Restricted stock units (RSUs) and equity-settled stock appreciation rights (SARs)
result into share issuance while cash settled SARs are contractual cash liability
which is in turn tied to share value but with no allotment or dilution involved. Putting
all these categories in an undifferentiated manner under Section 42 & 62 would
impose heavy compliances around private placement and share issuance; effectively
on instruments which do not alter the capital structure. Further, cash settled SARs do
not trigger Section 42 at a threshold level as they do not involve allotment or transfer
of securities under Section 62 at all. Clarify that regulated digital security tokens and
tokenised ESOPs are eligible under IFSCA-approved frameworks".

(vi) " `One size fit all' penalty is disproportionate. Levy lower penalty for
Contravention of procedural/ administrative default relating to private placement.
[Example adjudication orders:

 Timing of Form filing incorrect - INR 10,000 (RoC Chennai)

 Funds used before Form filing INR 1 lakh to 2 lakh (RoC Pune)]

 Replace prosecution (i.e. fine) on statutory auditor and cost auditor with monetary
penalty."

                                                      194
26.4 Examination by the Committee:

26.5.1 Regarding the redundancy of the term "securities, in section 42, and strictness
of the proposed penalty under the clause, the Ministry submitted:

"(i) The proposed amendment is a drafting change. Section 42 is substantively
concerned with private placement of securities, and the marginal heading is being
aligned accordingly. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,
2026 may be retained without any change.

(ii) While strict penalties are warranted for serious violations of the private placement
framework, section 42 prescribes obligations of varying nature and consequence.
The requirements under subsections (1) to (5) of section 42, relating to the manner
of making a private placement, issuance of the offer only to identify persons,
adherence to the prescribed limits on offerees, prohibition on overlapping private
placement offers, and receipt of subscription money only through banking channels,
constitute the principle substantive safeguards governing private placements. These
provisions are fundamental to preserving the integrity of the private placement
framework, Maintaining separate bank account for receipt of application money is
connected to restriction on its utilization for any purpose other than those specified
under said proviso to sub section (6). It cannot be treated as merely a technical
default as non-maintenance of separate Bank account could lead to receipt of money
in company's existing account, consequent fungibility and possible utilization of said
money before allotment of shares or securities resulting into contravention of proviso
of sub section (4) which is of serious nature. Similarly, sub-section (6), which
requires allotment of securities within the prescribed period, mandates refund of the
application money with interest where allotment is not completed within the stipulated
time, and restricts the utilisation of application money until allotment or refund,
directly protects investor interests and safeguards subscription funds. Diversion or
premature utilisation of money, contrary to the statutory restrictions, directly
undermines investor protection and the integrity of the private placement framework
and therefore merits stringent consequences. Hence, the provision in the Corporate
Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

26.5.2 As regards the suggestion pertaining to scope and operational aspects of
employee incentive schemes and the prescription of appropriate safeguards for their
implementation, the Ministry submitted following response:

                                                      195
         "The suggestion relates to the scope and operational aspects of employee
incentive schemes and the prescription of appropriate safeguards for their
implementation. The proposed amendment is intended to enable companies to issue
securities under schemes linked to the value of the share capital of a company, while
the detailed framework governing such schemes, including their applicability and
eligibility criteria, is to be prescribed separately. The suggestion is duly noted. It will
be addressed in the relevant rules. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

26.5.3 The Ministry in regard to confirmation that the RSU/SAR enabling provision

is not limited to listed companies and codifying that promoters and founder-directors

of recognised startups are eligible to participate in RSU/SAR schemes, submitted the

following:

"The proposed amendment is intended to enable companies to issue securities
under schemes linked to the value of the share capital of a company, while the
detailed framework governing such schemes, including their applicability and
eligibility criteria, is to be prescribed separately. Accordingly, the suggestions
regarding the classes of companies to which such schemes may apply and the
eligibility of promoters and founder-directors of recognised start-ups to participate
therein would be considered, as appropriate, while framing the relevant Rules.
Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained
without any change."

26.5.4 Regarding insertion of a anchoring definition in sub section 2 for further clarity
on the clause the Ministry apprised that, the proposed amendment seeks to
recognize employee compensation schemes. The specific schemes covered by the
provision, and the conditions governing their implementation, would be appropriately
prescribed under the Rules. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change.

26.5.5 The Ministry in respect of suggestion mentioned at Sl. No. (v) suggesting
insertion of "under a scheme involving restricted stock units or equity-settled stock
appreciation rights" after employees' stock option, informed that the proposed
amendment to section 42 is an enabling provision intended to expand the category of
employee compensation schemes. The specific schemes covered by the provision,
and the conditions governing their implementation, may be appropriately prescribed
under the Rules. Therefore, any clarification regarding the applicability of section 42
to cash-settled Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs) or other schemes that do not
involve the issue of shares may therefore be dealt with through the Rules. Hence,
the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without
any change.

                                                      196
26.5.6.  In respect of levying of disproportionate Penalty following `one size fit

all' view, the Ministry stated as mentioned below:

"While strict penalties are warranted for serious violations of the private placement
framework, section 42 prescribes obligations of varying nature and consequence.
The requirements under sub-sections (1) to (5) of section 42, relating to the manner
of making a private placement, issuance of the offer only to identified persons,
adherence to the prescribed limits on offerees, prohibition on overlapping private
placement offers, and receipt of subscription money only through banking channels,
constitute the principle substantive safeguards governing private placements. These
provisions are fundamental to preserving the integrity of the private placement
framework., Maintaining separate bank account for receipt of application money is
connected to restriction on its utilization for any purpose other than those specified
under said proviso to sub section (6). It cannot be treated as merely a technical
default as non-maintenance of separate Bank account could lead to receipt of money
in company's existing account, consequent fungibility and possible utilization of said
money before allotment of shares or securities resulting into contravention of proviso
of sub section (4) which is of serious nature. Similarly, sub-section (6), which
requires allotment of securities within the prescribed period, mandates refund of the
application money with interest where allotment is not completed within the stipulated
time, and restricts the utilisation of application money until allotment or refund,
directly protects investor interests and safeguards subscription funds. Diversion or
premature utilisation of application money contrary to the statutory restrictions,
directly undermines investor protection and the integrity of the private placement
framework and therefore merits stringent consequences. Hence, the provision in the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

26.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

26.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 26 of the Bill seeks to amend section 42
of the Companies Act, 2013 in the following manner:

(i) The marginal heading of section 42 by substituting the word "shares"
with the word "securities".

(ii) Sub-section (2) to insert the words "or such other scheme linked to the
value of the share capital of a company", after the words, "employee stock
option", in order to recognise instruments such as Restricted Stock Units and
Stock Appreciation Rights, in addition to Employee Stock Option Plans, as
executive compensation to be issued with approval of shareholders.

                                                      197
(iii) Sub-section (10) to replace the words "which may extend to", with the
words "equivalent to" to bring in more transparency in levy of penalties.

26.6.2 The Committee after examining the suggestions and the responses
thereto of the Ministry, are of the opinion that the marginal heading correction
reflects that Section 42 is substantively concerned with private placement of
securities, and the marginal heading is being aligned accordingly. Further,
section 42 already governs the private placement of all securities, not just
shares, and this removes a longstanding drafting inconsistency. Further, the
extension to "other schemes linked to share value" in order to recognise
instruments such as Restricted Stock Units and Stock Appreciation Rights is a
forward-looking change to accommodate emerging equity-linked instruments.
Further, the move to a fixed penalty formula in sub-section (10) again reflects
the broader shift away from open-ended, discretionary fines.

The Committee further note the concerns raised in respect of the lack of
requisite clarity on the scope and coverage of schemes under the expression
"or such other scheme linked to the value of the share capital of a company"
in section 26(2). The Committee in this regard, agree with the justification and
clarifications submitted by the Ministry that proposed amendment is intended
to enable companies to issue securities under schemes linked to the value of
the share capital of a Company, while the detailed framework governing such
schemes, including their applicability and eligibility criteria, is to be prescribed
separately under the Rules. The Committee acknowledges that the issue needs
to be adequately addressed, so that genuine employee incentive schemes, are
covered and appropriate safeguards prevent their misuse. The Committee
desire that the aforementioned concerns of the stakeholders seeking clarity on
the Schemes to be covered must be satisfactorily addressed by timely
formulation of clear and comprehensive rules, regulations and procedural
guidelines. The Committee after detailed scrutiny of the suggestions received
and responses submitted by the Ministry, accept the proposed provisions
under this clause, in entirety, without any modification.

                                               CLAUSE - 27

27. Clause 27 of the Bill seeks to insert new Section 43A after Section 43
of the Companies Act, 2013.

27.1 Provision proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026

After section 43 of the principal Act, the following section shall be inserted, namely:--

`43A. (1) A company, set up and incorporated in the International Financial Services
Centre, shall issue and maintain its share capital in a permitted foreign currency:

Provided that a company set up and incorporated in the International Financial
Services Centre prior to the commencement of the Corporate Laws (Amendment)
Act, 2026 may convert its share capital from Indian rupee to a permitted foreign
currency within such period and in such manner, as may be specified by regulations
by the International Financial Services Centres Authority, in consultation with the
Central Government:

Provided further that a company referred to in the first proviso shall not be permitted,
after the commencement of the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026, to issue
any share capital without converting its share capital into a permitted foreign
currency.

(2) A company referred to in sub-section (1), maintaining its share capital in a
permitted foreign currency shall prepare and maintain its books of account, and other
relevant books and papers, financial statements and all other records in the
permitted foreign currency:

Provided that if the International Financial Services Centres Authority permits, such
company may present such books of account and other relevant books and papers,
financial statements and other records in Indian rupee.

(3) The Central Government may, in such manner as may be prescribed, require that
a company referred to in sub-section (1) shall use permitted foreign currency for the
purpose of filing, submitting or delivering any documents under section 398.

(4) Every company referred to in sub-section (1) shall pay fees, fines and penalties
under this Act and the rules made thereunder in Indian rupees.

(5) In this section, the expressions--
                                                      199
(a) "International Financial Services Centre" shall have the same meaning as
assigned to it under clause (g) of sub-section (1) of section 3 of the International
Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019;

(b) "International Financial Services Centres Authority" shall have the same meaning
as assigned to it under clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 3 of the International
Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019; and

(c) "permitted foreign currency" means a currency which may be specified by the
International Financial Services Centres Authority in consultation with the Central
Government.'.

27.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013)

New Section being Inserted after section 43 of the Principal Act.

27.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"This clause proposes a new section 43A to facilitate IFSC companies by allowing
the issue and maintenance of share capital in a foreign currency permitted by IFSCA.
It also provides a framework for existing companies to transition from Indian rupees
to such foreign currency and enables maintenance of books of account and financial
statements in that currency. This part provides definitional clarity by incorporating
definition references to the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act,
2019."

27.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

(i) "The provision enables alignment with the needs of IFSC entities, the mandatory
conversion of existing share capital and restriction on further issuance until such
conversion may pose practical challenges. It is suggested that Detailed transitional
and operational guidelines may be prescribed by the Government for conversion of
existing share capital into foreign currency, including timelines, methodology,
compliance requirements, and conditions for issuance of further share capital. In the
absence of clear procedures, companies may face difficulties in valuation, exchange
rate application, regulatory approvals, and compliance. Well defined guidelines would
facilitate smooth transition, reduce ambiguity, and ensure effective implementation."

(ii) "Ensure appropriate coordination between the provisions of Section 43A and
valuation requirements under Section 247. Since IFSC entities operate in a distinct

                                                      200
international financial environment, seamless interaction between foreign-currency
share capital provisions and valuation requirements would facilitate global
investment and reduce regulatory uncertainty."

(iii) " Retain the IFSC provisions and the new SEBI/IFSCA trust-to-LLP conversion
routes, which allow IFSC companies to maintain their capital, books, and filings
entirely in a permitted foreign currency. However, because implementing these
routes involves regulatory overlap among the MCA, IFSCA, SEBI, CBDT, and the
RBI, it is recommended that all related rules be carefully coordinated. The guidelines
governing foreign currency filings, conversion mechanics, and tax reporting be
finalized together in consultation with industry participants. Ultimately, stakeholders
emphasize that this comprehensive, unified framework must be published before the
provisions officially come into force to ensure a smooth transition. Propose for
extending the conversion period for existing IFSC companies/LLPs to a minimum of
three years with an explicit tax-neutrality/stamp-duty exemption, and permitting
genuinely India-facing IFSC entities to opt out of the mandatory foreign-currency
requirement, noting that DIFC/ADGM impose no such currency mandate."

(iv) " Extend the conversion period for existing IFSC companies/LLPs to a minimum
of three years with an explicit tax-neutrality/stamp-duty exemption, and permitting
genuinely India-facing IFSC entities to opt out of the mandatory foreign-currency
requirement, noting that DIFC/ADGM impose no such currency mandate."

(v) " Indian law does not recognise the Simple Agreement for Future Equity( SAFE)
instrument used internationally for early-stage funding, forcing startups into time-
consuming Shareholder Agreements/CCPS structures requiring upfront valuation
(commonly taking around 10 months versus 24-48 hours abroad). A new Section
43A is proposed recognising SAFE as a distinct contractual instrument that converts
compulsorily into equity on a qualifying event (priced round, liquidity event, or an
outer date of not more than 10 years), carries no right of repayment or interest, with
the conversion price fixed at conversion by a registered valuer, issued by private
placement to identified investors, and ranking as an equity-linked instrument on
liquidation (after creditors but before shareholders). A consequential amendment to
Section 53 is also proposed to ensure such conversions are not void as an issue at a
discount."

(vi) " Need for clarity on the treatment of subsequent issuances of shares and the
related regulatory and tax implications under the proposed framework. For instance,
the issuance of ESOPs which also carries tax implications would require a clearly
defined framework for both Indian and foreign currency issuances. Similarly, a
structure framework would be needed for the conversion of debt into equity, as
evolving business requirements may necessitate such conversions, particularly when
the original debt and the resulting equity are denominated in different currencies. The
proposed framework introduces flexibility in the denomination of share capital and
related transactions. Clarity on subsequent issuances and conversions would reduce
interpretational issues, facilitate compliance and provide certainty to companies,
investors and other stakeholders."

                                                      201
(vii) Insertion of a third and fourth proviso to proposed Section 43A (1) as stated
below:

" Provided also that no such conversion shall be given effect to except in accordance
with a valuation determined by a registered valuer under Chapter XVII, and the
company shall give notice of the proposed conversion, together with such valuation,
to its shareholders in such manner as may be prescribed: Provided also that any
shareholder objecting to the valuation may, within thirty days of such notice, apply to
the Tribunal, and the Tribunal may, after hearing the company and the objecting
shareholders, confirm, modify, or direct redetermination of the valuation, and the
conversion shall be given effect to in accordance with the valuation as so confirmed,
modified, or redetermined." The following may be added in clause 4 of the proposed
section 43A:

"Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, for the purposes of any
recovery, enforcement, or insolvency proceeding under any other law for the time
being in force, the value of share capital issued or maintained in a permitted foreign
currency under this section shall be calculated in Indian rupees at such rate of
exchange and as on such date as may be prescribed.

While mandated conversion is a welcome step, a valuation-fairness check may be
inserted. This will ensure shareholder protection by mandating valuation by an
independent registered valuer with an option to object the conversion rate before the
Tribunal. Also, proposed section 43A is silent on how the capital must be valued in
case of the IFSC entering recovery or insolvency proceedings. While the 2026 bill
cannot amend laws such as SARFAESI, 2002; RDBI, 1993 and IBC 2016; it may be
worthwhile to fix a prescribed rupee conversion mechanism so that the
corresponding enforcement bodies do not develop ad hoc methodologies on
exchange rate."

(viii) "Provision to draw balance sheet in foreign currency and not in INR will not be
appropriate for non-financial entities located in the IFSC or entities not regulated by
IFSCA. It is suggested that such a provision should be only for financial institutions in
the IFSC and regulated by IFSCA. While financial institutions in IFSC and regulated
by IFSCA are treated as persons resident outside India, other non-financial entities in
IFSC or entities not regulated by IFSCA are persons resident in India, under FEMA
1999."

(ix) "Auditing, scrutiny, investigation etc. would become difficult for Income-tax and
all other regulatory agencies, therefore, cautioned that the freedom to prepare books
in foreign currency may be misused. The books may be required to be maintained in
permitted foreign currency as well as in Indian rupee. "

(x) "Permit issuance of tokenised shares and blockchain-based cap tables
recognised under IFSCA regulations was the proposal of yet another stakeholder."

                                                      202
27.5 Examination by the Committee:

27.5.1 The Ministry on the suggestion regarding the operational and transitional
concerns regarding conversion of existing share capital into foreign currency under
section 43A, submitted that:

"The operational and transitional concerns raised are noted and would be taken into
consideration during the Rule-making process. Hence, the provision in the Corporate
Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

27.5.2 The Ministry regarding the appropriate coordination between the provisions of
Section 43A and Section 247, submitted that:

"The suggestion is in the nature of smoothing out implementation and coordination
between the International Financial Services Authority and the appointment of
registered valuers under Section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013. It may be
addressed without any amendments to the proposed provision under the
Amendment Bill, through clarifications and subordinate legislation, if required."

27.5.3 Suggestion is agreeing to the proposed amendment. LLP Act has an
established mechanism of conversion of other entities into LLP, which is presently
provided in Second to Fourth Schedule. Thus, the conversion mechanism is well laid
out which ensures that the existing liabilities and covenants are protected and the
converted entity is able to run its business in a seamless manner. As such the
threshold for investor consent has been reviewed and it is proposed to based on
value terms.

27.5.4 Regarding the proposal for extending the conversion period for existing IFSC
companies/LLPs a minimum of three years with an explicit tax-neutrality/stamp-duty
exemption, and permitting genuinely India-facing IFSC entities to opt out of the
mandatory foreign-currency requirement, the Ministry assured that suggestion would
be considered while framing of regulations by IFSCA.

27.5.5 The Ministry in connection with the suggestion to recognise the SAFE
instrument used internationally for early-stage funding, forcing startups into time-
consuming Shareholder Agreements/CCPS structures requiring upfront valuation,
submitted that it will examine the suggestion in consultation with relevant
stakeholders.

27.5.6 The Ministry with reference to suggestion seeking clarity on the treatment of
subsequent issuances of shares and the related regulatory and tax implications
under the proposed framework submitted that the proposed section 43A(1) clearly

                                                      203
provides for conversion and issuance of share capital into permitted foreign currency.
Matters relating to specific transactions, including ESOPs, conversion of debt into
equity, and the applicable regulatory, accounting and tax implications, are governed
by the relevant legal and regulatory framework and may be addressed, where
required, under applicable subordinate legislation. Therefore, it may not be required
to incorporate a transaction specific provision in section 43A. Hence, the provision
in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change.

27.5.7 As regards the proposal for Inserting third and fourth proviso to proposed

Section 43A (1) the Ministry gave following response:

"The proposed section 43A is intended to provide an enabling framework for the
issuance and maintenance of share capital in a permitted foreign currency by
companies incorporated in the IFSC. The manner and timeline for conversion will be
specified by IFSCA. Matters relating to recovery, enforcement, and insolvency
proceedings are governed under their respective statutory frameworks. Hence, the
provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change."

27.5.8 Regarding the Provision disapproving drawing balance sheet in foreign
currency and not in INR, the Ministry responded that the proposed provision is
intended to facilitate business operations in IFSCs by enabling eligible companies to
prepare financial statements in a permitted foreign currency. Restricting the benefit
only to financial institutions regulated by IFSCA would narrow the scope of the reform
and undermine its objective.

27.5.9.  In respect of suggestion pointing towards downsides of preparing

books in foreign currency, the Ministry, stated that the proposed provision does not

prevent regulatory authorities from carrying out audit, scrutiny or investigation.

Requiring companies to maintain books of account in both foreign currency and

Indian rupees would increase the compliance burden and defeat the objective of

facilitating business operations in IFSCs. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws

(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change.

27.5.10. The Ministry submitted that the permission for issuance of tokenised
shares and blockchain-based cap tables recognised under IFSCA regulations would
be regulated by IFSCA. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment)
Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change.

27.5.11. The Ministry in respect of the scope and ambit of the rule making
powers under clause 27, submitted the following response:

                                                      204
"It proposes to prescribe the manner in which a Specified International Financial
Services Centre LLP shall use permitted foreign currency. These provisions
demonstrate that the delegation is directed at procedural flexibility. The legislature
has already determined that such modes are permissible; the executive is merely
tasked with specifying how they are to be operationalised. Given the rapidly evolving
nature of corporate governance practices, such delegation is not only permissible but
necessary to account for evolving practices."

27.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

27.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 27 of the Bill seeks to insert new
section 43A in the Companies Act to provide for the requirements in respect of
issue and maintenance of share capital, preparation and maintenance of books
of account, filing, submitting or delivering documents by companies set up
and incorporated in the IFSC jurisdiction in a permitted foreign currency. The
`Notes on Clauses' of the Ministry informs that presently; the Companies Act
does not include specific provisions to enable companies to prepare accounts
or financial statements in foreign currencies. Therefore, considering the nature
of companies set up in IFSC jurisdiction, new section 43A has been proposed.
The Committee observe that it provides a framework for existing companies to
transition from Indian rupees to such foreign currency enabling maintenance
of books of account and financial statements in that currency and provides
definitional clarity by incorporating definition references to the International
Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019.

The Committee observe that this is a substantial and enabling structural
change for IFSC incorporated companies and responds to the practical
difficulty for companies operating in the IFSC whose business, investor base,
and functional currency is foreign-currency-denominated were nonetheless
required to maintain share capital and records in Indian rupees, creating
currency-mismatch. Therefore, upon examination and after threadbare
analysis of the views of the Ministry and stakeholders, the Committee are of
the considered view that the amendment proposed in Clause 27 is a forward
looking provision to bring the companies-law treatment of IFSC entities into
closer alignment with international financial centre practice and address a

                                                      205
practical difficulty faced by companies operating in the IFSC, that would help
promoting the ease of doing Business. Therefore, the Committee concurs with
the justifications of the Ministry and accept the Clause 27 as proposed without
any modification.

28.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment expands section 62(1)(b) to cover schemes other than ESOPs that
are linked to the value of a company's share capital, to align with evolving forms of
employee compensation. It will help in recognising schemes such as Restricted
Stock Units (RSUs) and Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs), in addition to Employee
Stock Option Plans (ESOPs), by including schemes linked to the value of the share
capital of a company, thereby providing flexibility in structuring executive
compensation."

28.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

                                                      207
(i) " Since 62(1)(b) deals with the issue of shares, Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs)
entitle employees to a bonus equal to the increase in the company's stock price over
a pre-determined period. Cash-Settled SARs (where no shares are issued) should
remain outside the purview of Section 62. The proposed amendment recognizes
instruments such as Restricted Stock Units and Stock Appreciation Rights, in
addition to Employee Stock Option Plans, as executive compensation to be issued
with approval of shareholders."

(ii) "The phrase "scheme linked to the value of share capital" (and "value of share
capital") be defined/clarified to exclude any scheme that does not involve issuance of
equity shares. Accordingly, limit special resolution and compliance requirements to
schemes involving actual issuance of shares - specifically exclude (i) value-linked
schemes with no shares (e.g. phantom stock) and (ii) schemes involving transfer (not
issuance) of shares."

(iii) "The Committee Report has deliberated on inclusion of RSUs and SARs to be
recognized under the Companies Act through enabling provisions however, there are
certain other shared based employee benefits such as ESPS and GEBS which is
provided for under SBEB &SE Regulations, that should also be regulated under the
Companies Act and Rule 12 of the Share Capital and Debenture Rules. Therefore, to
ensure that the Companies Act and the Rules are aligned with the SBEB & SE
Regulations, the Company Law Committee, 2022 ("CLC") should consider amending
Section 62(1)(b) of the Companies Act and Rule 12 of the Share Capital and
Debenture Rules.

Section 62(1)(b) of the Companies Act may accordingly be amended in the following
way:

b) to employees under a scheme of employees' share based schemes stock option,
subject to special resolution passed by company and subject to such conditions as
maybe prescribed; or

Rule 12 of the Share Capital and Debenture Rules may accordingly be amended in
the following way:

1. Employee stock options ("ESOPs") to include stock appreciation rights ("SARs"),
restricted stock units ("RSUs") and other share based employee benefits such as
employee stock purchase schemes ("ESPS"), general employees benefit schemes
("GEBS"), etc except sweat equity shares. Clarificatory language as mentioned

                                                      208

28.5 Examination by the Committee:

28.5.1 The Ministry in respect of keeping Cash-Settled SARs (where no shares are
issued) outside purview of Section 62, submitted that:-

"The proposed amendment to section 62(1)(b) an enabling provision intended to
expand the category of employee compensation schemes. The specific schemes
covered by the provision, and the conditions governing their implementation, may be
appropriately prescribed under the Rules. Therefore, any clarification regarding the

                                                      211
applicability of section 62(1)(b) to cash-settled Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs) or
other schemes that do not involve the issue of shares may therefore be dealt with
through the Rules. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,
2026 may be retained without any change."

28.5.2 Regarding the scope and coverage of schemes `linked to the value of share
capital' of the company, the Ministry submitted:

"This suggestion seeks clarification regarding the scope and coverage of schemes
linked to the value of share capital of the company. The proposed amendment is
intended to enable companies to issue securities under schemes linked to the value
of the share capital of a company, while the detailed framework governing such
schemes, including their applicability and eligibility criteria, is to be prescribed
separately. The suggestion is duly noted. It will be addressed in the relevant rules.
Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained
without any change."

28.5.3 The Ministry in respect of the specific schemes covered by the provision, and
the conditions governing their implementation, submitted following response:

"The proposed amendment covers the suggestion. The proposed amendment to
section 62(1)(b) an enabling provision intended to expand the category of employee
compensation schemes. The specific schemes covered by the provision, and the
conditions governing their implementation, may be appropriately prescribed under
the Rules. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may
be retained without any change."

28.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

28.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 28 of the Bill seeks to amend clause (b)
of sub-section (1) of section 62 of the Companies Act to include the words "or
under such other scheme linked to the value of the share capital of the
company", after the words "under a scheme of employees' stock option", in
order to recognise instruments such as Restricted Stock Units and Stock
Appreciation Rights, in addition to Employee Stock Option Plans, as executive
compensation to be issued with approval of shareholders. The explanation to
clauses provides that amendment expands section 62(1)(b) to cover schemes
other than ESOPs that are linked to the value of a company's share capital, to

                                                      212
align with evolving forms of employee compensation. It will help in
recognising schemes such as Restricted Stock Units (RSUs) and Stock
Appreciation Rights (SARs), in addition to Employee Stock Option Plans
(ESOPs), by including schemes linked to the value of the share capital of a
company, thereby providing flexibility in structuring executive compensation.
The Committee take note of the Ministry's clarification that the proposed
amendment to section 62(1)(b) is an enabling provision intended to expand the
category of employee compensation schemes and the specific schemes
covered by the provision, and the conditions governing their implementation,
may be appropriately prescribed under the Rules. Upon examination and after
considering the views of the Ministry and stakeholders, the Committee
observe that the amendments proposed in Clause 28 are necessary as it gives
companies a clearer statutory basis to design and implement equity-value-
linked incentive plans beyond conventional ESOPs. Therefore, the Committee
accept the Clause 28 as proposed without any modification.
