29.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment to section 68 seeks to provide flexibility in buy-back offers for such
class or classes of companies as may be prescribed. It enables a higher limit for buy-
back (up to such percentage of paid-up capital and free reserves as may be
prescribed) and permits an additional buy-back offer within a year, subject to a
minimum gap of six months between two offers.

The amendment to Section 68(5) seeks to include securities issued under schemes
linked to the value of the share capital of a company, in line with similar amendments
to section 62.

Under Section 68(6), the omission of the requirement for verification of the
declaration of solvency by affidavit is provided for ease of compliance.

The amendment under Section 68(8) seeks to include securities issued under
schemes linked to the value of the share capital of a company, in line with similar
amendments to section 62.

                                                      217
The amendment to Section 68(11) replaces the existing fine-based punishment with
a penalty framework. The amendment is part of broader decriminalisation exercise
under the bill. Further, the expansion of the definition of "specified securities" aligns
the provision with amendments to section 62."

29.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

(i) "(a) limits of buy back in case of listed companies should be as specified by
SEBI. Similarly, the cooling off period between the two buyback offers for listed
companies should also be specified by SEBI; (b) Provided further that in case of a
listed company, the limits of buy-back referred to in clause (c) shall be as specified
by the Securities and Exchange Board of India; (c) Provided further that in case of a
listed company, the cooling-off period between two buy-back offers referred to in
clause (g), shall be as specified by the Securities and Exchange Board of India;"

(ii) "Optionality to undertake more than one buyback offer may be provided to all
companies meeting the debt-equity ratio provided in section 68(2)(d) and not
restricted to only debt free companies. Accordingly, the Notes on clause 29 and
relevant Rules may be amended accordingly. Section 68(2)(d) of the Act mandates
companies to have a post buy-back debt: equity ratio of 2:1. If two buyback offers are
to be permitted within a period of one year, then the debt: equity ratio post the
second buyback offer may be retained at 2:1 as per provisions of section 68(2)(d).
Section 68 provides for enough safeguards protecting financial stability of companies
even if two buyback offers are made in a year. Essential criteria for providing multiple
buy-back offers should be that during a period of 12 months all buyback offers taken
together should not result in buyback offer of >10% of paid up capital and free
reserves with board approval (68(2)(b)) and offer of >25% of paid up capital and free
reserves with shareholders' approval (68(2)(c)). Multiple buy-back offers within a
period of one year would help following type of investors: a. Investors of infrequently
traded or delisted companies. b. Investors holding the physically held share
certificates."

(iii) "The limits up to which a company can buy back its shares needs clarity. On
one hand, Section 68 provides that a company can buy back its shares up to 25% of
its paid-up capital and free reserves. On the other hand, the proviso states that in
case of buy back of equity shares, the limit shall be reckoned as 25% of total paid-up
equity capital. It appears that for buy back of equity shares, there are two limits the
total amount of buy back (i.e., number of shares X amount to be paid per share)
should not exceed 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves, and the total number of
shares to be bought back should not exceed 25% of total paid-up equity capital.
Hence, it is suggested that these aspects should be amply clarified. For companies
following Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), there may be a possibility that a
preference share is classified under liability. There is ambiguity in how such limits
should then be applied and determined as paid up capital under Companies Act,
2013."

                                                      218
(iv) "SEBI Buy-back Regulations to remain primary."

(v) "Permission for buy-backs by start-ups, small companies, unlisted companies
and wholly-owned subsidiaries through a simplified and expedited process,
particularly where there are no secured creditors, by relaxing procedural
requirements if possible. The Committee may also consider prescribing differentiated
buy-back limits based on the company's leverage, solvency position, and financial
health, while retaining the mandatory Board declaration of solvency to safeguard the
interests of stakeholders. Further, the Committee should include an illustrative
example to clarify the operation of the proposed proviso permitting specified classes
of companies to undertake up to two buy-backs within a period of one year, subject
to a minimum interval of six months between the closure of the first buy-back and the
commencement of the second buy-back. The proposed approach will facilitate
efficient capital restructuring while safeguarding the interests of creditors and
shareholders. Retaining the mandatory Board declaration of solvency will provide
adequate safeguards without imposing unnecessary procedural or documentation
requirements. Further, the inclusion of an illustrative example will provide greater
clarity on the computation of the prescribed timelines, reduce interpretational
ambiguity, and facilitate the consistent implementation of the provision."

(vi) "The suggested provision is:

"Provided further that such class or classes of companies, as may be prescribed,
may make upto two offers of buy-back within a period of one year, subject to no offer
of buy-back being made earlier than a period of six months reckoned from the date
of the closure of the preceding offer of buyback."

                                                      OR

"Provided further that for such class or classes of companies, as may be prescribed
no offer of buy-back under this subsection shall be made within a period of six
months reckoned from the date of the closure of the preceding offer of buyback, if
any."

The proposed proviso appears to enable such class or classes of companies, as
maybe prescribed, to undertake up to two buy-backs within a period of one year by
reducing the cooling-off period between two buybacks from one year to six months.
However, the proposed proviso stipulates that the "second buy-back during the year"
shall not be made earlier than six months from the date of closure of the preceding
offer of buy-back. The reference to the "second buy-back during the year" may give
rise to interpretational ambiguity, as the period contemplate dunder the proviso isa
rolling period of one year reckoned from the date of closure of the preceding offer of
buy-back, rather than a fixed calendar year or financial year. Since the relevant one-
year period would shift with each successive buy-back, the identification of a
particular offer as the "second buyback during the year" may lead to uncertainty in

                                                      219
the application of the provision. The two proposed alternative suggestions aim to
address this ambiguity."

(vii) "Clarification is needed whether spillover of the first buy back offer is permitted
to the second offer without any approvals, or whether separate approvals will be
required for each buy back offer. Further whether the thresholds for buy back will
apply per financial year/per offer. While this proposal gives an option to undertake
two tranches of buy back in a year, it would be necessary to clarify applicability of the
threshold, meaning of `as well whether the unfulfilled buy back portion can be
undertaken without going through the approval process."

(viii) "Whether the enhanced buyback framework should extend to eligible growth-
stage private companies. This way early Angel Investors will get timely exit
increasing Investor confidence. Buy-backs provide an efficient partial liquidity
mechanism for early investors and employees without requiring a full secondary sale
process. Extending eligibility to growth-stage private companies would help Angel
Investors invest more in the start-ups ecosystem".

(ix) "Clause 29 allows the Government to set custom limits for specific companies
and permitting up to two buy-backs per year with a six-month gap. Two provisos may
be inserted under Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 - one under Section
68(2)(c) and another under Section 68(2)(g), stating that for listed companies, the
limits of buy-back and cooling-off periods between two buy-back offers shall be as
specified by SEBI, respectively.

Proposed revised draft clause:

In section 68 of the principal Act,--

(a) in sub-section (2),--

(i) in clause (c), for the proviso, the following provisos shall be substituted, namely:--

"Provided that in case of such class or classes of companies, as may be prescribed,
the buy-back may be up to such per cent. of aggregate of paid-up capital and free
reserves, as may be prescribed:

Provided further that in case of a listed company, the limits referred to in clause (c)
shall be as specified by the Securities and Exchange Board by making regulations in
this behalf;

...............
                                                      220
(ii) in clause (g), after the existing proviso, the following proviso shall be inserted,
namely:--

"Provided further that such class or classes of companies, as may be prescribed,
may make up to two offers of buy-backs within a period of one year reckoned from
the date of the closure of the preceding offer of buy-back, if any, if the second buy-
back during the year is not made earlier than six months from the date of closure of
the preceding offer for buy-back during the year.;

Provided further that in case of a listed company, the cooling-off period between two
buy-back offers referred to in clause (g), shall be as specified by the Securities and
Exchange Board by making regulations in this behalf;"

Listed companies have large number of public shareholders, and any buy-back by
such companies can significantly affect share prices, public shareholding, market
liquidity, and investor interests. Therefore, permissible buy-back limits and minimum
interval between two buy-backs may need to be revised from time to time in line with
changing market conditions. In terms of Section 68(2) (f) of the Companies Act,
2013, the buy-back of the shares or other specified securities listed on any
recognised stock exchange is in accordance with the regulations made by the
Securities and Exchange Board in this behalf. Since, SEBI is the regulator
responsible for overseeing the regulations with respect to listed companies and
protecting the interests of investors. Therefore, empowering SEBI to determine these
parameters would provide necessary flexibility to respond quickly to evolving market
conditions while ensuring adequate investor protection and orderly market
functioning."

(x) "Proposed amendments may be reviewed that the Companies Act should not
prescribe a statutory limit of two buy-back offers within a financial year. Instead, the
Act may continue to provide the enabling framework, while leaving it to the Board, in
coordination with SEBI, to determine the appropriate frequency and conditions for
buy-backs through rules and regulations. The proposed amendments to Section 68
introduce a more flexible and calibrated framework for buy-back of securities,
particularly for prescribed classes of financially sound companies. The proposed
enhancement of buy-back limits would provide greater flexibility in capital
management and facilitate efficient deployment of surplus capital. Further, the
extension of restrictions on buy-backs to schemes linked with the value of share
capital under Section 62(1)(b) ensures consistency in the regulatory treatment of
comparable capital-related transactions. The proposal to dispense with the
requirement of affidavit-based verification of the declaration of solvency would
simplify procedural compliance without diluting the underlying financial safeguards.
In addition, the proposed decriminalisation of certain contraventions relating to buy-
backs, by substituting civil penalties for criminal sanctions, reflects a balanced and
facilitative regulatory approach. It is also pertinent to note that the Securities and
Exchange Board of India (SEBI), at its Board meeting held on 19 June 2026,
approved the reintroduction of the open market buy-back mechanism through the
stock exchange route with effect from 1 August 2026. SEBI has further decided that

                                                      221
buy-backs through the stock exchange route shall be completed within 66 working
days from the opening of the offer. These measures are intended to make the buy-
back process more efficient, responsive and aligned with prevailing market
conditions. In light of the above regulatory developments, it is recommended that the
proposed proviso permitting prescribed classes of companies to undertake up to two
buy-back offers within a single financial year may be omitted, to greater operational
flexibility in capital restructuring by the prescribed classes of financially sound
companies."

(xi) "Flexibility of two buy-backs a year and removal of the affidavit requirement is
a welcome step, but cautions that repeated buy-backs (up to 25% of issued capital)
could reduce free float and increase price-manipulation risk. Therefore, capping each
buy-back at 10% (maximum 20% in a year) and requiring shareholder approval
where cumulative buy-backs in a year exceed 10% of issued capital."

(xii) "Replace the fixed percentage buy-back cap with a principles-based
solvency/distributable-reserves test as the primary constraint (as in Delaware and
the UK), retaining a percentage cap only as a disclosure trigger. Recommends
extending the 'two buy-backs a year' relaxation to all listed companies with a clean
compliance/solvency record, rather than confining it to a class prescribed later by
rules."

(xiii) "The existing statutory limit for buybacks under Section 68 of the Companies
Act, 2013 should continue to be prescribed in the Act itself and should not be
delegated entirely to subordinate legislation. At the same time, if the policy objective
is to provide greater flexibility for specific classes of companies, such as companies
with low debt and strong balance sheets, an enabling provision may be considered
whereby the Act continues to prescribe the existing 25% limit as the baseline
threshold, while empowering the Central Government to prescribe a higher limit for
specified classes of companies through rules, subject to appropriate safeguards and
eligibility conditions. The buyback framework is a significant capital allocation and
shareholder return mechanism that directly impact investor expectations and
corporate financial planning. The existing limit of 25% is presently embedded in the
Act thereby providing certainty, stability and legislative oversight. Shifting the
determination of such limits entirely to rules may create regulatory uncertainty and
reduce predictability for companies and investors. This approach would preserve
certainty regarding the existing statutory framework while allowing targeted
relaxations for deserving class of companies without compromising investor
confidence or regulatory predictability."

(xiv) "The Committee Report has discussed Section 68 of the Companies Act and
sought clarity concerning the stage at which shares arising out of employee benefit
schemes by companies that grant stock options (such as ESOPs) can be bought
back. The Committee Report, where the Committee Report has deliberated
concerning the stages at which shares arising out of employee benefit schemes can
be bought back and have recommended that the Explanation at the end of Section
68 should be amended and the words "which have been exercised" may be inserted

                                                      222
after the words "stock option", as the various conditions for a buyback cannot be
satisfied if options are being bought back are agreed upon. Further, to ensure that
companies have the flexibility to settle employee stock options for cash, through a
private contractual arrangement, without requiring to go through the buyback
process, and the requirements of Section 68 of the Companies Act is restricted to
securities in the form of shares or debentures, the CLC should consider inserting the
words "which have been exercised" after the words "stock option" from Explanation I
to Section 68 of the Companies Act. Section 68 of the Companies Act may
accordingly be amended in the following way:

"[...]

Explanation I.--For the purposes of this section and section70, "specified securities"
includes employees' stock option which have been exercised or other securities as
may be notified by the Central Government from time to time."

(xv) "It is recommended that the clause be retained, subject to the clarification that
the rules prescribing an enhanced buy-back limit shall require that the enhanced limit
be exercised only pursuant to a special resolution and upon a solvency certification
by the auditor. Buy-back flexibility is a genuine capital-management reform, long
sought for cash-rich unlisted companies and consistent with the J.J. Irani philosophy
of enabling capital reorganisation with creditor safeguards. Because buy-back
directly implicates creditor protection, tying any enhanced percentage to shareholder
special resolution and solvency assurance preserves the balance of section 68 while
allowing calibrated liberalisation through rules."

(xvi) "The significant buybacks will reduce the free float of the company especially
if instituted in close succession. The Companies Act, 2013 allows buybacks of up to
25% of issued capital which may significantly reduce the free float of a company
which increases the risk of price manipulation while also giving the promoters
additional control in voting matters. The Securities and Exchange Board of India
(SEBI) Buy-Back of Securities Regulations, 20181 and the Companies Act, 2013
require shareholder approval via a Special Resolution for buybacks of over 10% of
issued capital. Within the Asia Pacific region, this is similar to regulations in Australia
that require shareholder approval for a buyback of more than 10% of voting shares
over the prior 12 months. Given that the proposed amendment to Section 68 would
allow up to two buy-backs within a single financial year, we recommend careful
monitoring on the extent of the permitted buy-backs especially if there could be a
second buyback in the same financial year and then repeated again after another six
months in the next financial year. It is recommended that each buyback instituted
should be for up to 10%, i.e. a maximum of 20% in a financial year, and that
shareholder approval should be required if cumulative buy-backs in a single financial
year would be over 10% of issued capital."

(xvii) "Define "scheme linked to the value of share capital" (including "value of share
capital"), limit buyback restrictions to employee schemes involving actual share

                                                      223
issuance and clarify that the 25% capital-plus-reserves limit is a minimum threshold,
with the Government empowered to prescribe higher limits or exemptions for
specified classes of companies."

29.5 Examination by the Committee:

29.5.1 The Ministry in respect of specifying the limits of buy back in case of listed
companies by SEBI, submitted that:

"At present, the proposed amendment discusses buy-back provisions for all
companies. Specific caveats for a class or classes of companies will be considered
at the rule-making stage. While SEBI is the sectoral regulator for listed companies,
the principal framework governing buy-backs is contained in Section 68 of the
Companies Act, 2013, which applies uniformly to all companies. Prescribing different
buy-back limits and cooling-off periods for listed companies through SEBI regulations
may lead to fragmentation of the statutory framework and reduce legislative
uniformity. Matters such as the permissible extent of buy-back and the minimum
interval between buy-back offers are fundamental aspects of the statutory regime
and are more appropriately prescribed under the Companies Act and the rules made
thereunder. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may
be retained without any change."

29.5.2 The Ministry in respect of optionality to undertake more than one buyback
offer, submitted that:

"Clause 29 of the Amendment Bill enables higher buy-back limits and an additional
buyback offer in a year only for "prescribed classes of companies," with the actual
eligibility criteria to be notified through rules rather than fixed in the Act itself.
Accordingly, the suggestion does not require any amendment to the Companies Act,
2013 and will be considered, if required, at the rule-making stage. Hence, the
provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change."

29.5.3 The Ministry in regard to specifying the Limits up to which a company can buy
back its own shares submitted that:-

"The suggestion has been accepted. Accordingly, the relevant provision will be
amended to provide the necessary clarification regarding the limits applicable to buy-
back of shares."

                                                      224
29.5.4 Regarding the suggestion that SEBI Buy-back Regulations to remain
primary, the Ministry has stated:

"The amendments are enabling provisions empowering the Central Government to
prescribe different buy-back limits and frequency for specified classes of companies.
These have been proposed in consultation with SEBI. The proposed amendments
are enabling provisions intended to provide flexibility for such class or classes of
companies as may be prescribed. The existing requirement under section 68(2)(f)
that buy-backs of listed securities be undertaken in accordance with the applicable
SEBI regulations remains unchanged. Therefore, the provisions do not dilute the
regulatory framework applicable to listed companies under the SEBI Act and
regulations made thereunder. The Companies Act and the SEBI regulatory
framework operate harmoniously within their respective statutory domains. Hence,
the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without
any change."

29.5.5 With regard to the suggestion to simplify and relax buy-back procedures for
start-ups, small companies, unlisted companies, and wholly-owned subsidiaries, the
Ministry has submitted:

"The proposed amendments to section 68 are enabling in nature and empower the
Central Government to prescribe, through rules, the class or classes of companies
eligible for enhanced buy-back limits and multiple buy-backs within a year, along with
the applicable conditions. Differentiated buy-back limits based on the company's
leverage, solvency position, and financial health - not acceptable as upper limit
provide flexibility to companies to undertake buy-back with varying percentage of
buy-back. Accordingly, the suggestions relating to simplified procedural requirements
for specified categories of companies, differentiated buy-back limits based on
objective financial parameters, and the inclusion of appropriate clarificatory guidance
to facilitate consistent implementation of the provision, pertain to matters of
implementation and may be examined while framing the relevant Rules. Hence, the
provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change."

29.5.6 In the context of drafting the proviso that permits certain classes of
companies to undertake up to two buy-backs within a year, with a reduced cooling-off
period of six months, the Ministry has submitted:

"The proposed proviso is intended to permit such class or classes of companies, as
may be prescribed, to undertake up to two buy-backs within a rolling period of one
year, subject to a minimum interval of six months between successive buy-backs."

                                                      225
29.5.7 The Ministry in respect of the clarification needed on the mechanics of
multiple buy-back offers within a year, has stated as follows:

"The proposed amendment is intended to provide flexibility to specified classes of
companies by permitting up to two buy-back offers within a period of one year,
subject to the prescribed conditions. The suggestions regarding the approval
requirements for successive buy-back offers, the applicability of the prescribed
thresholds, and the treatment of any unutilised portion of an approved buy-back
pertain to the operational framework for implementation of the provision. These
aspects will be examined while framing the relevant Rules to ensure clarity and
consistent implementation. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment)
Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

29.5.8 The Ministry with regard to applicability of enhanced buyback framework
responded that proposed amendment is intended for listed companies. Hence, the
provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change.

29.5.9 In respect of the suggestion recommending insertion of two under Section
68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 one under Section 68(2)(c) and another under
Section 68(2)(g), the Ministry stated as under:

"The provisions relating to the eligibility, limits and conditions for buy-backs form part
of the substantive framework under section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, which
governs a company's power to undertake a buy-back. The proposed amendments
are intended to modify this framework and, accordingly, it is appropriate that the
prescription of the applicable classes of companies, limits and conditions continues
under the rule-making framework of the Companies Act. The existing SEBI regulatory
framework governing the manner in which listed companies undertake buy-backs,
including market conduct and investor protection requirements, remains unaffected.
Accordingly, it is not considered necessary to provide separate rule-making powers
to SEBI in respect of the matters proposed under section 68. Hence, the provision in
the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

29.5.10 On the proposal seeking review of the amendments for prescribing a
statutory limit of two buy-back offers within a financial year, the Ministry submitted
that:

"The proposed amendment seeks to modify the substantive statutory framework
under section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, by permitting such class or classes of
companies, as may be prescribed, to undertake up to two buy-back offers within a
period of one year, subject to the conditions specified therein. Accordingly, the

                                                      226
frequency of permissible buy-backs forms part of the statutory framework under the
Act and it is not proposed to leave this aspect entirely to subordinate legislation.
Further, the recent regulatory changes introduced by SEBI in relation to the buy-back
framework do not necessitate any modification to the proposed amendment, which
operates within the framework of section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013. Hence, the
provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change."

29.5.11. Suggestion, recommending capping each buy-back at 10% and
requiring shareholder approval where cumulative buy-backs in a year exceed 10% of
issued capital was responded to by the Ministry as stated below:

"The proposed amendments are intended to provide an enabling framework under
which the Central Government may prescribe the class or classes of companies
eligible for the buy-back limits and multiple buy-backs within a year, along with the
applicable conditions. The suggestion to prescribe a statutory limit of 10 per cent for
each buy-back, an aggregate annual limit of 20 per cent, and an additional
shareholder approval requirement based on cumulative buy-backs during the year
would alter the statutory framework proposed under the amendment, and therefore,
may not be appropriate. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment)
Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

29.5.12 As regards the suggestion recommending extension of the 'two buy-backs
a year' relaxation to all listed companies with a clean compliance/solvency record,
the Ministry submitted that:

"The suggestion to replace the statutory buy-back limits under section 68 with a
principles-based solvency and distributable reserves test would substantially alter the
existing statutory framework governing buy-backs under the Companies Act, 2013.
Further, the proposed amendment is intended to operate as an enabling provision,
empowering the Central Government to prescribe, through rules, the class or classes
of companies eligible for enhanced buy-back limits and multiple buy-backs within a
year, along with the applicable conditions. Accordingly, it is not proposed to specify
eligible classes of companies in the Act itself. Hence, the provision in the Corporate
Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

29.5.13 The Ministry in response to the suggestion recommending existing statutory
limit for buybacks under Section 68 to continue to be prescribed in the Act itself and
not to be delegated entirely to subordinate legislation, provided the following :

      "The amendment proposes to empower Central Government to prescribe the
class or classes of companies, and the percentage of the aggregate of paid-up

                                                      227
capital and free reserves, up to which a buyback may be made by such prescribed
class or classes of companies. The financial thresholds are subject to periodic
revision based on inflation, administrative cost, and market conditions. Embedding
these in primary legislation would render the statute inflexible and quickly outdated.
Further, the policy decision to impose a threshold is contained in the statute itself;
only the quantum of its determination is delegated. Hence, the provision in the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

29.5.14 In response to the suggestion for including an explanation on "specified

change.

29.5.15 Suggestion for exercising enhanced limit only pursuant to a special

"This would be appropriately dealt with during framing of subordinate legislation. At

Specific caveats for a class or classes of companies will be considered at the rule-
making stage."

29.5.16 The statutory ceiling of 25% and the requirement of shareholder approval
for buy-backs above 10% are considered sufficient safeguards. The same
safeguards are applicable to each and every buyback. The proposal would lead to
overall reduction in the statutory ceiling and may force many companies to have 2
buy-backs in a year, even when 1 buy-back would suffice. Hence, the provision in the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change.

29.5.17 In regard to defining the expression "scheme linked to the value of share

29.5.18 When asked to clarify the applicability of the clause 29 and import of `such

                                                      228
     "Sir, in the entire Companies Act -- whether it is to do with exemptions or to do
with provisions or applicability -- there are two aspects. We have moved away from
individual exemptions or exemptions to companies by name - let us say Section 8
Companies. We have moved to a concept of class of companies. So, by class of
companies, they share some common characteristics. It could be a class of
companies - listed companies or unlisted companies. It could be a class of
companies to do with public companies above a certain turnover. Take the example
of NFRA. We have certain class of companies which come under NFRA. It means
that all listed entities, all public companies, have a certain turnover. So, this concept
of class of companies is there as an omnibus thing in the Act to allow the Act to be
flexible to prescribe proportionate rules or regulations depending on the kind of
companies. So, as far as this purchasing the securities is concerned, this particular
provision has come on the request of SEBI. So, it is essentially meant for listed
companies. There are only 7,000 companies.

make up to two offers of buybacks within a single year. The use of "class or classes"
is a well established legislative device incorporate law, enabling dynamic calibration
without frequent statutory amendments. The essential policy, i.e., that differential
compliance may be warranted, is determined by the legislature; only the identification

would render the statute inflexible and quickly outdated. Further, the policy decision
to impose a threshold is contained in the statute itself; only the quantum of its
determination is delegated."

                                                      230
29.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

29.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 29 of the Bill seeks to amend Section
68 of the Principal Act in the following manner:

(i) In clause (c) of sub-section (2) of section 68 of the Companies Act to
provide that prescribed class or classes of companies may buy-back shares
up to such per cent of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves as
may be provided by rules.

(ii) To insert a proviso to clause (g) of sub-section (2) thereto to allow
prescribed class or classes of companies to make up to two offers of buy-
backs within a period of year in such a manner that the second buy-back
during the year is not made earlier than six months from the date of closure of
the preceding offer for buy-back during the year.

(iii) To amend clause (c) of sub-section (5) of section 68 of the Companies
Act, 2013 to include the words "or a scheme linked to the value of the share
capital of a company referred to in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 62"
after the words "sweat equity".

(iv) To omit words "and verified by an affidavit" in sub-section (6) so that
declaration of solvency to be filed for the purposes need not be in the form of
an affidavit.

(v) To convert the fine under sub-section (11) into penalties as the offence is
being decriminalised.

    The Committee note that Clause 29 of the Bill seeks to substantially amend
Section 68 of Company law 2013 to provide flexibility in buy-back offers for
such class or classes of companies as may be prescribed. Buy-back through
tender offers is an efficient way of returning surplus funds to shareholders and

                                                      231
it is proposed to allow prescribed class of companies to avail such
mechanism. The Committee find that these are enabling provisions allowing a
higher limit for buy-back permitting an additional buy-back offer within a year,
subject to a minimum gap of six months between two offers. The Committee
observe that eligible companies gain meaningfully greater flexibility in capital
management through additional buy-backs and, potentially, higher buy-back
ceilings.

         The Committee further note that under Section 68(6), the omission of the
requirement for verification of the declaration of solvency by affidavit is
provided for ease of compliance. Removing the affidavit requirement reduces
procedural cost. The amendment under Section 68(8) seeks to include
securities issued under schemes linked to the value of the share capital of a
company, in line with similar amendments to section 62. Further, the
amendment to Section 68(11) replaces the existing fine-based punishment with
a penalty framework as part of broader decriminalisation exercise under the
bill.

         The Committee also take note of the views of stakeholders received on
the proposed amendments. While some stakeholders have endorsed and
welcomed the amendments, the others have shared their apprehensions
about the possible impact of buy-backs by big listed companies on share
prices, market stability, among others. The Committee however, are of the
view that the advantages of having flexibility in buy-backs outweighs its
drawbacks.

29.6.2.  The Committee in this regard take cognizance of lack of requisite

clarity on the permissible buy-back limits of 25% on paid-up capital, free

reserves and on equity shares as the case may be. There is also need to

clarify the reckoning of year for determining two buy backs and the

computation of six months gap between the previous and following buy back.

The Committee therefore, recommend following modifications to clause (c) &

         232
(g) under section 68(2) to remove above referred inconsistencies. The revised

"In section 68 of the principal Act,--

       (a) in sub-section (2),--

       (i) in clause (c), for the proviso, the following provisos shall be

30. Clause 30 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 77of the Companies Act,
2013.

30.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

In section 77 of the principal Act, in sub-section (1), after the second proviso, the
following proviso shall be inserted, namely:--

`Provided also that for such class or classes of companies, as may be prescribed,
the period of "sixty days" referred to in clause (b) of the second proviso shall be read
as "one hundred and twenty days":'.

30.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013)

77. Duty to register charges, etc 77. (1) It shall be the duty of every company
creating a charge within or outside India, on its property or assets or any of its
undertakings, whether tangible or otherwise, and situated in or outside India, to
register the particulars of the charge signed by the company and the charge-holder
together with the instruments, if any, creating such charge in such form, on payment
of such fees and in such manner as may be prescribed, with the Registrar within
thirty days of its creation:

* * * * *

Provided also that any subsequent registration of a charge shall not prejudice any
right acquired in respect of any property before the charge is actually registered:

* * * * *

30.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"This amendment proposes to provide additional time for registration of charges
under section 77 for such class or classes of companies as may be prescribed for
ease of doing business."

30.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:
                                                      235
(i) "Extend the prescribed timeline from 120 days to 180 days. Alternatively, the
Committee may consider introducing a graded condonation mechanism whereby
delays beyond 120 days may be regularised by the ROC or the RD upon the
applicant demonstrating sufficient cause, without judicial proceedings. Considering
the practical challenges involved in obtaining lenders' approvals in some cases and
completing security documentation, the proposed approach will protect lenders'
security interests and prevent the inadvertent invalidation of charges due to
procedural delays. It will also promote timely compliance and improve the overall
efficiency of the charge registration process."

(ii) "Clause 30 proposes to increase the "further period" to register charges from 60
to 120 days, making the total time available for registration of charges by companies
to 180 days.

Suggestion: The time period as applicable (i.e., 120 days in total) under the existing
provisions under the Companies Act, 2013 may continue to apply on listed entities
and to be listed entities.

Proposed revised draft clause 30

In section 77 of the principal Act, in sub-section (1), after the second proviso, the
following proviso shall be inserted, namely:--

`Provided also that for such class or classes of companies, as may be prescribed,
the period of "sixty days" referred to in clause (b) of the second proviso shall be read
as "one hundred and twenty days", except in case of listed companies or those
companies which intend to get their securities listed on any recognised stock
exchange in India:'.

(i) As per Section 2(16), a charge means an interest or lien created on the property
or assets of a company (or any of its undertakings), and it includes a mortgage. (ii)
Section 77 requires registration of charge within 30 days by paying standard normal
fee to the Registrar of Companies (ROC), extendable by 30 more days with a late
fee, and another 60 days (120 days in total) with an ad-valorem fee. (iii) Once
registered, the charge becomes a public document. This prevents fraud and protects
the lender's interest. (iv) Clause 30 of the Bill proposes extending this final window of
"60 days" to "120 days" for prescribed class of companies, raising the maximum
timeline from 120 days to 180 days. (v) Any increase in timelines for registration of
charge may undermine transparency and investor safety, especially for `listed
entities' and during IPO evaluations for `to be listed entities'. (vi) Further, any such
extension could lead to public investments being made based on outdated data, and
therefore may have ramification to the interest of investors. (vii) Thus, the time period
as applicable (i.e., 120 days in total) under the existing provisions under the

                                                      236
Companies Act, 2013 may continue to apply on listed entities and to be listed
entities."

(iii) "Additional safeguards may be prescribed where delay in registration of
charges exceeds the existing period. Although extended timelines may ease
compliance, delayed registration may adversely affect lenders. Therefore,
Registration of Charges in favour of banks should be accorded priority and time-
bound processing."

(iv)  "The proposed amendment may be reviewed in line with the greater

transparency, improved credit discipline, and more efficient dissemination of

information in the public domain. Although extended timelines may ease compliance,

delayed registration may adversely affect lenders. Therefore, Registration of Charges

in favour of banks should be accorded priority and time-bound processing."

(v) "(a) It is suggested that the following change be carried out under Section 82(1)
of the Act:

"A company shall give information to the Registrar in the prescribed form, of the
payment or satisfaction in full of any charge registered under this Chapter within a
period of thirty ninety days from the date of such payment or satisfaction."

(b) It is also suggested that while a timeline may be prescribed for filings to ensure
compliance discipline, delayed registration or satisfaction should be permitted upon
payment of additional fees, as may be prescribed."

30.5 Examination by the Committee:

The corresponding replies of the Ministry to the suggestions of stakeholders are as
under:

30.5.1 "The Amendment Bill expressly amends Section 77 of the Companies Act,
2013 to provide for additional 120 days from the original 60 day extension for
registration of charges for certain class or classes of companies as may be
prescribed. This is intended for small companies. The provision in the Amendment
Bill therefore provides companies with the facility to regularise non-registration of
charges via the first and second provisos to Section 77, 2013 encapsulating the
second proposal for a graded condonation mechanism. The Central Government
maintains the ability to prescribe fees as deemed fit under the provisos, including ad
valorem fees to be charged by Registrar. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

                                                      237
30.5.2 "This suggestion seeks to retain the existing timeline for registration of
charges in respect of listed companies and companies proposing to list their
securities. Proposed amendment is intended for Small companies based on the
request from MSME associations supported by Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium
Enterprises. The suggestion is duly noted. It will be addressed in the relevant rules
as the amendment is applicable only for the class of companies as may be
prescribed by the Central Government. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

30.5.3 "Suggestion will be considered during framing of subordinate legislation.
The proposal to prioritise charges in favour of banks to ensure time-bound
processing would be considered at the rule making stage. Hence, the provision in the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

30.5.4 "The Amendment Bill provides an additional window of time to a certain
class or classes of companies as may be prescribed for registering charges that may
be created. As the amendment does not propose a blanket extension of the timeline,
the majority of companies may still be obligated to register charges within the 60
days period. The additional time has been intended for small companies which may
benefit from the relaxed compliance requirements under the Amendment Bill, further
promoting ease of business. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

30.5.5 "Provisions of section 82 already provides for delayed filing satisfaction of
charge with an additional fees. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

30.5.6 During the clause-by-clause deliberations on the Bill on 16.7.2026, the
Committee sought to know the consequences for Company withholding information
about the creation of charge, the Secretary, MCA clarified:

"Sir, there are two things for that. First of all, it is in the interest of the company to
show the charge and then it is very important on behalf of the person who is giving
the charge to insist         It is because tomorrow
when he goes to IBC, it helps. So, the responsibility comes more from the person
who is giving the loan rather than the person who is taking the loan. He would not
like to do it. But there are certain companies who would like to show good credit
record. So, they will show the ROC showing that they have got the charge and have
also satisfied the charge. So, it creates a record. "

                                                      238
30.5.7 During the Clause-by-Clause deliberations on 17.7.2026 the Committee
pointed out that if the legislative intent was to provide the relief to `Small Companies'
or Companies in category of such class or classes of companies, then why it does
not find specific mention in the provision, the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs
deposed the following:

",       ,            
           If the Committee feels, we will do
that.     ,         `  ' 
   ,             
 There are not the other big companies, because this is a very important
financial discipline.       ,       
        100       "

30.5.8 The Ministry in respect of `Rule framing powers' enshrined in the clause 30,
submitted that:

" It proposes to prescribe the class or classes of companies for which the period of
"sixty days" shall be read as "one hundred and twenty days". The use of "class or
classes" is a well established legislative device incorporate law, enabling dynamic
calibration without frequent statutory amendments. The essential policy, i.e., that
differential compliance may be warranted, is determined by the legislature; only the
identification and periodic revision of such classes is delegated."

30.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

30.6.1 The Committee note that clause 30 of the Bill seeks to insert proviso in
sub-section (1) of section 77 of the Companies Act to provide that for
prescribed class or classes of companies such as, small companies the period
of "sixty days" referred to in clause (b) of second proviso shall be replaced
with "one hundred and twenty days" so that such class or classes of
companies get 60 additional days for filing e-forms relating to the registration
of charges, in the interest of ease of compliances. The Committee take note
that the proposed amendment intends to provide additional time for
registration of charges under section 77 for class or classes of companies in

                                                      239
category of small companies which may benefit from the relaxed compliance
requirements for ease of doing business. The Committee, however, are of the
view that the use of class of companies in section instead of specific mention
of class intended to be benefitted, itself do not bring out clear legislative intent
to extend the relaxation to small companies or such or others in the category.
The Committee, therefore, while supporting the core objectives of the
proposed amendments, recommend that section 77 may be reworded and now
be read as given under:
"In section 77 of the principal Act, in sub-section (1), after the second proviso,
the following proviso shall be inserted, namely:--
`Provided also that for such class or classes of small companies, as may be
prescribed, the period of "sixty days" referred to in clause (b) of the second
proviso shall be read as "one hundred and twenty days.' "

                                               CLAUSE - 31

31. Clause 31 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 88 of the Companies Act,
2013.

31.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,2026

In section 88 of the principal Act, after sub-section (2), the following sub-section shall
be inserted, namely: --

"(2A) No notice of any trust, whether express, implied or constructive, shall be
entered in the register of members or debenture holders maintained under sub-
section (1).".

31.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013)

Section 88. Register of members, etc.--

(1) Every company shall keep and maintain the following registers in such form and
in such manner as may be prescribed, namely: --

(a) register of members indicating separately for each class of equity and preference
shares held by each member residing in or outside India;

(b) register of debenture-holders; and

(c) register of any other security holders.

(2) Every register maintained under sub-section (1) shall include an index of the
names included therein.

31.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"This clause proposes to amend section 88 to clarify that no notice of any trust shall
be entered in the register of members or debenture holders. Accordingly, the trustee
shall be recorded as the legal owner in the register, while the trust may be entered as
the beneficial owner as per the relevant provisions of the Act."

                                                      241
31.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

(i) "Clarify that, while the Companies Act, 2013 does not expressly prohibit the
recording of trusts in the register of members, it continues to recognise the long-
standing principle that a company acknowledges only the registered holder of
securities and not beneficial interests arising under trust arrangements. The
proposed clarification will prevent any misinterpretation that the beneficial ownership
reporting obligations have been diluted and will preserve transparency in the
ownership and control framework."

(ii) "A transitional provision may be inserted to clarify the treatment of notices of
trust that have already been entered in the register of members or debenture holders
prior to the commencement of the proposed amendment. The proposed insertion of
subsection(2A) prohibits the entry of notice of any trust, whether express, implied or
constructive, in the register of members or debenture holders. However, the
proposed amendment is silent on the treatment of notices of trust that may already
have been recorded in such registers before the amendment comes into force. In the
absence of a transitional provision, ambiguity may arise as to whether companies
are required to remove such existing entries or whether they may continue to remain
in the register notwithstanding the amendment. It is, therefore, suggested that a
transitional provision should be introduced to clarify the treatment of existing entries."

(iii) "The clause be retained, subject to the insertion of the following Explanation:
"Explanation. -Nothing in this sub-section shall affect the obligation to make
declarations of beneficial interest under section 89 or the obligations under section
90." Reinstating the 1956 Act rule protects companies from being drawn into disputes
between trustees and beneficiaries and gives certainty to the register- the trustee is
the member. The Explanation forecloses any argument that the provision dilutes the
beneficial-ownership transparency framework (sections 89-90), which operates on a
different plane."

(iv)     "Permit blockchain-based beneficial ownership registers recognised by

IFSCA."

31.5 Examination by the Committee:

31.5.1 The corresponding replies of the Ministry on the suggestions given above:

(i) "The amendments does not affect the beneficial ownership disclosure and
reporting framework under the Companies Act, 2013. Obligations relating to

                                                      242
disclosure of beneficial interest in shares under section 89 and disclosure of
significant beneficial ownership under section 90, together with the rules made
thereunder, continue to apply in full. Companies remain obligated to obtain, maintain
and file the prescribed declarations and records relating to beneficial ownership
wherever applicable."

(ii) "The Ministry accepted the suggestion for the inclusion of a mechanism by which
trusts already registered as members are struck from the register pursuant to the
amendment to Section 88 of the Companies Act, 2013."

(iii) "The Ministry in response to the suggestion stated that the proposed provision
only clarifies that notices of trusts shall not be entered in the register of members or
debenture holders. It does not affect the operation of sections 89 and 90 relating to
declarations of beneficial interest and significant beneficial ownership. Accordingly,
the suggested Explanation is not necessary. Hence, the provision in the Corporate
Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without change."

(iv) "The Ministry submitted that issue related with permitting blockchain-based
beneficial ownership registers recognised by IFSCA would be appropriately dealt, if
required, during framing of subordinate legislation."

31.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

31.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 31 of the Bill seeks to insert a new sub-
section (2A) in section 88 of the Companies Act to provide that no notice of
any Trust, whether express, implied, or constructive, shall be entered in the
register of members or debenture holders as maintained under sub-section (1)
of the said section. Accordingly, the trustee shall be recorded as the legal
owner in the register, while the trust may be entered as the beneficial owner as
per the relevant provisions of the Act. The Committee however, at the same
time, underscores that there is a need for clarity regarding the treatment of
notices of trust that have already been entered in the register of members or
debenture holders prior to the commencement of the proposed amendment. In
the absence of requisite clarity, uncertainty may persist whether the existing
entries to be removed or should they continue to remain in the register
notwithstanding the amendment. The Committee, therefore, while

                                                      243
acknowledging the need of procedural streamlining recommend for providing
a transitional period under which trusts already registered as members are
struck from the register pursuant to the amendment. Thus, after threadbare
analysis of the justification of the Ministry and stakeholder's submissions, the
Committee recommend that in section 88 of the principal Act, after sub-section
(2), the following sub-section shall be inserted, namely: -
"(2A) No notice of any trust, whether express, implied or constructive, shall be
entered in the register of members or debenture holders maintained under
sub-section (1):
Provided that every company, existing on or before the commencement of the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026, which is required to comply with the
provisions of this sub-section, shall make necessary changes in the entries in
the register referred to in sub-section (1) within a period of one year from the
date of such commencement.".
