132A(3) provides for a penalty for failure to furnish any document or return or any
other information under sub section (2). Same is of procedural in nature and hence
does not require different penalties for individual and firm."

41.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee

41.6.1.  The Committee take note that the amendment under Clause 41,

132A (1) seeks to insert a new section 132A to require auditors of specified

companies and bodies corporate to intimate details of his/ its registration with

ICAI to the NFRA. The requirement in respect of filing with NFRA and penalty

framework for non-compliance and misreporting have also been provided. The

Committee observe that suggestions were made regarding registration and

annual return-filing portal for auditor intimation to NFRA (s.132A) that is

interoperable with existing ICAI and MCA21/V3 portals, so auditors are not

required to separately re-file substantially the same registration particulars

with multiple authorities.

                            361
The Committee find that the Ministry has agreed that the Clause needs to be
modified to require only bodies corporate to file details of auditors and for
companies which are under the ambit of NFRA.

During examination the Committee also took note of the concerns expressed
by the stakeholders that the proposed amendments seek to significantly
expand NFRA's powers. Apprehensions were raised that the issuance of
directions under this provision may result in punitive consequences disguised
as directions. Consequently, it was suggested that the phrase `as may be
specified by regulations' be replaced with `as may be prescribed'.

Concurring with the above view, the Committee recommend that the provision
of 132A (1) be redrafted as under:

"(1) Every body corporate, other than a company as defined in clause (20) of
section 2, covered under sub-section (4) of section 132 shall, within fifteen
days of appointment of an auditor under sub-section (1) of section 139, inform
the National Financial Reporting Authority, the particulars of the auditor
appointed by such body corporate within such period, in such form and
manner and on payment of such fees payable to the said Authority as may be
prescribed."

In this regard the Committee further recommends that Ministry consider
creation of a National Single Window System (NSWS) for all regulatory
approvals across central, state, and local authorities, integrating all relevant
permissions into one digital platform. A single-window digital platform will cut
compliance requirements, ensure transparent governance, and fast-track
business growth and have a remarkable impact on ease of doing business
which is the primary objective behind the present and other legislations being
introduced by the Government.

41.6.2.  The Committee observe that the language of 132A (2) required

amendment so as to bring it in consonance with the redrafted version of

Section 132 A (1) above. The Committee therefore recommend that section 132

A (2) may now be read as under:

"(2) The auditors of companies or class of companies or bodies corporate
referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (4) of section 132, shall file such
documents or returns or information with the National Financial Reporting

                                                      362
Authority, in such form and manner, within such period, and on payment of
such fees, as may be prescribed."

41.6.3.  Further, the Committee take note of the suggestions concerning

rationalisation of the penalty amount(s) proposed under Clause 41, 132A (3).

The Committee observe that the Ministry has expressed agreement to

suggestion for rationalisation and reduction of penalty amounts. Therefore, the

Committee after consideration of the suggestion and the reply of the Ministry

desire that the penalty amounts be reduced and thus recommend that 132 A (3)

be amended as under:

"(3) A person, required to furnish any document or return or any other
information under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), who fails to furnish any
document or return or any other information, shall be liable to penalty of not
less than ten thousand rupees and in case of continuing failure with a further
penalty of one hundred rupees for each day during which such default
continues, subject to a maximum of five lakh rupees, if such person is an
auditor or an audit firm."

For 132 A (4) after (4)c,

"then, without prejudice to any other action which may be taken under any law
for the time being in force, such person shall be liable to a penalty of not less
than twenty thousand rupees, and in case of continuing failure with a further
penalty of two hundred rupees for each day during which such default
continues, subject to a maximum of ten lakh rupees, if such person is an
auditor or an audit firm."

41.6.4.  The Committee understand that Clause 41, 132 C seeks to insert a

new section 132C to empower the NFRA to issue directions to auditors in

public interest or in the interest of investors, creditors or other stakeholders,

along with a penalty framework for non-compliance.

The Committee note the suggestion to strengthen the provisions by
incorporating clear statutory safeguards. These include defining key terms like
"public interest," functionally separating investigation from adjudication, and
establishing objective criteria for exercising powers and imposing penalties.

                           363
The Committee also observe that the Ministry in its reply have stated that the
provision is part of the broader set of insertions to strengthen the NFRA, on
the lines of other regulators. Moreover, according to the Ministry, the
expression "public interest" is a well-established legislative expression and
has been used in several statutes. At the same time the Ministry has agreed
that Proposed Section 132C should be suitably modified to require NFRA to do
inquiry/review before issuing such directions.

Accordingly, in view of the above, after careful consideration of the Powers
being granted to NFRA, the suggestion to include safeguards and the reply of
the Ministry, the Committee recommend that the section 132 C be amended as
under:

"132C. (1) In exercise of its functions under this Act, where the National
Financial Reporting Authority is satisfied that it is necessary in public interest
or the interest of investors or creditors or other persons concerned, it may,
after making an enquiry, in the manner that is prescribed, give such directions
to auditors of companies, class of companies or bodies corporate referred to
in clause (a) of sub-section (4) of section 132, as it may consider appropriate."

41.6.5.  The Committee further observe the need to amend section 132C(2)

in order to rationalize the penalty framework on similar lines as the changes

being made in 132 A. Accordingly, the Committee recommend that under Sub

Clause 132 C, (2) the amount of penalty be reduced and section 132 C (2) be

amended as under:

"Section 132C(2) Whoever fails to comply with any direction given under sub-
section (1), shall be liable to a penalty of not less than twenty thousand
rupees, and in case of continuing failure with a further penalty of two hundred
rupees for each day during which such default continues, subject to a
maximum of ten lakh rupees, if such person is an auditor or an audit firm."

41.6.6. The Committee note that Clause 41 inserts a new section 132D to
provide a framework for inquiry, adjudication and imposition of penalties by
the NFRA, including powers to summon persons, enforce attendance, and
recover penalties, along with a provision for appeal to the Appellate Tribunal.
The Committee agree with the suggestion that the power to examine a person
on oath constitutes a standard enabling provision conferred upon independent
regulators within the domestic legislative framework and thus the same
deserves to be incorporated in section 132D (2). The Committee observe that

                                                      364
the Ministry accepts the suggestion and is of the view that the power to
examine a person on oath is a necessary corollary to the power to summon
and enforce attendance for the purpose of conducting an effective inquiry.
Similar powers are already available under the Companies Act, 2013, and are
also vested in other statutory authorities such as the Income Tax Authorities.
Thus, after careful consideration of the suggestion and reply of the Ministry
the Committee recommend that Clause 132 D (2) may be reframed as under:

"(2) While holding an inquiry, the National Financial Reporting Authority shall
have power to summon and enforce the attendance of any person acquainted
with the facts and circumstances of the case to give evidence and examine
them on oath or to produce any document, which in the opinion of the said
Authority, may be useful for or relevant to the subject matter of the inquiry and
if, on such inquiry, it is satisfied that the person has failed to comply with the
provisions of any of the sections specified in sub-section (1), it may impose
such penalty as it considers appropriate in accordance with the provisions of
any of those sections."

41.6.7.  Further, The Committee note with concern the proposed provision

in Clause 132D stipulating that `penalties imposed by the National Financial

Reporting Authority (NFRA), if unpaid, may be recovered as arrears of land

revenue'. Stakeholders have suggested that the amount of any penalty

imposed under this section and section 132 of this Act if not paid, may be

recovered by the National Financial Reporting Authority, in accordance with

the proposed section 454B under Clause 103. The Committee find that Clause

103 of the Bill inserts new section 454B which seeks to provide the procedure

for recovery of amounts by the Recovery Officer if a person fails to pay the

penalty imposed under the Act. It, inter alia, provides that the Recovery Officer

shall have the power to seek assistance of local district administration while

exercising powers under this section.

The Committee observe that such stringent recovery mechanisms, as provided
under the present Clause 41 132 (D) (3), are traditionally reserved for sovereign
dues and tax-related defaults and considered draconian. In the view of the
Committee the new subsection 454B proposed under Clause 103 provides a
robust framework for recovery of penalty due. Accordingly, the Committee
desire that provision under Clause 132D (3) may be amended as follows:

"132D (3) The amount of any penalty imposed under section 132 and sub-
section (3) of section 132A and this section, if not paid, may be recovered by
the National Financial Reporting Authority, in accordance with section 454B"

                                                      365
41.6.8.     The Committee observe that Clause 41, seeks to insert a new

section 132I to empower the NFRA to levy fees or other charges on auditors of

specified companies and bodies corporate, in such manner as may be

specified by regulations. The Committee were apprised of the concerns of the

stakeholders that the provision, in its current form, also grants wide and

unguided discretion to prescribe fees and "other charges" through

regulations, without any principles, limits, or legislative safeguards, which may

lead to arbitrary imposition and regulatory overreach. The Committee also

considered the reply of the Ministry that these provisions are consistent with

those conferred on other regulators such as SEBI, CCI and IBBI, and are

intended to establish NFRA as an independent audit sectoral regulator with

comprehensive powers necessary for effective supervision, enforcement and

regulation. The Committee are of the considered opinion that the power under

proposed section 132 I may remain with the Central Government and should

be prescribed by rules allowing for legislative oversight. Accordingly, the

Committee recommend that in section 132 I, the words `specified by it by

regulations' may be substituted with `prescribed'.

41.6.9.     The Committee note the provisions under Clause 41 of the Bill,

specifically the proposed section 132J, grants regulation-making powers to the

National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA). The provision grants wide and

residuary powers to the National Financial Reporting Authority to frame

regulations "for carrying out its functions," including matters relating to

investigation, reporting, fees, and enforcement. During examination the

Committee were apprised that NFRA does not presently have explicit powers

akin to Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) under Section 469 of the

Companies Act, 2013 to frame and lay regulations before Parliament. In the

absence of such enabling provision, the validity of NFRA issuing regulations,

particularly those intended to have statutory effect may be open to legal

challenge.

Stakeholders have raised concerns that such broad and open-ended
delegation, may result in excessive delegation of legislative powers and enable
creation of a parallel regulatory framework without adequate legislative
oversight. The Committee are of the considered opinion that scope of
regulation making powers be clearly defined and limited primarily to
procedural and operational aspects. Substantive matters such as the manner
of investigation, and the recovery of penalties may be governed through rules
framed by the Central Government, subject to Parliamentary oversight, rather
than through regulations framed by NFRA itself, in order to avoid excessive
delegation and preserve legislative accountability

                                                      366
The Committee observe that substantive changes have been recommended by
the Committee to the regulation making provisions of NFRA. In particular the
manner of investigation under clause (a) of sub-section (4) of section 132 and
the manner of recovery of the amount of penalty under sub-section (3) of
section 132D.

Accordingly, pursuant to the changes accepted in respective substantive
provisions necessary changes in the regulation making provisions have to be
carried out under section 132J.

Consequently, the Committee recommend that in clause 41, in the proposed
section 132J in sub-section (2), sub-clauses (a), (c), (d), (e) and (f) shall be
omitted and the other sub-clauses be renamed accordingly.

41.6.10. In this regard the Committee note that it has recommended
changes in Clause 41 to grant requisite flexibility to NFRA to govern its own
day-to-day internal workings w.r.t the meetings and the procedure to be
followed in such meetings. Accordingly, corresponding changes are required
to be made under Clause 41 in section 132 J(2)(b). Therefore, the Committee
recommend that the words `and Executive Body' may be added after the word
`Authority'. Thus section 132J(2)(b) may be amended to read as under:-

"The place and time of meetings of the Authority and executive body and the
procedure to be followed at such meetings under sub-section (10) of section
132"

41.6.11. The Committee note that NFRA was originally envisaged as an
oversight authority with a limited and clearly defined mandate in relation to
accounting and auditing standards for public interest entities, while regulation
of the Chartered Accountancy profession continued under the Chartered
Accountants Act, 1949.

However, the Committee feel that the expanded powers for registration,
investigation, delegated regulation-making powers and the proposed body
corporate status may broaden NFRA's role beyond its original oversight
function. In the considered opinion of the Committee this may result in overlap
with the statutory functions of ICAI, leading to regulatory duplication,
institutional fragmentation, increased compliance requirements, and
uncertainty regarding jurisdictional boundaries.

                                                      367
The Committee thus recommend that the Ministry take steps to ensure that
amendments to the Companies Act do not dilute or override the statutory
autonomy granted to ICAI under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. Instead,
the legislative framework must allow a harmonious coexistence where NFRA's
role under the Companies Act remains strictly focused on corporate financial
oversight, leaving professional development, standard-drafting foundations,
and primary domain matters to the statutory purview of ICAI.

41.6.12. The Committee observe that Clause 41, seeks to insert a new
section 132K to provide for transparency and periodic review in the regulation-
making process of the NFRA, including prior public consultation and review of
regulations at regular intervals, with an exception for urgent or internal
matters. In this regard, the Committee find that stakeholders have suggested
that the public at large should be provided a minimum of thirty days to
respond to the draft regulations under section 132 K and these features should
be expressly mentioned in the Act while leaving the detailed process to be
prescribed by the rules. The Committee agree with the view that the scope of
regulation making power vested with NFRA should preserve important
safeguards to prevent their misuse. The Committee therefore recommend that
the proviso to section 132 K after sub-clause (b) may be removed in entirety.

41.6.13. The Committee reviewed and deliberated upon the other new
subsections that are being proposed to be inserted viz. 132 - B, E, F, G, and H
After in depth consideration of the suggestions received from the stakeholders
and the rationale/replies/clarifications given by the Ministry of Corporate
Affairs, the Committee are of the view that they may be retained in their
present form.

42.5 Examination by the Committee:

42.5.1 In response to the suggestion that the AI and Digital Risk Statement should
require self-certification by the Board, the Ministry, in its written reply, stated as
under:

         "This would be addressed appropriately through Rules. Hence, the
         amendment under the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be
         retained without any change."

42.5.2 On the concern that the expressions "every observation or comment of
auditors" and "any qualification, reservation or adverse remark" used in the provision
are broad and subjective and may create uncertainty regarding the scope of the

                                                      371
Board's obligation to provide explanations or comments, the Ministry submitted as
under :-

         "Suggestion will be considered during framing of subordinate legislation. The
         suggestion discusses maintaining uniformity in language with existing auditing
         standards to ensure operational certainty for auditors when preparing
         statements. The suggestion would be considered at the rule making stage, as
         the Central Government is authorised to prescribe rules under Section 134, if
         required. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026
         may be retained without any change."

42.5.3. with respect to the suggestion that audit committee be composed only of
independent directors with appropriate financial/accounting skills, the Ministry, in its
written reply, stated as under:

         "The suggestion is to limit the composition of the audit committee to only
         independent directors. Currently, Section 177 of the Companies Act, 2013
         states that the Audit Committee (of a company obligated to form such
         committee) must comprise of `at least three directors with independent
         directors forming the majority'. Thus, effectively, independent directors play a
         significant role in the functioning of the Audit Committee under the extant
         provisions. An additional requirement to limit the membership of the Audit
         Committee to independent directors only , is not necessary at the statutory
         level of the Companies Act, 2013. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
         (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change." (Batch II, 142)

42.5.4. About the scope of the Board's obligation to comment on auditor
observations and the need to address emerging risks such as cyber threats, data
privacy, emerging technologies, sustainability and ESG, the Ministry, in its written
reply, stated as under:

         "The suggestion is already incorporated in in Section 134(3) of the Bill.
         Accordingly, the Board's Report is required to provide explanations or
         comments only on adverse. 2. The suggested disclosures relating to global
         uncertainties, cyber threats, data privacy, emerging technology risks, and
         sustainability/ESG are not uniformly mandated under the Act for all
         companies. Requiring such disclosures as a general requirement would
         increase the compliance burden, particularly for companies that are not
         subject to specific sectoral or regulatory reporting obligations. Hence, the
         provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained
         without any change." (Batch III, 113)

                                                      372
42.5.5. On the issue of reducing the frequency of board evaluations for wholly-owned

         in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
         change."

42.5.6. With respect to the suggestion that disclosure of blockchain governance,
digital-asset custody, cyber risk and token-reserve management , The Ministry in its

         "The Companies Act, 2013 and the rules made thereunder do not prescribe
         specific disclosures relating to blockchain governance, digital asset custody,
         smart contract audits, or token reserve management. Further, such matters
         may not be applicable to all companies and may vary depending upon the
         nature and activities of the company. As the existing framework provides for
         disclosure of material information and risks relevant to the company's affairs,
         introducing specific disclosures for emerging technologies at this stage may
         result in additional compliance requirements without uniform applicability.
         Hence, the amendment under the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026
         may be retained without any change."

42.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

42.6.1 The Committee note that the amendment proposed under Clause 42 to
section 134(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 seeks to enhance transparency in
the Board's Report by requiring the Board to provide explanations or
comments on specified observations, qualifications, reservations or adverse
remarks made by the auditors and to disclose the composition of the Audit
Committee, along with reasons where any recommendation of the Audit
Committee has not been accepted by the Board.

         The Committee note the concern raised by stakeholders that the
expressions "every observation or comment of the auditors" and "any
qualification, reservation or adverse remark" are broad and subjective. It was
pointed out that auditors' reports contain observations and statements arising
under different statutory and professional frameworks, including applicable

                                                      373
auditing standards, the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, internal financial
control reporting requirements and other applicable laws. The Committee are
of the view that the absence of clarity regarding the precise scope of the
Board's obligation may result in uncertainty, overlapping reporting
requirements and avoidable compliance requirements.

         The Committee, therefore, recommend that the rules and prescribed
reporting formats under section 134 clearly specify the categories of audit
observations, qualifications, reservations and adverse remarks requiring a
response from the Board. The terminology used should, as far as practicable,
be aligned with the relevant auditing standards and prescribed auditor
reporting formats. The framework should also clearly distinguish between
matters requiring a substantive explanation by the Board and routine or
technical observations already addressed through other statutory reporting
requirements.

         The Committee also note the suggestion that the proposed AI and
Digital Risk Statement should not remain a mere self-declaration by the Board
and should be subject to appropriate self-certification or verification. In view of
the increasing use of artificial intelligence and digital technologies in financial
reporting and corporate decision-making, the Committee recommend that the
applicable rules prescribe appropriate standards for Board-level oversight,
verification and accountability in respect of such disclosures. The Committee
further recommend that the need for appropriate certification or self-
certification of such statements be considered, wherever necessary, to ensure
that such disclosures are supported by adequate verification and that
accountability for the accuracy and integrity of material AI-driven or digitally
generated financial information is clearly established.

         The Committee further recommend that the above requirements be
suitably incorporated in the rules and prescribed reporting formats under
section 134 to ensure clarity, consistency and effective implementation. The
Committee recommend that Clause 42 of the Corporate Laws (Amendment)
Bill, 2026 be accepted without amendment.

i) "The increase in the CSR eligibility threshold will ease the compliance burden on

      Social, and Governance) disclosure in their annual reports. There are already
      BRSR reporting norms mandated for Listed entities and voluntary reporting on
      National Voluntary Guidelines on Social, Environmental and Economic
      Responsibilities of Business, 2011. Such guidelines should be made mandatory for
      companies falling under net profits above Rs 5 Crores. This proposal would not re-
      impose a spending obligation but would require such companies to report on
      relevant sustainability metrics or initiatives. It ensures that even if certain
      companies are no longer mandated to spend on CSR, they remain transparent
      about their environmental and social footprint. This approach aligns with global
      trends toward sustainability reporting and encourages continued voluntary
      engagement in responsible business practices. It is further suggested that if the

      proposed in Clause 43(b)(ii) of the Bill. Raising the CSR threshold will reduce
      operational burdens and provide more flexibility for many companies, but it also
      means fewer businesses are obliged to publicly disclose their community and
      environmental contributions. Without an adjustment, a company could have
      significant operations and social impact yet provide no transparency simply
      because its net profit falls below 10 crore. Requiring a basic ESG or sustainability
      report for companies that are sizable in other respects (like revenue or industry
      footprint) keeps stakeholders informed about those companies' environmental and
      social practices. This measure helps fill the potential transparency gap created by
      the higher CSR threshold. It shifts focus from mandated spending to disclosure,
      thereby maintaining public insight into corporate sustainability efforts in line with
      modern corporate governance expectations."

xi) "Section 135 (1) (a) may not be amended as by virtue of this amendment, we are
      excluding the companies having net profits of 5 crores to 10 crores from the
      applicability of CSR, this may adversely impact the society as a whole. Section 135
      (10) may not be added as this may lead to an unguided delegated power."

xii) "Suggests deleting the proposed clause (10) proposed to Section 135 entirely. The
      newly proposed Section 135 (10) empowers the Central Government to exempt
      entire classes of companies from all provisions of Section 135. This raises
      concerns regarding the extent of executive discretion in relation to a substantive
      statutory obligation. As presently drafted, the provision effectively permits the
      executive to nullify, a substantive policy obligation enacted by Parliament. Notably,
      no parameters, criterior guardrails are specified for the exercise of this power. In
      the absence of such safeguards, the Central Government could, in theory, exempt
      all private companies, all companies below a certain turnover threshold, or all
      companies in a specified sector, without any requirement for Parliamentary
      oversight or scrutiny. Such unfettered discretion undermines the legislative intent
      underlying the CSR framework. CSR awareness and CSR consciousness has
      grown dramatically among large and medium-sized companies, which now look at
      CSR to build a strategic fit with the community and environment in which they
      operate.7 The Report of the High level Committee on Corporate Social
      Responsibility 2018 records that the primary objective of CSR was to promote
      responsible and sustainable business philosophy at a broad level and encourage
      companies to come up with innovative ideas and robust management systems to
      address social and environmental concerns of the local area and other needy areas
      in the country.8 The Report's data shows that CSR spending is not confined to the
      largest companies alone. Companies in lower CSR obligation slabs constitute a
      substantial part of the CSR mandate with 7,970 companies in FY 2017-18 having a
      prescribed CSR amount below 10 lakh and 9,317 companies having a prescribed
      CSR amount between 10 lakh and 50 lakh.9 The report further notes that the
      projects related to education and health have received maximum CSR funds
      almost every year post 2014- 15 followed by projects falling in the domain of rural

                                                           379
      development.10 Another notable observation is that the number of companies with
      CSR spending more than their prescribed amount suggest that broad class-based
      exemptions, if framed without adequate safeguards, may materially reduce the
      number of companies participating in CSR and thereby diminish the overall CSR
      contributions. It bears emphasis that the Supreme Court has recently held, in M.K.
      Ranjitsinh & Others v. Union of India 12 that CSR obligations are not mere
      voluntary acts of charity but constitute the fulfilment of a constitutional obligation.
      The Court observed that a corporation, as a legal person and a key organ of
      society, shares the fundamental duty under Article 51A(g) of the Constitution to
      protect and improve the natural environment. (Para 38) In this context, empowering
      the executive to exempt entire classes of companies from CSR obligations without
      Parliamentary scrutiny would effectively permit the dilution of a constitutionally
      mandated duty. It is pertinent to note that Section 462 of the Companies Act, 2013
      already provides a mechanism for exempting classes of companies from the
      provisions of the Act in the public interest. Importantly, Section 462 incorporates a
      safeguard by requiring that such notifications be laid before each House of
      Parliament, thereby ensuring a measure of legislative oversight. The rationale for
      creating an additional, parallel exemption power under Section 135 (one that lacks
      the accountability mechanisms prescribed under Section 462) is unclear and
      warrants clarification."

xiii) To increase the time period for transferring the unspent amount earmarked for
      ongoing project after three years on similar lines that of proposed amendment for
      transfer of unspent amount after completion of financial year.

    43.5 Examination by the Committee:

    43.5.1. In response to a suggestion requiring disclosure from companies that fall out
    of mandatory CSR due to the higher threshold, under Section 135, the Ministry of
    Corporate Affairs in its written submission stated as under:

             "The core principle of the proposed amendment to increase the threshold to
             INR 10 crore is to ease compliance burdens on companies. Having a tiered
             system of compliance requirements for companies having different financial
             parameters may prove contradictory. It is further suggested that if the
             company fails to spend the unspent CSR amount within 3 years from the date
             of transfer, the timeline for transfer of such amount to funds specified in
             Schedule VII should be extended from 30 days to 90 days. This would be in
             line with the change proposed in Clause 43(b)(ii) of the Amendment Bill.
             Hence, the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 shall be modified
             accordingly."

                                                           380
43.5.2 About raising CSR thresholds reducing mid-sized firms' social accountability
and favours shifting toward mandatory ESG/sustainability disclosure instead, under
Section 135; the Ministry in its written reply stated as under:.

         "Noted. It may be noted that CSR and ESG are distinct regulatory concepts.
         CSR, under Section 135 of the Companies Act, requires eligible companies to
         undertake expenditure on social, environmental and developmental activities.
         In India, ESG reporting is regulated primarily by SEBI's BRSR (Business
         Responsibility and Sustainability Report) which mandates the top 1000 listed
         companies, basis market capitalisation, to disclose standardised information
         relating to environmental, social and governance matters, including
         sustainability related risks, governance, policies, due diligence and prescribed
         ESG indicators. Further, SEBI introduced the BRSR Core framework
         prescribing a set of ESG indicators, which is being implemented in a phased
         manner, for specified classes of companies. Listed companies, not falling
         under the prescribed threshold, including companies listed on SME exchange,
         may voluntarily file BRSR reports."

43.5.3 On the issue of extending the CSR exemption to IFSC branch entities and
IFSC-incorporated finance-company SPVs, under Section 135, Ministry of Corporate
Affairs in its written submission stated as under:

         "Ambiguity, if any, would be appropriately addressed through Rules. The
         proposed amendment to subsection 10 of Section 135 states that such `class
         or classes of companies, which fulfil such conditions, as may be prescribed'
         would not be obligated to undertake CSR. Hence, the amendment under the
         Corporate (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change.

43.5.4 On the issue of exempting Section 8 companies from CSR obligations under
Section 135, the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate affairs while deposing before the
Committee submitted as under:

         "Section 8 companies have been incorporated for a specific purpose which
         may not align with Schedule VII, and that exempting them purely because
         they are Section 8-incorporated would let profit-making entities avoid the
         specific redistributive obligation which Section 135 is designed to impose.
         Elaborating this position, the Ministry informed that approximately 178 Section
         8 companies presently fall within the CSR net, with aggregate CSR spend of
         Rs. 101.55 crore, and that funds received by such companies for
         implementing CSR on behalf of other companies are not counted towards
         their own net profit for the purpose of CSR applicability. In response to queries

                                                      381
        from the Committee on why Section 8 (non-profit) companies should be
        compelled to spend on CSR, the Ministry cited the examples of NPCI, NDDB
        and FICCI-type organisations, which possess substantial income/surplus and
        are accordingly brought within the CSR mandate where net profit -- termed
        'surplus' for Section 8 companies -- exceeds the prescribed threshold. On a
        further query from the Committee regarding audit of such expenditure with
        reference to Schedule VII, it was submitted by the Ministry that CSR
        expenditure by Section 8 companies is auditor-certified and forms part of the
        annual disclosure and CSR-2 filing accompanying the annual return.

43.5.5 On the concern that companies ceasing to meet the CSR applicability
thresholds may immediately discontinue their CSR obligations, thereby disrupting
ongoing multi-year CSR projects and adversely affecting beneficiaries and

        companies. It would be considered during framing of subordinate legislation.
        Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be
        retained without any change"

43.5.6 On the suggestion to increase the timeline for transfer of unspent CSR

        provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained

43.5.7 Regarding the suggestion of permitting blockchain-based CSR tracking and

43.5.8  On the question of removal of reference to Section 198 of the

Companies Act from the explanation, the Ministry in its written reply stated as under:

        382
         "Section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, read with the Companies
         (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014, already provide a clear
         framework for determination of net profit for CSR purposes. The explanation
         to Section 135 specifies that "net profit" shall be calculated in accordance with
         the provisions of Section 198 of the Act, with certain exclusions as prescribed.
         The existing provisions provide sufficient clarity for determining CSR
         obligations. Hence, the amendment under the Corporate Laws (Amendment)

43.5.9 Regarding the suggestion on incentivising voluntary CSR and widening the
permissible CSR fund uses. The Ministry in its written response stated as under:

         "The provisions relating to Corporate Social Responsibility are governed
         under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Schedule VII and
         the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014. The
         existing framework provides sufficient flexibility to eligible companies to
         undertake CSR activities in the areas specified under Schedule VII. Further,
         the Companies Act framework does not provide for separate incentives for
         CSR contributions by small and mid-sized companies or for empowering
         sectoral regulators to prescribe additional areas of CSR utilisation. Introducing
         such sector-specific provisions would affect uniformity in the CSR framework.
         Hence, the amendment under the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026
         may be retained without any change"

43.5.10 On the issue of raising CSR thresholds would reduce the social
accountability of mid-sized firms, the Ministry in its written reply stated as under:

         "The proposed amendments aim to simplify compliance and provide flexibility
         while maintaining the effectiveness of the CSR framework. The applicability of
         CSR provisions and rule-making powers are reviewed considering policy
         objectives and ease of compliance. Hence, the amendment under the
         Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
         change."

43.5.11 On the suggestion deleting clause (10) to Section 135 with defined criteria
(insolvency, new-company status, sectoral overlap) for CSR exemption notifications,
the Ministry in its written reply stated as under:

         "It proposes to prescribe class or classes of companies and conditions to be
         fulfilled by them. The use of "class or classes" is a well-established legislative

                                                      383
device in corporate law, enabling dynamic calibration without frequent
statutory amendments. The essential policy, i.e., that differential compliance
may be warranted, is determined by the legislature; only the identification and
periodic revision of such classes is delegated. Hence, the amendment under
the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change

43.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

43.6.1  The Committee note that the proposed amendments to Section

135 of the Companies Act, 2013 seek to rationalise the Corporate Social

Responsibility (CSR) framework by easing the compliance requirements on

small companies, enhancing the threshold for applicability of CSR from a net

profit of 5 crore to 10 crore, providing additional time for transfer of unspent

CSR amounts to the designated account, enhancing the threshold for

constitution of the CSR Committee, and enabling exemption of such class or

classes of companies as may be prescribed. The Committee observe that the

revision of the CSR threshold would reduce the compliance requirements for a

large number of small and medium-sized companies, enabling them to devote

greater resources towards business expansion and operational efficiency,

while ensuring that the CSR framework remains focused on companies with

relatively greater financial capacity. However, the Committee are of the view

that the proposed power to exempt "such class or classes of companies as

may be prescribed" is broad and lacks statutory guidance, thereby amounting

to excessive delegation of legislative power. The Committee, therefore,

recommend that the words "as may be prescribed" be omitted. The Committee

        387
further note that the consequential amendments proposed under Clause 43(c)
and Clause 43(d), relating to the extension of the timeline for transfer of
unspent CSR amounts to the designated account and the enhancement of the
threshold for constitution of the CSR Committee, are intended to provide
greater operational flexibility and simplify compliance processes without
diluting corporate accountability towards CSR obligations. The Committee are
of the view that these amendments strike an appropriate balance between
regulatory facilitation and preserving the underlying objectives of the CSR
framework. Accordingly, the Committee accept the provisions contained in
Clause 43(a), 43(c) and 43(d) of the Bill as proposed.

The Committee also observe that, while Clause 43 proposes to extend the
period for transferring the unspent CSR amount remaining at the end of a
financial year from thirty days to ninety days, no corresponding amendment
has been proposed in respect of the transfer of the unspent amount earmarked
for an ongoing project after the completion of the third financial year. The
Committee are of the view that both provisions govern analogous procedural
requirements and should provide a uniform compliance timeline. In order to
ensure consistency in the statutory framework and to provide companies with
a reasonable timeframe for effecting such transfers, the Committee
recommend that the corresponding provision relating to ongoing projects be
amended on similar lines by substituting, for the words "specified in Schedule
VII, within a period of thirty days", the words "specified in Schedule VII, within
a period of ninety days".

The Committee are in agreement that CSR funds should not be utilised
through any implementing agency, including organisations, trusts, societies,
non-governmental organisations and Section 8 companies, that is in
contravention of any law for the time being in force or is prohibited from
receiving such funds under any statutory provision or order of a competent
authority. The Committee are of the considered view that any CSR contribution
made to an entity included in a duly notified negative list should not qualify as
CSR expenditure for the purposes of compliance under Section 135 of the

                                                      388
Companies Act, 2013. The Committee further recommend that the criteria for
inclusion of any entity in such a negative list should be objective, transparent
and based solely on statutory provisions or orders passed by a competent
authority, so as to ensure certainty, fairness and uniform application. The
Committee also recommend that the restriction should operate only for the
period and subject to the conditions specified in the relevant notification, and
that an appropriate statutory mechanism be provided for removal of an entity
from the negative list upon the cessation of the grounds that led to its
inclusion. Accordingly, the Committee recommend that Clause 43 of the Bill
may be suitably modified to incorporate the above safeguards within the
statutory framework.

Subject to the above recommendation for amendment to Clause 43, and
prescribing a negative list of entities ineligible to receive CSR contributions,
the Committee recommend that Clause 43 of the Bill be accepted with the
following modification:

"43. In section 135 of the principal Act,--

(a) in sub-section (1), for the words "five crore", the words "ten crore, or such
sum as may be prescribed" shall be substituted;

      (b) in sub-section (6),--

            (i) for the words, brackets and figure "amount remaining unspent under
            sub-section (5)", the words, brackets and figure "unspent amount
            under sub-section (5)" shall be substituted;

            (ii) for the words, "company within a period of thirty days", the words
            "company within a period of ninety days" shall be substituted;

            (iia) for the words and figures "specified in Schedule VII, within a period
            of thirty days", the words and figures "specified in Schedule VII, within
            a period of ninety days" shall be substituted;

                                                      389
            (ba) after sub-section (8), the following sub-section shall be inserted,
            namely: --

            "(8A) (1) The Central Government may, by notification, specify any
            organisation, trust, society, company registered under section 8 or
            such other entity as may be prescribed, to which any contribution
            made towards Corporate Social Responsibility activities shall not be
            treated as expenditure incurred under this section.

            (2) The Central Government shall maintain a list of the organisations,
            trusts, societies, companies and entities notified under sub-section
            (1).

             (3) No organisation, trust, society, company or entity shall be specified under
             sub-section (1), except on the basis of a prohibition, restraint, disqualification or
             other restriction imposed under any law for the time being in force, or pursuant
             to an order of a Court or any competent statutory or regulatory authority.

             (4) Every notification issued under sub-section (1) shall specify the period for
             which, or the conditions subject to which, the inclusion of such organisation,
             trust, society, company or entity in the list referred to in sub-section (2) shall
             remain in force, and the Central Government shall remove such entity from such
             list upon the cessation of the grounds for such inclusion, in such manner as
             may be prescribed.";

            (c) in sub-section (9), for the words "fifty lakh rupees", the words "one
            crore rupees or such higher amount as may be prescribed" shall be
            substituted; (d) after sub-section (9), the following sub-section shall
            be inserted, namely:--

            "(10) Such class or classes of companies which fulfil such conditions,
            as may be prescribed, shall not be required to comply with the
            provisions of this section."

         The Committee further note the suggestions received from certain
stakeholders for permitting companies to discharge, wholly or partly, their
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) obligations through contributions in
kind, such as products, technology, infrastructure, equipment and professional
expertise, particularly where such contributions are capable of generating
greater social impact in sectors such as healthcare, education and disaster
management. The Committee also note that the proposal of the National
Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) to treat the free-of-cost supply of

                                                      390
products for disaster relief as eligible CSR expenditure is presently under
consideration and that valuation principles under the GST framework have
been suggested for determining the value of such contributions.
The Committee are of the considered view that recognising in-kind
contributions, where appropriately regulated, has the potential to enhance the
effectiveness, flexibility and impact of CSR initiatives by enabling companies
to leverage their core competencies and resources for public benefit. At the
same time, the Committee recognise that such a framework must adequately
address concerns relating to objective valuation, transparency, auditability and
accountability. The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Government
examine the feasibility of permitting CSR contributions in kind through an
appropriate statutory or regulatory framework, incorporating robust
safeguards, including objective valuation norms, independent verification,
appropriate disclosure and reporting requirements, and effective monitoring
mechanisms, so as to prevent misuse or overvaluation while ensuring that the
objectives and integrity of the CSR framework are fully preserved.

44. Clause 44 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 139 of the Companies Act,
2013.

44.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

   In section 139 of the principal Act, after sub-section (11), the following sub-section shall
   be inserted, namely:--

   "(12) Such class or classes of companies which fulfil such conditions as may be
   prescribed shall not be required to appoint auditors under this Chapter."

44.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013):

139. Appointment of auditors.--(1) Subject to the provisions of this Chapter, every
company shall, at the first annual general meeting, appoint an individual or a firm as
an auditor who shall hold office from the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion
of its sixth annual general meeting and thereafter till the conclusion of every sixth
meeting and the manner and procedure of selection of auditors by the members of
the company at such meeting shall be such as may be prescribed:

*  *  *  *        *

Provided further that before such appointment is made, the written consent of the
auditor to such appointment, and a certificate from him or it that the appointment, if
made, shall be in accordance with the conditions as may be prescribed, shall be
obtained from the auditor: Provided also that the certificate shall also indicate
whether the auditor satisfies the criteria provided in section 141: Provided also that
the company shall inform the auditor concerned of his or its appointment, and also
file a notice of such appointment with the Registrar within fifteen days of the meeting
in which the auditor is appointed. Explanation.--For the purposes of this Chapter,
"appointment" includes re-appointment. (2) No listed company or a company
belonging to such class or classes of companies as may be prescribed, shall appoint
or re-appoint-- (a) an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive
years; and (b) an audit firm as auditor for more than two terms of five consecutive
years: Provided that-- (i) an individual auditor who has completed his term under

five years from the completion of his term; (ii) an audit firm which has completed its

                                                      392
term under clause (b), shall not be eligible for re-appointment as auditor in the same

the date of appointment no audit firm having a common partner or partners to the

financial year, shall be appointed as auditor of the same company for a period of five
years: 1 [Provided also that every company, existing on or before the
commencement of this Act which is required to comply with the provisions of this

manner in which the companies shall rotate their auditors in pursuance of sub-
section (2). Explanation.--For the purposes of this Chapter, the word "firm" shall
include a limited liability partnership incorporated under the Limited Liability

                                                      393
the case of failure of the Board to appoint such auditor within the next thirty days, it

44.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

    "The amendment seeks to relax the requirement of mandatory appointment of
    auditors under section 139 by exempting such class or classes of companies,
    subject to prescribed conditions, from appointing auditors."

44.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders

i)  It was suggested that the blanket exemption be removed from Statutory

    Audit to class of companies. Even if it is provided to small companies there

    are a plethora of companies wherein turnover and Capital is below 10

    Crores, however the Capital of Rs 10 Crores was deployed 15 years back in

    a Real Estate project which would be now worth 350 Crores. Thus, merely

    measuring a Company and its severity on Capital or Turnover is not

    394
         appropriate. The nuances of this exemption would be great as how will the
         requirement of true & fair view on the financial statements shall be complied
         in the absence of a Statutory Audit. As an alternative to complete audit
         waivers, regulators could consider measures like simplified audit standards
         or limited scope audits for small businesses. Such options would reduce
         costs and administrative burdens while retaining the key benefits of
         independent financial oversight. Additionally, the Government should consult
         with stakeholders (industry, professional bodies like the ICAI, etc.) when
         formulating the specific rules and align any exemption thresholds with those
         in tax and other regulations for consistency. We also recommend that certain
         companies always remain subject to audit - for example, small companies
         that are part of larger corporate groups or that have bank or institutional
         borrowings, since they still require independent scrutiny. Finally, as an
         alternative to complete audit waivers, regulators could consider measures
         like simplified audit standards or limited scope audits for small businesses.
         Such options would reduce costs and administrative burdens while retaining
         the key benefits of independent financial oversight A statutory audit by an
         independent professional is fundamental to corporate governance and
         financial credibility, even for smaller firms. Audits help detect fraud, ensure
         accurate financial reporting (including tax compliance), and instil discipline in
         financial management. If companies with nontrivial operations were to go
         entirely without audits, it would pose risks for stakeholders such as lenders,
         investors, and tax authorities due to the lack of reliable financial information.
         International practice shows that easing audit requirements is usually
         reserved for only the smallest or dormant entities, not for active companies
         of significant size. By keeping any new audit exemption tightly limited, we
         can avoid unintended gaps in oversight that could undermine confidence in
         financial disclosures particularly for group companies, where unaudited
         subsidiaries might weaken the reliability of consolidated accounts. In short,
         any exemptions should be sparingly granted to ensure that the vast majority
         of businesses continue to benefit from the assurance that audits provide.

ii) "There is no objection in principle to enabling exemption of prescribed
         classes of companies from the requirement to appoint auditors under the
         Chapter. However, the eventual impact of this clause will depend entirely on
         the classes and conditions prescribed. Since this may affect market
         confidence, compliance architecture and audit ecosystem functioning, the
         Ministry may suggest that exemptions be narrowly targeted, transparently
         justified and confined to cases where the ease-of-doing business gains are
         clear and the governance risk is low."

iii) "Rules under the new subsection should require every exempted company
         to obtain a declaration from the officer responsible for financial affairs,
         confirming that financial statements present a true and fair view and comply
         with applicable law. Statutory audit acts as a critical safeguard for the
         reliability and credibility of financial statements. An outright exemption
         without an accountability substitute could weaken regulatory oversight."

                                                    395
iv) "Exemption threshold should be formulated considering following factors:
         Public interest (Primary criteria) e.g exclude companies having loans from
         banks/ financial institution over INR 5 crores, NBFCs or entities registered
         with Financial Intelligence Unit of Department of Revenue. Alignment with
         Income tax/ GST. Global practices e.g. US/ UK. Clarify consequential
         implications e.g. Adoption of accounts in AGM. Buy-back provisions require
         audited/ limited reviewed financial statements. Monetary threshold (i.e. paid-
         up capital and turnover) for identification of small companies may not uphold
         public interest in all scenarios. Alignment with other statues critical for
         streamlining compliance burden."

v) "Clarify whether IFSCA Sandbox entities qualify for simplified audit
         requirements. Encourages innovation while maintaining regulatory
         oversight."

vi) It is recommended that the clause be modified as follows: "(12) Such class
         or classes of companies, not being public companies, which fulfil such
         conditions relating to paid-up capital turnover, aggregate borrowings and
         public interest, as may be prescribed, shall not be required to appoint
         auditors under this Chapter, subject to such alternative certification or self-
         declaration requirements as may be prescribed." Audit exemption for the
         smallest companies follows mature-jurisdiction practice (the UK small
         companies audit exemption; Singapore's "small company" concept), and is a
         defensible ease-of doing-business measure However, an unbounded
         delegation - under which any class of company could be exempted from
         audit - is excessive: audited financial statements underpin credit decisions,
         tax administration and the deposit/borrowing framework. Confining the
         power to non-public companies by objective statutory parameters, with
         alternative assurance, preserves the reform while safeguarding the
         credibility of financial reporting.

        399
44.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

44.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 44 of the Bill seeks to insert a new sub-
section (12) in Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013 to enable the Central
Government to exempt such class or classes of companies, subject to such
conditions as may be prescribed, from the requirement of appointing statutory
auditors. The Committee observe that the proposed amendment is intended to
reduce the compliance requirement on low-risk and small companies,
particularly newly incorporated and micro enterprises, for whom the cost of
mandatory statutory audit may be disproportionate to the scale of their
operations. The Committee further note that the preparation and filing of
financial statements, annual returns and other statutory compliances would
continue to remain mandatory and that the conditions governing such
exemption would be prescribed through subordinate legislation, taking into
account relevant factors, such as borrowings, assets and other appropriate
parameters, so as to balance the objective of ease of doing business with the
need to preserve financial discipline, transparency and stakeholder
confidence.

The Committee, however, are of the view that extending the enabling provision
to all classes of companies may have unintended implications for
transparency and stakeholder protection. In the opinion of the Committee, the
proposed exemption should be confined to private companies only, as such
companies generally have a limited shareholder base and comparatively lower
public interest implications. Restricting the exemption to private companies
would achieve the objective of reducing compliance requirement for small
businesses, while ensuring that the public companies, whose affairs have a
wider bearing on investors, creditors and other stakeholders, continue to
remain subject to statutory audit requirements.

The Committee, therefore, recommend that Clause 44 of the Bill be modified to
provide that the power of the Central Government to exempt companies from
the requirement of appointing statutory auditors shall be exercisable only in
respect of such class or classes of private companies, subject to such
conditions as may be prescribed. This would adequately balance the objective
of ease of doing business with the need to safeguard transparency,
accountability and stakeholder confidence in the corporate sector.

Accordingly, Clause 44 of the Bill be modified as under:

                                                      400
44. In section 139 of the principal Act, after sub-section (11), the following sub-
section shall be inserted, namely:--
"(12) Such class or classes of private companies, which fulfil such
conditions as may be prescribed, shall not be required to appoint auditors
under this Chapter and the reference to the requirement of having audited
financial statements for determining any financial information in accordance
with the provisions of the Act or the rules made thereunder shall be construed
accordingly, as if there is no requirement for audit.".

45. Clause 45 of the Bill proposes to amend Section 141 of the Companies
Act, 2013.

45.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026

    45. In section 141 of the principal Act, in sub-section (1), after the proviso, the following
    proviso shall be inserted, namely:--

    "Provided further that every partner of the firm shall be a person who has been registered
    with a statutory institute or body established under a law in India having powers of such
    registration.".

45.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013)

         141. Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications of auditors.

    141. (1) A person shall be eligible for appointment as an auditor of a company
    only if he is a chartered accountant: Provided that a firm whereof majority of
    partners practising in India are qualified for appointment as aforesaid may be
    appointed by its firm name to be auditor of a company.

    * *  *       *                                               *

45.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment seeks to insert a second proviso in section 141(1) to strengthen
accountability for audit firms."

45.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

i)       It is suggested that this proposed proviso be reconsidered, and that the

         existing Section 141(1) framework be retained. The current requirements

         already ensure that those who actually perform and sign audits are qualified

            402
           CAs in good standing; an additional blanket mandate that every firm partner
           hold an Indian statutory registration is unnecessary and could hinder the
           operation of the audit firms. This broad restriction would adversely affect
           multi-disciplinary firms by forcing them to restructure partnerships with
           experts who may not be members of a statutory institute (e.g., IT specialists,
           MBAs, or foreign-qualified professionals). It would impose compliance costs
           without clear benefits for audit quality."

  ii) It was further suggested that Section 141 of the Companies Act already
           ensures that where a firm, including a limited liability partnership, is
           appointed as an auditor of a company, only the partners who are chartered
           accountants shall be authorised to act and sign on behalf of the firm and a
           majority of the partners in such a firm have to be chartered accountants
           holding a certificate of practice. Requiring `every' partner in such the firm to
           be registered with an Indian statutory body may undermine the
           government's own push for encouraging multidisciplinary partnership firms
           as, among others, IT specialists, MBAs, foreign qualified professionals,
           forensic experts who need to be part of such MDPs who may not have the
           benefit of membership or registrations with any statutory body and will not
           be entitled to become partners in the such firms.

  iii) "Introduce mandatory certification for Digital Asset Auditors and Blockchain
           Assurance Professionals. Crypto businesses require specialised audit
           capabilities."

45.5 Examination by the Committee:

45.5.1 On the issue of mandatory Indian statutory registration for all partners of an
audit firm under Section 141(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the ministry in its written
response stated as under:

     "Clause 45, proposing amendments to section 141, shall be modified to omit the
     proposed proviso requiring every partner of an audit firm to be registered with a
     statutory institute or body established under a law in India. This would provide
     the requisite flexibility to accommodate professionals possessing relevant
     expertise while avoiding an unduly restrictive statutory requirement. Hence, the
     Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 shall be modified accordingly."

45.5.2 On the issue of introducing mandatory certification for digital assets and
blockchain, the Ministry in its written response stated as follows:

                                                      403
"suggestion has been examined. At present, there is no specific requirement
under the Companies Act, 2013 for mandatory certification of digital asset
auditors or blockchain assurance professionals. As these areas are evolving and
may not be applicable to all companies, introducing such a requirement under
the Act may not be appropriate at this stage. Hence, the amendment under the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change"

45.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

45.6.1         The Committee note that Clause 45 of the Corporate Laws

(Amendment) Bill, 2026 seeks to amend Section 141(1) of the Companies Act,

2013, by inserting a proviso requiring that every partner of an audit firm shall

be a person registered with a statutory institute or body established under a

law in India.

         The Committee observe that stakeholders and professional bodies
raised strong concerns against this proposed blanket mandate, emphasizing
that the existing framework under Section 141 of the Companies Act, 2013,
already provides sufficient safeguards. Currently, where a firm or Limited
Liability Partnership (LLP) is appointed as an auditor, a majority of the partners
practicing in India must be qualified Chartered Accountants, and only partners
who are Chartered Accountants are authorized to act and sign on behalf of the
firm.

         The Committee are of the considered view that mandating Indian
statutory registration for every partner in an audit firm is unnecessary and
counterproductive as it will affect the constitution of multi-disciplinary
partnership firms. The Committee feel such a rigid restriction would adversely
affect Multidisciplinary Partnerships (MDPs) by preventing them from
inducting domain experts such as IT specialists, MBAs, forensic analysts, or
foreign-qualified professionals who may not be registered with an Indian
statutory body. This would create operational friction, increase compliance
requirement, and contradict the Government's ongoing initiative to encourage
holistic and multidisciplinary partnership firms.

         Accordingly, the Committee recommend that the proposed proviso to
Section 141(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, as contained in Clause 45 of the
Bill, may not be accepted and is to be omitted from the Bill.

46. Clause 46 of the Bill proposes to amend Section 144 of the Principal Act

46.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

Provided further that the restriction under this section shall also apply for a period of three years
after the auditor or audit firm has completed his or its term under sub-section (2) of section 139:

Provided also that"

46.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013):

        144. Auditor not to render certain services.--

        An auditor appointed under this Act shall provide to the company only such
        other services as are approved by the Board of Directors or the audit
        committee, as the case may be, but which shall not include any of the
        following services (whether such services are rendered directly or indirectly to
        the company), or its holding company or subsidiary company, namely:--

         (a) accounting and book keeping services;

        (b) internal audit;

        (c) design and implementation of any financial information system;

        (d) actuarial services;
                                                      405
        (e) investment advisory services;

        (f) investment banking services;

        (g) rendering of outsourced financial services;

         (h) management services; and

        (i) any other kind of services as may be prescribed: Provided that an auditor or

        section before the closure of the first financial year after the date of such
        commencement.

         Explanation.--For the purposes of this sub-section, the term "directly or
        indirectly" shall include rendering of services by the auditor,--

        (i) in case of auditor being an individual, either himself or through his
