        (ii) in case of auditor being a firm, either itself or through any of its
                  partners or through its parent, subsidiary or associate entity or through
                  any other entity, whatsoever, in which the firm or any partner of the firm
                  has significant influence or control, or whose name or trade mark or
                  brand is used by the firm or any of its partners

46.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

        "The amendment seeks to prohibit auditors of prescribed class of companies
        to provide non audit services."

                                                      406
46.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

  i) It has been recommended that a calibrated, risk-based approach to any
           additional restrictions on non-audit services and advise against
           implementing a blanket ban on all non-audit services as contemplated. The
           current law already prohibits key non-audit services that threaten auditor
           independence, and a total prohibition on any other services is too broad and
           goes beyond widely followed international norms. If additional safeguards
           are deemed necessary, a more targeted approach would be preferable: for
           example, exempt clearly low-risk services like routine tax compliance and
           confine any ban to services provided to the Indian company and its Indian
           parent or subsidiaries. Additionally, terms like "management services" in
           Section 144 should be clearly defined in the rules to remove ambiguity in the
           scope. We further suggest that the proposed three-year post-audit service
           ban be reconsidered and not pursued. Extending a prohibition on providing
           services of any period, after an audit engagement ends, is unprecedented
           globally and may have nil to very limited incremental benefits in practice. It
           could unduly restrict both companies and audit firms, reducing available
           choices for needed services and increasing costs, especially for specialized
           or mid-sized firms. Given the robust independence measures already in
           place, adding this extra post-engagement restriction appears unnecessary
           and would place Indian practices at a competitive disadvantage. Auditor
           independence is already safeguarded by multiple layers of regulation:
           Section 144's targeted restrictions, the ICAI's Code of Ethics (aligned with
           international standards), oversight by audit committees, mandatory auditor
           rotation, and NFRA's regulatory reviews. These measures collectively
           mitigate conflicts of interest without resorting to extreme prohibitions.
           Indeed, no major international jurisdiction imposes an all encompassing ban
           on non-audit services or requires a lengthy post audit "cooling-off" for firms.
           Introducing a sweeping ban (especially coupled with a three-year post-
           tenure restriction) could have significant unintended consequences. It would
           limit companies' flexibility in obtaining expert services from their auditors,
           potentially increase compliance costs, and disproportionately impact smaller
           audit firms who often balance audit and non-audit work. This could ironically
           drive companies to concentrate more advisory work with a few large firms,
           reducing competition. Moreover, there is no evidence that forbidding
           services after an auditor has left an engagement improves audit quality.
           Once an audit relationship ends, the risk of undue influence on financial
           reporting largely dissipates, and other regulations address any remaining
           conflicts.

  ii) "Define "Non-audit services" or Prescribe permitted services (Proviso no. 1)
           We humbly request that the first new proviso is amended to replace the
           words "any non-audit services" with "any non-audit services, as may be
           prescribed". The prescription can, by way of illustration be "all non-audit
           services, except the following..." Illustrative list of permissible non-audit
           services: a) Limited review reports on quarterly unaudited financial results
           under SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations,

                                                      407
         2015 ("LODR") b) Certificates of net worth or financial position required by
         lenders, regulatory bodies, or counterparties from statutory auditors under
         contractual or statutory obligations c) Tax certifications under Form 3CEB
         (transfer pricing) under Section 172 of the Income Tax Act, 2025 or reporting
         in Form 3CA or Form 3CB d) Audits prescribed by Section 63 of the Income
         tax Act, 2025 e) Certifications of revenue or eligible expenditure for
         government scheme purposes, including under the PLI schemes
         administered by various Ministries, where the statutory auditor's certification
         is expected Certificates required from statutory auditors under FEMA and
         RBI regulations, including for remittances, overseas investments, and
         external commercial borrowings g) Comfort letters or agreed-upon
         procedures reports required by investment banks for public issuances,
         where the statutory auditor has already conducted the underlying audit
         procedures h) Reports for ESG Assurance (including or Assessments over
         the BRSR reporting of audit client) whether required by clients or otherwise
         i) Assurance re Post rotation cooling-off period (Proviso no. 2) We humbly
         request that the second new proviso imposing the three-year post rotation
         cooling-off is deleted and consider requiring that any non-audit services
         engagement by the outgoing auditor during the financial year immediately
         following rotation be subject to prior Audit Committee approval, with an
         obligation to disclose such engagement in the Board's report under Section
         134.".

iii) "Cooling-off period of three years after cessation as auditors may not be an
         effective safeguard against audit independence Cooling-off period should be
         replaced with other measures. It is inconsistent with the cooling-off
         requirements by other regulators in India it was further suggested Complete
         restriction on non-audit services prevents companies from using the
         valuable expertise, skills, and deep understanding of their trusted auditors.
         Companies should be allowed to hire their auditors for non-audit work,
         provided they get strict approval from both the Audit Committee and the
         Board of Directors. This ensures the company benefits from expert guidance
         while maintaining proper checks and balances Limit the 3-year restriction
         only to high-risk services. Further, allow flexibility for holding and subsidiary
         entities to use the non-audit services where there is no conflict. Audit
         Committee can approve such cases."

iv) "The proposal states that the restrictions on providing NAS would apply for a
         period of 3 years post completion of term by the statutory auditor. A
         combined reading of the proposed amendments to Section 144 suggests
         that an auditor would not be able to provide Non-Audit Services (NAS) to the
         company or its holding or subsidiary company for a period of more than 13
         years (considering the 10- year period as auditor and 3-year period post the
         conclusion of the Annual General Meeting of the Company, where the
         statutory auditor would be mandatorily rotated). Further, as the Companies
         Act currently has a cool-off period of 5 years for the statutory auditors, it
         would imply that neither audit nor non-audit services can be provided for that
         3-year period to the company or its holding or subsidiary company. The

                                                    408
         following implications may be considered in this regard: - Lack of choices of
         professionals for companies which engage multiple auditors in their Group -
         No international precedent - Impact on formation of multi -disciplinary
         partnership (MDP) structure - May not be aligned with overall objective of
         the Amendment Bill of `ease of doing business ' - May impact availability of
         right skill set to meet business requirements - Enabling safeguards are
         already in place to maintain auditor independence and integrity, including: o
         oversight by audit committees o restrictions under current Section 144
         during audit term o regulatory inspections and oversight - Applicability if
         auditor is not reappointed post completion of 5 -year term or there is a mid -
         term resignation (say in 9th year) Position in case of joint audits since two
         (or more) audit firms would be involved - Specific sector regulators (such as
         the RBI)"

v) "Class of companies to which the extended restriction is to be applied (say,
         only to Public interest entities (PIEs)). - Clarity, as a part of Rules, on
         permissible services (such as, ESG assurance, SOC assurance, issuance of
         other certificates, transfer pricing audits, tax services etc.) - Clarity on the
         term `management services' in clause 144(h) - Global practices (such as
         under IESBA, SEC framework The implications of the proposed amendment
         in the following situations may be considered: - Groups with diversified
         businesses carried through separate legal entities with the ownership held
         by a single parent entity - Holding company is a private equity (PE) company
         - May not be aligned with the overall objective of the Amendment Bill of
         `ease of doing business; and `ease of compliance'.

vi) "Limit restriction to large listed companies. Small audit firms will face
         challenge as they provide multiple services to small companies. Such
         blockage will impact many aspects. Small audit firms rely on multi-service
         offerings; blanket restriction harms MSMEs. The strength of any professional
         services market depends upon the presence of a wide range of participants.
         Businesses benefit when they can choose from firms that differ in size,
         specialization, industry expertise and service approach. Over the past
         decade, many Indian mid-sized firms have invested heavily in Quality control
         systems; Technology platforms; Sector-specific expertise; Training and
         development; Risk management frameworks; and Audit methodologies
         aligned with global standards. These investments have enabled such firms
         to compete effectively and provide companies with credible alternatives to
         larger networks. A competitive marketplace encourages innovation,
         enhances service quality and reduces excessive dependence on a limited
         number of market participants. Accordingly, any regulatory reform that
         affects the structure of the profession should be evaluated not only from a
         governance perspective but also from a competition perspective. They
         further stated that a healthy audit ecosystem requires firms of varying sizes
         to coexist and compete. Large professional organizations generally possess
         Extensive client bases; International affiliations; Significant financial
         resources; Broad geographic reach; Mid-sized firms compete by: Developing
         industry expertise; Building long-term client relationships; Offering

                                                    409
         specialized services; and Providing partner-level attention. The proposed
         amendments may disproportionately affect firms in the growth stage, thereby
         making it more difficult for them to expand and compete effectively. Over
         time, such restrictions may contribute to increased concentration of work
         among a smaller number of firms, reducing diversity within the profession.
         From a public policy perspective, excessive concentration may create
         systemic risks and reduce resilience within the audit market".

vii) Concern relates to possible inconsistencies between different regulatory
         frameworks. Even if certain companies are exempted from audit under the
         Companies Act, they may continue to be subject to audit, certification, or
         verification requirements under the Income-tax Act, GST laws, banking
         regulations, or investor agreements. As a result, businesses may continue to
         incur compliance costs without obtaining the benefits associated with a
         comprehensive statutory audit. Such inconsistencies may create confusion
         and uncertainty rather than simplification. India has emerged as one of the
         world's fastest growing major economies and has consistently sought to
         align its corporate governance framework with international best practices.
         Several significant reforms have already been implemented over the last
         decade, including mandatory auditor rotation, enhanced reporting
         requirements, strengthened Audit Committee oversight, introduction of
         NFRA, and tighter professional standards These reforms have positioned
         India among jurisdictions with one of the most comprehensive auditor
         independence frameworks. In this backdrop, it is important to examine
         whether the proposed amendments are aligned with international practice
         and whether they are likely to achieve the intended objectives. A review of
         major jurisdictions such as the United States, United Kingdom, Canada,
         Australia, Singapore, and various European countries indicates that while
         restrictions exist on conflict-prone services during an audit engagement,
         broad post-audit restrictions extending for three years are generally not
         followed. Similarly, most developed jurisdictions adopt a risk-based
         approach towards non-audit services rather than imposing blanket
         prohibitions on all services. Accordingly, the proposed amendments appear
         to go beyond internationally accepted norms despite India already having
         extensive independence safeguards. An often-overlooked consequence is
         the impact on market diversity. India has invested significant effort over
         several decades in developing a broad-based audit profession comprising
         large, medium and small firms. A blanket prohibition on non-audit services
         may weaken the business model of mid-sized firms that rely on diversified
         service offerings. Large multinational networks typically possess greater
         scale and geographic reach. Smaller and mid-sized firms, however, build
         expertise through long-term client engagement and multidisciplinary service
         delivery. Restricting these opportunities may unintentionally increase
         concentration within the professional services market. This outcome would
         run contrary to the broader objective of encouraging competition and
         expanding professional capacity. Further the alternative has been suggested
         that Instead of a blanket prohibition: · Continue prohibiting high-risk
         services. · Permit low-risk services subject to safeguards. · Clearly define
         restricted activities. · Limit restrictions to services creating genuine

                                                    410
           independence threats. Such an approach would preserve independence
           while maintaining efficiency and competition.

  viii) "Define separate standards for Smart Contract Audit, Cyber Audit and
           Financial Audit. Smart contract audits differ fundamentally from statutory
           audits ".

46.5 Examination by the Committee:

         In response to the suggestions the Ministry submitted the following:-

46.5.1. On the issue of proposed prohibitions on non-audit services by statutory
auditors, the Ministry in its written response stated as under:

             "a. In the first proviso in section 144, the terms "as may be prescribed"
             shall be inserted after the words "non-audit services", thereby enabling the
             definition of non-audit services to be prescribed through Rules. b. In the
             second proviso in Section 144, the reference to "three years" would be
             reduced. The new cooling off period is under discussion and examination.
             Hence, the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 shall be modified
             accordingly."

46.5.2. On the issue of penalty frameworks for corporate non-compliances, the
Ministry in its written response stated as under:

             "The suggestion discusses taking a proportional approach for imposition of
             penalties for contraventions by small companies. The suggestion is noted,
             and the current regime has been drafted in consideration of this suggestion
             with small companies enjoying relaxed thresholds compliance
             requirements and corresponding penalties for contraventions under the
             Companies Act. Hence, the amendment under the Corporate Laws
             (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

46.5.3. On the issue of defining non-audit services under Proviso 1, the Ministry in its

             "To provide adequate flexibility while ensuring that only such services as

46.5.5. Further on the issue of post-tenure restrictions on non-audit services (NAS),

46.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

46.6.1.  The Committee note that Clause 46 of the Bill seeks to amend

Section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013, by introducing additional restrictions

on the provision of non-audit services by auditors or audit firms of such class

or classes of companies as may be prescribed. The proposed amendment

further provides for a three-year restriction on the provision of non-audit

services to the company, its holding company or subsidiary company after the

completion of the auditor's term, besides providing a transitional period for

auditors already rendering such services.

         The Committee observe that the proposed amendments seek to
strengthen auditor independence and address potential conflicts of interest
arising from the provision of non-audit services. The Committee, however,
note the concerns raised by various stakeholders regarding the broad scope
of the proposed restrictions, the absence of clarity regarding the class of
companies to which the enhanced restrictions would apply and the categories
of services that would be regarded as non-audit services. The Committee
further note that a blanket prohibition on all non-audit services may
unnecessarily restrict legitimate and low-risk professional services and may
create uncertainty regarding the services intended to be covered by the
restriction.

         The Committee are, therefore, of the considered opinion that the
implementation of the proposed restrictions should adopt a calibrated and

                                                      413
risk-based approach, with due regard to the need to preserve auditor
independence while avoiding unintended restrictions on legitimate
professional services, particularly in the case of small companies, MSMEs and
smaller audit practices. The Committee, accordingly, recommend that the
Ministry utilise its delegated rule-making powers to restrict the application of
the enhanced prohibitions on non-audit services to specified high-risk entities
or Public Interest Entities, thereby safeguarding small companies, MSMEs and
smaller audit practices from disproportionate administrative and compliance
requirements.

         The Committee further note that the proposed first proviso prohibits
auditors or audit firms from providing "any non-audit services" to the
company or its holding or subsidiary company. The Committee are of the view
that the scope of such prohibition should be clearly defined to ensure legal
certainty and prevent inconsistent interpretation and implementation. The
Committee, therefore, recommend that the words "as may be prescribed" be
inserted after the words "any non-audit services", thereby enabling the
prescription of specific categories of non-audit services to which the
restriction would apply. The Committee further recommend that the
subordinate legislative framework clearly identify the services covered by the
prohibition and, where appropriate, permit legitimate and low-risk professional
services, subject to appropriate safeguards to protect auditor independence
and prevent actual or perceived conflicts of interest. The Committee further
recommend that the expression "management services" be replaced with
"management functions" so as to provide greater clarity regarding the scope
of the restriction. The Committee, therefore, recommend that Clause 46 be
suitably amended to provide that the prohibition shall apply to such non-audit
services "as may be prescribed" and to replace the expression "management
services" with "management functions".

         With regard to the proposed three-year restriction on the provision of
non-audit services after completion of the auditor's term, the Committee note
the concerns raised by various stakeholders regarding the length and scope of
the proposed cooling-off period and its possible implications for the
availability of professional expertise, choice of service providers and the cost
of compliance. The Committee further note that the proposed three-year
restriction may be particularly onerous in cases involving group companies,
joint audits, mid-term resignation or non-reappointment of auditors.

         The Committee are of the considered view that a proportionate and risk-
based approach would balance the objective of safeguarding auditor
independence with the need to preserve access to specialised professional

                                                      414
services. The Committee, therefore, recommend that the proposed three-year
cooling-off period be reduced to one year. The Committee, therefore,
recommend that Clause 46 of the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 be
modified to provide for flexibility and relaxation through the following
changes:
"46. In section 144 of the principal Act,--

      (a) in clause (h), for the words "services; and", the words "functions; and"
           shall be substituted;

      (b) in the proviso, for the words "Provided that", the following shall be
           substituted, namely:--

      "Provided that an auditor or audit firm of such class or classes of
      companies, as may be prescribed, shall not provide, directly or indirectly,
      [***] non-audit services, as may be prescribed, to the company or its holding
      company or subsidiary
      Provided further that the restriction under this section shall also apply for a
      period of [***] one year after the auditor or audit firm has completed his or
      its term under sub-section (2) of section 139:
      Provided also that".

47.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendments seek to decriminalise offences under section 147 by replacing
fines with a penalty-based regime for specified contraventions. They also expand
the scope of sub-section (2) to expressly include contraventions of section 143
(other than sub-section (12)) and section 146. The amendment is part of the
broader decriminalisation exercise under the Bill."

47.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

i) "No penal action, prosecution or adverse professional consequence should be
         initiated against any person, including professionals, unless one is found guilty
         with a negative mensrea and the same is established through due process of
         law on a judicial forum. The proposed and existing delegation of such powers
         with Registrar of Companies, Regional directors and other administrative
         machinery is not justified and will result in harassment and corruption. 2.
         Prosecution and Fine should be limited to cases of diversion of funds or
         criminal misuse of funds of a material amount of Rs. 10 Crores or more as
         maybe prescribed. 3. Arrest powers under corporate and economic laws
         should be significantly curtailed and should be reserved only for exceptional
         cases involving threats to national security, sovereignty, defence of India,
         terrorism financing, or similar grave offences. The businessman should not be
         subjected to criminal action in case due to bad weather and circumstances,
         the Companies are not able to meet their financial commitments."

ii) It has been suggested that the Bill brings Section 143 (excluding sub-section
         12) within auditor liability under Section 147 exposing auditors to two sets of
         proceedings (NFRA/ICAI and Companies Act, 2013 Act) for same breach of
         accounting and auditing related matters. It has been requested that only one
         set of proceedings should apply; additionally, auditors cannot avail
         compounding (or of proposed settlement mechanism), which is available only
         to directors and officers.

      417
iii) "Insertion of sub-clause making statutory auditors liable to prosecution for
         contravening specified duties and attendance provisions instead of blanket
         penalty. It has been submitted that One size fit all" penalty is disproportionate
         and to levy lower penalty for contravention of procedural/ administrative
         default relating to private placement. [Example adjudication orders: Timing of
         Form filing incorrect - INR 10,000 (RoC Chennai). Funds used before Form
         filing INR 1 lakh to 2 lakh (RoC Pune)] Replace prosecution (i.e. fine) on
         statutory auditor and cost auditor with monetary penalty of INR 2 crore for
         procedural/ administrative defaults might appear as a tax gathering exercise.
         Levy penalty basis: Amount of disproportionate gain/ unfair advantage.
         Amount of loss to an investor. Repetitive nature of default. Criminal sanctions
         on auditors: Incongruent with Bills objective to decriminalize. Disproportionate
         when company/ management is not subject to criminal sanction."

iv) Introduction of a proportional compliance framework for regulated Digital
         Asset Startups to avoid excessive compliance burden during early-stage
         operations.

47.5 Examination by the Committee:

47.5.1  Addressing the issue of civil penalties for regulatory non-compliance

and criminal offences requiring culpability, the Ministry stated as under:

                 "The Companies Act distinguishes between civil penalties for objective
        regulatory non-compliance and criminal offences requiring culpability. Many
        corporate law obligations are statutory compliance requirements where liability
        is intentionally based on failure to comply, irrespective of intent. 2. The
        Companies Act, 2013 provides for prosecution in respect of a range of serious
        offences, including fraud, false statements and furnishing false evidence
        under sections 447, 448 and 449, as well as other misconduct affecting the
        integrity of corporate governance and investor protection. Restricting
        prosecution only to cases involving diversion or misuse of funds exceeding
        Rs. 10 crore would unduly narrow the enforcement framework. 3. The
        Companies Act, 2013 already follows a calibrated enforcement framework,
        under which imprisonment is generally reserved for serious offences such as
        fraud and other wilful misconduct, while numerous procedural and technical
        defaults have been decriminalised and made subject to civil penalties through
        the in-house adjudication mechanism. The present amendment to section 147
        further advances this approach by replacing criminal sanctions with penalties
        for specified procedural contraventions relating to auditor appointment and
        compliance requirements. Accordingly, the proposed curtailment of arrest
        powers and replacement of criminal liability with civil penalties may not be
        warranted. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,
        2026 may be retained without any change.

                                                     418
47.5.2. On the issue of exposing auditors to two sets of proceedings namely under
NFRA/ICAI and Companies Act, 2013, Ministry have submitted as under:

                  `The provisions of Section 147 and 132 operate differently. Jurisdiction
         of NFRA is specified in NFRA Rules while Section 147 applies to all auditors.
         Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be
         retained without any change.'

47.5.3. With respect to suggestion regarding making statutory auditors liable to
prosecution for contravening specified duties and attendance provisions instead of
blanket penalty and levying of lower penalty for contravention of procedural/
administrative defaults, the Ministry have submitted as under:

                  `The Companies Act distinguishes between civil penalties for objective
         regulatory non-compliance and criminal offences requiring culpability. It has
         been further stated that the Act already follows a calibrated enforcement
         framework, under which imprisonment is generally reserved for serious
         offences such as fraud and other wilful misconduct, while numerous
         procedural and technical defaults have been decriminalised and made subject
         to civil penalties through the in-house adjudication mechanism. Section 147
         further advances decriminalization approach by replacing criminal sanctions
         with penalties for specified procedural contraventions relating to auditor
         appointment and compliance. Further 446B of the Act provides for lesser
         penalties for small companies, OPC, startup company and producer company.
         Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be
         retained without any change.'

47.5.4. With respect to the proportional compliance framework for regulated Digital
Asset Startups, the Ministry has submitted as under:

                  `The Companies Act, 2013 provides a uniform corporate compliance
         framework based on the nature and size of companies Digital asset-related
         activities are subject to applicable sector-specific regulations, wherever
         applicable. Introducing a separate compliance framework under the
         Companies Act for digital asset startups may not be appropriate at this stage.
         Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be
         retained without any change.'

                                                      419
47.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

47.6.1  The Committee note that Clause 47 of the Bill seeks to amend

Section 147 of the Companies Act, 2013, as part of the broader objective of

decriminalising procedural and technical defaults under the Companies Act,

2013. The proposed amendment provides for the substitution of criminal fines

with monetary penalties in respect of specified contraventions relating to

auditor appointment and related compliance requirements, while also

expressly including contraventions of Section 143, other than sub-section (12),

and Section 146 within the scope of sub-section (2) of Section 147.

         The Committee observe that the proposed amendment seeks to
establish a more calibrated enforcement framework by distinguishing between
procedural and technical non-compliances, which may appropriately be
addressed through monetary penalties, and serious misconduct warranting
criminal consequences. The Committee further note the Ministry's submission
that the Companies Act, 2013 already follows such a differentiated
enforcement approach, wherein imprisonment is generally reserved for
serious offences involving fraud, false statements and other wilful misconduct,
while procedural and technical defaults are increasingly dealt with through
civil penalties and in-house adjudication. The Committee also note that
Section 446B provides for lesser penalties in respect of certain classes of
companies, including small companies, One Person Companies, start-up
companies and producer companies.

         The Committee have also examined the concerns regarding the possible
exposure of auditors to parallel proceedings under Section 147 of the
Companies Act, 2013 and the regulatory framework administered by the
National Financial Reporting Authority or the Institute of Chartered
Accountants of India. The Committee note the Ministry's clarification that the
jurisdiction and scope of proceedings under Section 147 and Section 132
operate under distinct statutory frameworks, with the jurisdiction of the
National Financial Reporting Authority being specified under the relevant

                                                      420
Rules, while Section 147 applies generally to auditors in respect of specified
contraventions under the Companies Act, 2013. The Committee also note the
Ministry's submission that a separate compliance framework under the
Companies Act, 2013 for digital asset-related start-ups may not be appropriate
at this stage, as such activities, wherever applicable, are subject to sector-
specific regulatory frameworks.

         The Committee, while taking note of the views and suggestions received
from stakeholders and the clarifications furnished by the Ministry, are of the
view that the proposed amendment appropriately advances the objective of
decriminalising procedural and technical defaults while retaining criminal
sanctions for serious misconduct and culpable violations. The Committee
further observe that the proposed framework, read with the existing provisions
providing for proportionate penalties for specified classes of companies,
seeks to balance the objectives of effective enforcement, corporate
accountability and ease of doing business.

         Accordingly, taking into account the justifications and clarifications
furnished by the Ministry, the views and suggestions received from
stakeholders and experts, and the deliberations held by the Committee, the
Committee recommend that Clause 47 be accepted without any amendment.

48.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

         "The amendment seeks to empower Central Government to provide for
standards for cost accounting.

         The amendment seeks to allow firms of cost accountants, subject to
prescribed eligibility and registration safeguards. It also incorporates a consequential
drafting correction to provide that "Cost and Works Accountants" be changed to
"Cost Accountants." (Comparative pg. 91)

this section by replacing the punishment with penalties for specific defaults, while
retaining existing consequences for other contraventions. The amendment is part of
the broader decriminalisation exercise under the Bill."

48.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

i) "Liberalization of Cost Records & Cost Audit Requirements. Remove
         mandatory cost record maintenance and cost audit as statutory obligations for
         all classes of companies. Repeal Section 148 of the Companies Act, 2013

                                                      425
         and delete the Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014. May be
         included in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 by repealing Section
         148."

ii) "Existing cost accounting standards do not capture node infrastructure and
         blockchain operations. Hence, Develop Digital Infrastructure Cost Accounting
         Standards for Blockchain Networks and Digital Asset Custodians."

iii) "Fixing responsibility on the officer actually charged with the function, with
         listed/unlisted differentiation and capped continuing penalties, is proportionate
         and consistent with the penalty architecture adopted across the Bill.
         Accordingly, it is recommended that the proposed clause be retained as
         drafted."

iv) The suggestion is that mandatory registration with a statutory professional
         institute or body should not be made an absolute precondition for participation
         in or formation of a Multi-Disciplinary Partnership (MDP). Such a requirement
         may constrain the development of MDPs by excluding specialised
         professionals and subject-matter experts working in emerging or
         interdisciplinary fields--such as management consultants, AI and data-
         security experts, ESG specialists and forensic experts--where a statutory
         professional body or formal regulatory framework may not yet exist. It is
         therefore suggested that eligibility for participation in an MDP should be based
         on recognised qualifications, relevant professional experience and
         demonstrated expertise, rather than statutory registration alone. Making
         statutory registration a mandatory precondition may also not be aligned with
         the objective of accessing the wider global consulting and auditing talent pool
         and may reduce the availability of qualified experts in emerging and
         interdisciplinary fields.

48.5 Examination by the Committee:

48.5.1 On the Suggestion of repealing mandatory cost-record and cost-audit
requirements for all companies the Ministry has stated: -

                  "Cost audits provide a product-specific cost and quantity data which is
         not available in financial audit. The unit-wise, product wise, process-wise
         information derived from cost records facilitates informed decision making and
         analysing the data/information from competitiveness perspective of the
         audited Product/Sector/Industry/Organization. Cost audit is a potent tool for
         detecting and preventing frauds and is essential to support the functions of the
         Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO), GST Authorities, Income Tax

                                                      426
         Authorities which use cost audit reports extensively iii. Cost Audit Reports are
         critical for safeguarding government revenue by identifying "window dressing"
         in books of accounts. They reveal discrepancies where companies understate
         sales to related parties to reduce GST liability or overvalue inventory to secure
         higher bank loans. iv. Regulatory agencies such as the NPPA and the
         Department of Fertilizers use this costing data for subsidy determination and
         monitoring the prices of essential goods. Bodies like CERC use cost related
         data for their benchmark pricing for consumer products. This collaboration
         ensures transparency and effective enforcement across government
         operations. v. Cost audits verify Domestic Value Additions and per-unit costs
         for PLI incentives and Direct Benefit Transfers. The cost accounting records
         and cost audit report also facilitate both the DGTR to determine fair selling
         price and assess the nature of injury and dumping. vi. Cost structures prevent
         cartelization, predatory pricing and revenue leakages, protecting consumers
         from monopolistic exploitation. Cost Audit focus more on operational efficiency
         to drive down costs by detecting wastage and inefficiencies. Helps the
         company management to improve its performance, productivity,
         competitiveness and governance mechanism. Hence, the provision in the
         Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
         change."

48.5.2 On developing Digital Infrastructure Cost Accounting Standards for blockchain
networks and digital asset custodians the ministry in its written reply has stated as
under:

                  "The proposed insertion of section 148(1A) provides an enabling
         framework under which the Central Government may prescribe cost
         accounting standards or any addendum thereto after examination of the
         recommendations of the Institute of Cost Accountants of India. The proposed
         amendment is intended to provide a general enabling framework for
         prescribing cost accounting standards. It is not considered appropriate to
         incorporate sector-specific standards in the Act. Hence, the provision in the
         Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
         change."

48.5.3 On the issue of whether making registration with a statutory professional body
a mandatory requirement for participation in a Multi-Disciplinary Partnership may
exclude qualified experts from emerging and interdisciplinary fields that are not
governed by a statutory professional body, thereby restricting the formation and
functioning of such partnerships, the Ministry acknowledging the issue stated that
provision will be removed as it will affect the constitution of multi-disciplinary
partnership firms.

                                                      427
48.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

48.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 48 of the Bill seeks to amend Section
148 of the Companies Act, 2013, by empowering the Central Government to
prescribe standards of cost accounting or any addendum thereto, after
examination of the recommendations of the Institute of Cost Accountants of
India; permitting firms of cost accountants, subject to prescribed eligibility
requirements, to be appointed as cost auditors; and rationalising the penalty
framework for contraventions relating to cost records and cost audit by
replacing criminal punishment with monetary penalties for specified defaults.

         The Committee note the concerns regarding the compliance requirement
associated with mandatory cost records and cost audit, the adequacy of
existing cost accounting standards for emerging sectors such as blockchain
networks and digital asset custodians, and the proportionality of penalties for
procedural and administrative defaults. The Committee, however, are of the
view that cost records and cost audits serve important regulatory and public
policy objectives, while the proposed enabling framework for prescribing cost
accounting standards provides flexibility to address emerging sectors. The
Committee further observe that the proposed differentiated and capped
penalty framework, which fixes responsibility on the officer charged with the
relevant statutory function, is consistent with the objective of decriminalising
technical and procedural contraventions. The Committee, therefore,
recommend that the existing cost-record and cost-audit framework be
retained, along with the proposed enabling framework for prescribing cost
accounting standards and the proposed penalty provisions.

         The Committee further note the concern that mandatory registration with
a statutory professional institute or body may unnecessarily restrict the
participation of suitably qualified experts from emerging or interdisciplinary
fields where no statutory professional body or formal regulatory framework
may exist. The Committee are of the view that relevant qualifications,
professional experience and demonstrated expertise should be appropriately
recognised, subject to suitable safeguards, and that statutory registration
should not operate as an absolute bar to participation in multidisciplinary
professional partnerships.

         Accordingly, taking into account the justifications and clarifications
furnished by the Ministry, the concerns raised by stakeholders and experts,
and the deliberations held by the Committee, the Committee recommend that
Clause 48 be accepted with suitable modifications to ensure that the

                                                      428
framework for prescribing cost accounting standards remains responsive to
emerging and specialised sectors and that the requirement of mandatory
registration with a statutory professional institute or body does not operate as
an absolute bar to the participation of suitably qualified professionals and
experts in multidisciplinary professional partnerships. The Committee,
accordingly, recommend that Clause 48 (b) be modified as under:

49.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision :

                  "The amendments seek to harmonise sections 149(6)(e)(ii)(B) and
149(11) and provide greater regulatory flexibility by enabling prescription of a lower
pecuniary threshold than the existing ten per cent.

                  On Subsection 6A-

         The amendments seek to harmonise sections 149(6)(e)(ii)(B) and 149(11) and
provide greater regulatory flexibility by enabling prescription of a lower pecuniary
threshold than the existing ten per cent, it also expands the scope of related
provisions to include holding, subsidiary and associate companies."

49.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

i) An explanation should be added in this proviso to the effect that the
         Independent Director can continue to be appointed or reappointed in the
         capacity of Independent Director in the holding, subsidiary or associate
         company, till completion of his term specified under Sections 149(10) and
         (11). The proposed amendment in the Bill ignores the fact that their is already
         a shortage of Independent Directors. Adding the phrase "or its holding,
         subsidiary or associate compony" would eventually make the person Vacate
         his office in Holding/ Subsidiary/ Associate immediately. At least the provision
         should allow completion of the current term and no further continuance be
         undertaken to maintain the independence "n "Cooling off". It appears that the
         intent of the revised provision is to ensure that during the cooling-off period,
         an Independent Director (ID) should not have any pecuniary relationship with
         the company or its holding, subsidiary or associate companies. However,
         such a Director should be allowed to continue or re-appointed as ID in its
         holding, subsidiary or associate companies. A practical issue arises when an
         ID serves on multiple Boards with different appointment dates. In terms of the
         proposed amendment, upon completion of Mr. A's tenure as an ID in ABC Ltd.
         on 30th April 2026, he may be required to step down from XYZ Ltd. on the
         same date, as he would not be permitted to continue as an ID in a holding,
         subsidiary, or associate company beyond that date. Such an outcome could
         lead to an unintended and premature cessation of office in the associate
         company, potentially disrupting Board continuity and effectively nullifying the
         tenure previously approved by the shareholders of the concerned associate
         company.

ii) It has been suggested that proposed amendment should be dropped. The
         proposed amendment empowers the Government to prescribe a lower
         threshold for having pecuniary relationship with a legal / consulting firm, where
         the concerned Independent Director is a partner / proprietor / employee. The

                                                      436
         threshold of 10% for determining materiality of such transactions is sufficient
         and in line with other such thresholds prescribed under the Companies Act,
         2013."

iii) It has been suggested that the intent of the revised provision is to ensure that
         during the cooling-off period, an Independent Director (ID) should not have
         any pecuniary relationship with the company or its holding, subsidiary or
         associate companies. However, such a Director should be allowed to continue
         or re-appointed as ID in its holding, subsidiary or associate companies."

iv) The amendment to Section 149 validates the appointment of an Independent
         Director as an additional director but does not make corresponding changes
         to the enabling provision under Section 161 or the terminology in Schedule IV.
         Accordingly, it is suggested that Consequential amendments are therefore
         required to give full effect to the legislative intent and maintain internal
         consistency within the Companies Act, 2013. Therefore, consider introducing
         consequential amendments to Section 161, Section 149, and Schedule IV to
         give effect to the proposed amendment relating to independent directors.
         Specifically: - (i) Expressly empower the Board to appoint an Independent
         Director as an additional director (ii) Align terminology in Schedule IV.

v) Independent Directors provide objective, unbiased expertise. Serving one
         company within a business group does not compromise a director's
         independence toward other companies in that same group. Therefore, if an
         Independent Director leaves one group company, there should be no "cooling-
         off" period before another company in the same group can appoint them.
         Removing this restriction allows businesses to retain trusted, experienced
         leaders without harming corporate governance. Accordingly, it has been
         suggested to relax this requirement in Clause 49 (6A) (iii) of the Corporate
         Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026.

vi) "Board expertise is essential for technology-driven financial institutions. It has
         been suggested requiring at least one independent director with
         blockchain/cybersecurity/fintech expertise for significant IFSCA-regulated
         entities."

vii) Extending the look-back to the current year and counting additional-director
         stints toward tenure close two well-known circumvention routes and align the
         Act with LODR. Explanation 2 in particular addresses the practice of
         "evergreen" additional directorships. The carve-out for professional-firm
         partners is a sensible proportionality measure that avoids disqualifying
         candidates for de minimis firm-level dealings. It has been suggested that the
         clause be retained, subject to the clarification that the declaration under
         section 149(7) shall be the mode of compliance with sub-section (6A), so that
         the continuing obligation does not spawn a separate certification regime.

                                                      437
49.5 Examination by the Committee:

49.5.1. On the issue of clarifying that an Independent Director may continue in group
companies until completion of their statutory term under Sections 149(10)/(11). The
ministry has stated :-

                  "The suggestion proposes that Independent Directors complete their
         term in the group companies where they have already been appointed, even if
         their tenure in the original company has been completed. The amendment to
         include `or its holding, subsidiary or associate company' has been expressly
         proposed to ensure director independence, transparency and accountability.
         Accordingly, the suggestion to allow independent directors to complete their
         current terms of appointment in holding, subsidiary or associate companies
         would counter the intended proposal under Clause 49 of the Amendment Bill.
         Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be
         retained without any change."

49.5.2. On the suggestion to withdraw the amendment the Ministry has stated as
under:

                  "The proposed amendment to section 149 does not alter the existing
         threshold under the Act; it merely enables the Central Government to
         prescribe a lower threshold, if considered necessary, through subordinate
         legislation. This provides the flexibility to calibrate the materiality threshold for
         assessing the independence of independent directors in light of regulatory and
         market developments, without requiring a legislative amendment. Hence, the
         provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained
         without any change."

49.5.3. Regarding an Independent Director be allowed to continue/be reappointed in
group companies during the cooling-off period; The Ministry in its written response
has stated as under:

                   "The proposed amendment expressly extends the cooling-off
         restriction under the proviso to section 149(11) to the holding, subsidiary and
         associate companies of the company. This is to ensure that an individual
         completing the maximum permissible tenure as an independent director does
         not continue to remain associated with the same corporate group during the
         mandatory cooling-off period. Permitting appointment as an independent
         director in another company within the same group would dilute the
         effectiveness of the cooling-off requirement and the objective of preserving
         the independence of independent directors. Hence, the Ministry has proposed

                                                      438
         the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained
         without any change."

49.5.4. With respect to suggestion to make consequential amendments to Sections
161 and Schedule IV to align with the amendment to Section 149 permitting the
appointment of Independent Directors as additional directors the Ministry has stated:

                  "Section 161 already enables the Board to appoint "any person" as an
         additional director, subject to the provisions of the Act and the articles of the
         company. Accordingly, a person satisfying the eligibility requirements under
         section 149 may be appointed as an additional director. The proposed
         Explanation 2 to section 149 merely clarifies that the period served as an
         additional director shall be included in computing the tenure of an independent
         director and does not create a new power of appointment. Consequently, no
         corresponding amendment to section 161 or Schedule IV is considered
         necessary. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,
         2026 may be retained without any change."

49.5.5. On the suggestion to relax this requirement in Clause 49 (6A) (iii) regarding
"cooling-off" period of Independent Director, the Ministry in its written submission
stated as under:

                  "The proposed amendment extends the cooling-off requirement to the
         holding, subsidiary and associate companies to reinforce both the actual and
         perceived independence of independent directors across a corporate group.
         Given the close operational and governance linkages that may exist within
         such groups, permitting immediate appointment in another group company
         could dilute the effectiveness of the cooling-off period. Hence, the provision in
         the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
         change."

49.5.6. On the issue of prescribing specific technical expertise for Independent
Directors, the ministry opined that Prescribing specific technical expertise for
Independent Directors may not be appropriate as the skill requirements may vary
depending upon the nature of business and activities of the company. Further,
entities regulated by IFSCA may be governed by sector-specific requirements,
wherever applicable. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill,
2026 is proposed to be retained without any change.

49.5.7 On seeking clarification that the declaration under section 149(7) shall be the
mode of compliance with sub-section (6A), so that the continuing obligation does not
spawn a separate certification regime, the Ministry has stated that the suggestion will
be considered during rule making stage.

                                                      439
49.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

49.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 49 of the Bill seeks to amend Section
149 of the Companies Act, 2013, relating to the eligibility, continuing
independence and tenure of independent directors. The proposed
amendments seek to extend certain independence-related restrictions to the
current financial year; replace the reference to "company secretaries in
practice" with "secretarial auditors"; enable the prescription of a lower
pecuniary threshold for transactions involving legal or consulting firms;
require independent directors to continue to satisfy the prescribed eligibility
conditions during their tenure; extend the cooling-off restriction to the holding,
subsidiary and associate companies of the company; permit a limited
exception in respect of transactions of legal or consulting firms below the
prescribed threshold; and provide that the tenure served as an additional
director shall be counted towards the tenure of an independent director.

         The Committee observe that the proposed amendments seek to
strengthen the continuing independence of independent directors, prevent
circumvention of the prescribed tenure and cooling-off requirements, and
provide regulatory flexibility to calibrate the materiality threshold for assessing
potential conflicts of interest. The Committee also note the concerns raised
regarding the possible premature cessation of the tenure of independent
directors in group companies, the extension of the cooling-off restriction
across the corporate group, the proposed delegation of power to prescribe a
lower pecuniary threshold, and the absence of corresponding amendments to
Section 161 and Schedule IV. The Committee, however, note the clarifications
furnished by the Ministry that the proposed extension of the cooling-off
restriction is intended to preserve the actual and perceived independence of
independent directors across a corporate group; that the existing threshold is
not being altered but may be calibrated through subordinate legislation in
response to regulatory and market developments; and that Section 161 already
enables the appointment of any eligible person as an additional director, while

                                                      440
the proposed amendment merely clarifies that such tenure shall be counted for
the purposes of determining the tenure of an independent director.

         The Committee further note the concern that prescribing specific
technical expertise for independent directors of entities regulated by the
International Financial Services Centres Authority may not be appropriate, as
the skill requirements may vary depending upon the nature and activities of
the concerned entity and may be addressed, wherever necessary, through
sector-specific regulatory requirements. The Committee also note the
Ministry's assurance that the manner of compliance with the continuing
eligibility requirement under proposed sub-section (6A), including the role of
the declaration under sub-section (7), would be considered at the rule-making
stage. The Committee are of the view that the subordinate legislative
framework should ensure that the continuing compliance requirement does
not result in the creation of a separate or duplicative certification mechanism.

         Accordingly, taking into account the justifications and clarifications
furnished by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, the views and suggestions
received from stakeholders and experts, and the deliberations held by the
Committee, the Committee are of the opinion that the proposed amendments
seek to strengthen the framework governing the independence, eligibility and
tenure of independent directors while providing the necessary regulatory
flexibility to address evolving corporate and market circumstances. The
Committee, therefore, recommend that Clause 49 of the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 be accepted without amendment.

appointment.

         (6) (a) Unless the articles provide for the retirement of all directors at
every annual general meeting, not less than two-thirds of the total number of
directors of a public company shall--

         (i) be persons whose period of office is liable to determination by
retirement of directors by rotation; and

         (ii) save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act, be appointed by
the company in general meeting.

         (b) The remaining directors in the case of any such company shall, in
default of, and subject to any regulations in the articles of the company, also
be appointed by the company in general meeting.

         (c) At the first annual general meeting of a public company held next
after the date of the general meeting at which the first directors are appointed
in accordance with clauses (a) and (b) and at every subsequent annual
general meeting, one-third of such of the directors for the time being as are
liable to retire by rotation, or if their number is neither three nor a multiple of
three, then, the number nearest to one-third, shall retire from office.

         (d) The directors to retire by rotation at every annual general meeting
shall be those who have been longest in office since their last appointment,
but as between persons who became directors on the same day, those who
are to retire shall, in default of and subject to any agreement among
themselves, be determined by lot.

         (e) At the annual general meeting at which a director retires as
aforesaid, the company may fill up the vacancy by appointing the retiring
director or some other person thereto.

                                             443
                  Explanation.--For the purposes of this sub-section, "total number of
         directors" shall not include independent directors, whether appointed under
         this Act or any other law for the time being in force, on the Board of a
         company.

                  (7) (a) If the vacancy of the retiring director is not so filled-up and the
         meeting has not expressly resolved not to fill the vacancy, the meeting shall
         stand adjourned till the same day in the next week, at the same time and
         place, or if that day is a national holiday, till the next succeeding day which is
         not a holiday, at the same time and place.

                  (b) If at the adjourned meeting also, the vacancy of the retiring director
         is not filled up and that meeting also has not expressly resolved not to fill the
         vacancy, the retiring director shall be deemed to have been reappointed at the
         adjourned meeting, unless-- (i) at that meeting or at the previous meeting a
         resolution for the re-appointment of such director has been put to the meeting
         and lost; (ii) the retiring director has, by a notice in writing addressed to the
         company or its Board of directors, expressed his unwillingness to be so re-
         appointed; (iii) he is not qualified or is disqualified for appointment; (iv) a
         resolution, whether special or ordinary, is required for his appointment or re-
         appointment by virtue of any provisions of this Act; or (v) section 162 is
         applicable to the case.

                   Explanation.--For the purposes of this section and section 160, the
         expression "retiring director" means a director retiring by rotation.

50.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

         "The amendment seeks to strengthen enforcement of the Director
Identification Number (DIN) framework. The amendment is proposed for ensuring
proper enforcement by prescribing the circumstances and manner in which the
Director Identification Number of an individual may be deactivated or cancelled."

50.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

i) "A suitable relaxation or alternative mechanism may be provided for foreign
         directors with respect to annual DIR-3 KYC compliance, particularly where
         OTP-based authentication on foreign mobile numbers and MCA portal access
         poses practical challenges. Foreign directors often face persistent technical
         and operational difficulties in completing DIR-3 KYC (OTP issues, foreign
         mobile number restrictions, portal access). Automatic deactivation of DIN due
         to non-completion of DIR-3 KYC, despite genuine intent, creates compliance
         risks for companies and may result in unintended noncompliance."
                                                      444
ii) "Replace 'he has been allotted the' with 'he holds a valid' DIN. This clearly
         expresses the continuing obligation throughout the directorship tenure and
         removes interpretational ambiguity in the existing language. A director must
         hold a valid, non-deactivated/cancelled DIN -- not merely have been 'allotted'
         one."

50.5 Examination by the Committee:

50.5.1. On the issue of DIR-3 KYC compliance issues faced by foreign directors, the
Ministry in its written submission furnished as below:

                  "Suggestion will be considered appropriately during framing of
         subordinate legislation. The suggestion relates to procedural compliance with
         DIR-3 KYC and the deactivation of Director Identification Numbers. The
         proposed suggestion falls outside the scope of the statute. Practical difficulties
         faced by foreign directors in completing DIR-3 KYC are being examined
         separately through the relevant Rules. It is also to be noted that annual
         Director KYC requirement has been replace with once in 3 years KYC."

50.5.2 Regarding the suggestion seeking to replace a past event ("has been
allotted") with a continuing eligibility requirement ("holds a valid"), thereby removing
ambiguity regarding the status of the DIN during the director's tenure. The Ministry in
its written reply stated as under:

                  "The proposed suggestion is not accepted. However, the proposed
         amendment to Section 152 is being withdrawn. Further, suitable modifications
         are also being done in the proposed amendment under Section 154. Hence,
         the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 shall be modified accordingly."

50.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

50.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 50 seeks to amend sub-section (3) of
Section 152 of the Companies Act, 2013, to provide that no person shall be
appointed as, or continue to function as, a director unless such person has
been allotted a Director Identification Number (DIN) or such other prescribed
identification number, and that such number has not been deactivated or
cancelled. The Committee further note the concerns expressed by
stakeholders regarding the proposed linkage of a director's eligibility to
continue in office with the status of the DIN, particularly in view of practical

                                                      445
difficulties relating to DIR-3 KYC compliance, especially in the case of foreign
directors, the absence of a statutory grace period before deactivation, the need
for timely reactivation upon compliance, and the possibility of unintended
consequences for companies arising from technical or procedural lapses.
Certain stakeholders also sought clarity regarding the expression "other
number" and submitted that matters relating to DIN compliance are more
appropriately addressed through the existing statutory and regulatory
framework rather than by making the validity of the DIN a continuing statutory
condition for holding office as a director.

The Committee note that, during the course of examination, the Ministry has
informed the Committee that the proposed amendment to Section 152 is being
withdrawn and that Clause 50 is proposed to be omitted from the Bill, with
consequential modifications being made to the proposed amendments under
Section 154.

The Committee, therefore, recommend omission of Clause 50 of the Bill. At the
same time, the Committee are of the view that matters relating to DIR-3 KYC
compliance, the deactivation and reactivation of Director Identification
Numbers, facilitation of compliance by foreign directors, and other procedural
aspects of the DIN framework should continue to be addressed through
appropriately framed rules and administrative mechanisms, ensuring that
compliance requirements are effective, proportionate and do not result in
undue hardship or unintended disruption to the governance and functioning of
companies.

51. Clause 51 of the Bill proposes to amend Section 154 of the Companies

51.1 Provision proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

                  "(2) A person who has been allotted Director Identification Number
         under sub-section (1) shall submit such information towards verification of his

                  (3)(i) Where the person referred to in sub-section (2) does not comply

                                                      447
                  (a) the DIN was obtained by furnishing any false or incorrect

                  (i) deactivation of Director Identification Number shall mean the

51.3 Reasons/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

         "The amendment seeks to strengthen the framework relating to Director

51.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

i) Leaving the scope of discretion to deactivate or cancel DIN can be
         problematic and requires proper justification or rationale. (3) Where-- (a) the
         person referred to in sub-section (2) does not comply with the provisions of
         the said sub-section; or (b) the Director Identification Number has been
         allotted in contravention of the provisions of this Act or the rules made
         thereunder; or (c) a director has incurred disqualification in one or more
         companies pursuant to the provisions of section 164, or where the Tribunal or
         any competent court has passed an order in this regard, the Director
         Identification Number allotted to him shall be deactivated or cancelled, in such
         manner as may be prescribed, by the Central Government or the officer
         authorised by that Government in this behalf.

ii) "Safeguards against arbitrary cancellation; to support natural justice.
         Therefore, it is suggested providing opportunity of being heard before
         cancellation/deactivation."

iii) Section 155 prohibits possession of more than one DIN but does not provide
         any statutory mechanism for surrendering additional DINs. Consequently,
         individuals who inadvertently possess multiple DINs have no clear legal
         pathway to regularize their position, despite MCA permitting surrender
         administratively. A statutory provision enabling surrender of additional DINs
         would improve legal certainty, facilitate database cleansing, and strengthen
         the integrity of the DIN framework.

51.5 Examination by the Committee:

51.5.1 On the issue of clarification with respect to deactivation or cancellation of DIN
the Ministry has stated as under:

                                                      449
                   "Proposed amendment is being modified to bring more clarity on the
         grounds for cancellation and deactivation with proper safeguards. Hence, the
         provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 shall be modified
         accordingly."

51.5.2. On the suggestions involving an opportunity to be heard before cancellation
and deactivation of the DIN, the ministry has stated that it may be appropriately dealt
with at the rule making stage.

51.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

51.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 51 of the Bill seeks to amend Section
154 of the Companies Act, 2013, by providing a statutory framework for the
verification of particulars furnished by holders of Director Identification
Numbers (DINs) and specifying the circumstances and manner in which a DIN
may be deactivated or cancelled. The proposed amendment seeks to address
non-compliance with verification requirements, disqualification of directors,
obtaining a DIN through false or incorrect information, surrender of DIN in
prescribed circumstances and other specified situations. It also provides that
a reasonable opportunity of being heard shall be given before cancellation of a
DIN on the ground of false or incorrect information or suppression of material
facts.

The Committee note the concerns regarding the scope of discretion in the
deactivation or cancellation of DINs and the need for clear grounds and
adequate procedural safeguards to prevent arbitrary action. The Committee
are of the view that, given the significant consequences associated with the
deactivation or cancellation of a DIN, the statutory framework should clearly
define the grounds and consequences of such action and ensure that the
power is exercised in a transparent, reasoned and proportionate manner. The
Committee further emphasise that the principles of natural justice should be
adequately safeguarded and that a reasonable opportunity of being heard
should be provided, wherever the circumstances permit, before any adverse
action resulting in the deactivation or cancellation of a DIN is taken. The
Committee also recommend that the subordinate legislative framework should

                                                      450
prescribe clear procedures for a fair, transparent and time-bound procedure
for notice, rectification and reactivation of a DIN, particularly in cases of
procedural or verification-related non-compliance.

         The Committee further note that the proposed amendment to Section
154 establishes a comprehensive statutory framework governing the
deactivation and cancellation of Director Identification Numbers. Being the
principal provision governing the subject, Section 154 should
comprehensively regulate all matters relating to deactivation and cancellation
of DINs. The Committee are of the view that the corresponding provisions of
Sections 152 and 167 should be harmonised with the amended Section 154 so
as to ensure statutory consistency, avoid duplication and provide legal clarity.

         Accordingly, the Committee recommend that Clause 51 be accepted with
suitable modifications to clearly specify the grounds and safeguards
governing the deactivation and cancellation of DINs. The modified Clause 51
may be read as under:

"51. Section 154 of the principal Act shall be numbered as sub-section (1)
thereof and--

      (a) in the marginal heading, after the word "Allotment", the words
      "deactivation and cancellation" shall be inserted;

      (b) after sub-section (1) as so numbered, the following sub-sections shall
      be inserted, namely:--

           "(2) A person who has been allotted Director Identification Number under
           sub-section (1) shall submit such information towards verification of his
           particulars to the Central Government [***] at such intervals and in such
           manner, as may be prescribed.

      [***]

     (3) Where the person referred to in sub-section (2) does not comply
     with the provisions of the said sub-section the Director Identification
     Number allotted to such person shall be deactivated by the Central
     Government in such manner as may be prescribed.

   [***]

            (4) Where a director has incurred disqualification in one or more
     companies pursuant to the provisions of section 164, except on
     account of the proviso to clause (d) of sub-section (1) of that section,
     [***] the Director Identification Number allotted to him shall be
     deactivated [***], in such manner as may be prescribed [***].

[***]

     (5) Where a disqualification is incurred on account of the proviso to
     clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 164, the Director Identification
     Number allotted to him shall be cancelled in such manner as may be
     prescribed and such person shall not be eligible to apply for a Director
     Identification Number again.

(6) Where--

       (a) the Director Identification Number was obtained by furnishing any
       false or incorrect information or representation or by suppressing
       any material fact or information in any of the documents or
       declaration filed or made for obtaining such Director Identification
       Number; or

       (b) an application has been made for the surrender of the Director
       Identification Number, in case holder of Director Identification
       Number has died, or on account of any other grounds, as may be
       prescribed,

  then such Director Identification Number, shall be cancelled in such
  manner as may be prescribed.

       the Central Government.

     (i) deactivation of Director Identification Number shall mean the

subsists in terms of sub-section (4); and

     (ii) cancellation of Director Identification Number shall mean the
