                                                453
                                              CLAUSE - 51A

INSERTION OF NEW PROVISION

51A. New insertion of proviso in section 155 with regard to surrender of
additional Director Identification Numbers

51A.1 Examination by the Committee:

51A.1.1 During the examination of the proposed amendments to the Companies Act,
2013, the Committee noted that section 155 of the Act presently prohibits an
individual who has already been allotted a Director Identification Number (DIN) under
section 154 from applying for, obtaining or possessing another DIN. However, the
Committee observed that while the existing provision prohibits possession of multiple
DINs, it does not expressly provide a statutory mechanism for surrendering
additional DINs in cases where an individual is already in possession of more than
one DIN, whether on account of inadvertent duplication, legacy allotments, changes
in personal particulars, or other administrative reasons. The Ministry acknowledging
the above concern, proposed insertion of the following proviso to section 155 of the
principal Act:

       "Provided that an individual in possession of more than one Director
       Identification Number, shall make an application to surrender every such
       additional Director Identification Number in such manner within such time as
       may be prescribed."

51A.2 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

51A.2  The Committee note that the Director Identification Number

serves as a unique and permanent identifier for individuals acting as directors

and constitutes an important element of the corporate regulatory framework

for maintaining accurate records of directorships and ensuring effective

regulatory oversight.

                                     454
The Committee observe that while section 155 of the Companies Act, 2013
prohibits an individual from obtaining or possessing more than one Director
Identification Number, the Act does not presently provide an express statutory
mechanism requiring the surrender of additional Director Identification
Numbers where an individual is already in possession of multiple DINs.
Consequently, persons holding duplicate DINs, including those arising on
account of inadvertent allotment, legacy records or administrative errors, lack
a clear statutory process for regularising their position.

The Committee are of the view that providing an express statutory obligation
to surrender every additional Director Identification Number would facilitate
cleansing of the DIN database, preserve the integrity of the identification
framework, prevent duplication of records and strengthen regulatory
oversight. The Committee further note that prescribing the manner and time
within which such surrender is to be made through rules would provide the
necessary administrative flexibility while ensuring uniform implementation.

The Committee, therefore, recommend the insertion of the proposed proviso to
section 155 of the principal Act, as under:

In section 155 of the principal Act, the following proviso shall be inserted,
namely:-

         "Provided that an individual in possession of more than one Director
         Identification Number, shall make an application to surrender every such
         additional Director Identification Number in such manner within such
         time as may be prescribed."

                                               CLAUSE - 52

52. Clause 52 of the Bill proposes to amend Section 159 of the Companies
Act, 2013.

52.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

                  159. Penalty for default of certain provisions.--If any individual or
         director of a company makes any default in complying with any of the
         provisions of section 152, section 155 and section 156, such individual or
         director of the company shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to fifty
         thousand rupees and where the default is a continuing one, with a further
         penalty which may extend to five hundred rupees for each day after the first
         during which such default continues, subject to a maximum of five lakh
         rupees.

52.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013):

                  159: Penalty for Default of Certain Provisions:

                  If any individual or director of a company makes any default in
         complying with any of the provisions of section 152, section 155 and section
         156, such individual or director of the company shall be liable to a penalty
         which may extend to of fifty thousand rupees and where the default is a
         continuing one, with a further penalty which may extend to of five hundred
         rupees for each day after the first during which such default continues subject
         to a maximum of five lakh rupees.

52.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"Amendment in section 159 is proposed to fix the quantum of penalty by replacing
the discretionary penalty with a fixed amount and introducing a cap on continuing
penalties thereby removing adjudicatory discretion."

52.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

         By way of proposed amendment, a minimum penalty of Rs. 25 thousand may
         be introduced and the maximum penalty may be restricted to Rs. 50
         thousand, as it already stands in unamended provision. The proposed
         amendment substitutes the words "which may extend to "with the word "of" as
         a result of which it proposes to have a fixed penalty of Rs. 50 thousand.

                                                      456
Whereas the unamended provision prescribes for a penalty which may extend
to Rs.50 thousand thereby prescribing no minimum penalty and restricting the
maximum penalty to Rs.50 thousand.

52.5 Examination by the Committee:

52.5.1.  On the suggestion of having a minimum penalty of Rs 25,000 and

capping the maximum at Rs 50,000, the Ministry has stated the following: -

"The amendment in section 159 is proposed to fix the quantum of penalty by
replacing the discretionary penalty with a fixed amount and introducing a cap
on continuing penalty thereby removing adjudicatory discretion. The existing
penalty of INR 500 each day for continuing default is now proposed to be
capped at INR 5 lakhs. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change".

52.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

52.6.1.  The Committee note that Clause 52 of the Bill seeks to amend

Section 159 of the Companies Act, 2013, by replacing the expression "which

may extend to" with the expression "of", thereby providing for a fixed penalty

of 50,000 for defaults in complying with Sections 152, 155 and 156 of the Act.

The Clause further seeks to introduce a maximum ceiling of 5 lakh on the

additional penalty leviable for continuing defaults.

The Committee have considered the suggestion that a minimum penalty of
25,000 may be prescribed while retaining 50,000 as the maximum penalty, in
view of the fact that the existing provision does not prescribe a minimum
penalty and leaves the quantum of penalty to be determined, up to the
prescribed maximum, having regard to the facts and circumstances of each
case. The Committee also note the Ministry's submission that the proposed
amendment seeks to bring certainty and uniformity in the quantum of penalty
by removing adjudicatory discretion and, at the same time, introducing a cap
on the continuing penalty, which may otherwise accumulate without an upper
limit.

                                    457
The Committee are of the view that while certainty and uniformity in the levy of
penalties are important objectives, a fixed penalty may, in certain cases, result
in disproportionate consequences, particularly where the nature, duration and
circumstances of the default may vary. Considering that the proposed
amendment is intended to bring greater transparency and certainty in the levy
of penalties and that the continuing penalty is now proposed to be subject to
an overall ceiling of 5 lakh, the Committee accept the amendment proposed
under Clause 52 and recommend that the same may be retained without
modification.

                                                      458
                                               CLAUSE - 53

53.3. Reason/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the

53.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

i) "Request that such directors be permitted to hold office until next AGM without
         a separate general meeting (existing position - board fills casual vacancy
         subject to approval in next general meeting - may also be retained).  If
         enforced, restrict to listed and large unlisted public companies; exclude other

ii) "Conducting EGM within 3 months is costly for small/unlisted companies.
         Permit continuation till next AGM. Appointment in next AGM is best course if

iii) "It is recommended that the clause be modified as follows: in sub-sections (1)

         period to be obtained by postal ballot or e-voting without convening a general
         meeting. The mischief, additional directors continuing for years without
         shareholder ratification is real, and sub-section (5) rightly prevents boards

         almost immediately upon every board-level appointment, generating cost
         without governance gain. A six month limit, coupled with remote-approval
         mechanics, achieves shareholder primacy at proportionate cost. This is
         among the provisions most likely to create day one operational friction if
         enacted as introduced."

53.5 Examination by the Committee:

53.5.1. Regarding the suggestion that directors be permitted to hold office until next
AGM, the ministry has submitted:-

         "The proposed amendment appropriately strengthens shareholder oversight
         by ensuring that appointments of additional directors and directors appointed
         against casual vacancies are placed before members within a reasonable
         timeframe. Permitting such directors to continue until the next AGM, or limiting
         the requirement only to certain classes of companies, such as listed / large

                                                      461
         unlisted public companies, would dilute the objective of timely shareholder
         approval and may enable prolonged board appointments. Hence, the
         provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained
         without any change. "

53.5.2. "On the issue of permitting continuation in office till the next AGM the Ministry
has opined that provision is in the interest of corporate governance and with Virtual
EGMs being allowed, this would not entail additional financial burden."

53.3.3. "The Ministry with regard to the suggestion on extending the timeline has
stated that the proposed 3 months period is sufficient for appointment of a Director."

53.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

53.6.1 The Committee note that Clause 53 of the Bill seeks to amend Section
161 of the Companies Act, 2013, relating to the appointment of additional
directors and directors appointed against casual vacancies. The proposed
amendment seeks to provide that an additional director and a director
appointed to fill a casual vacancy shall hold office up to the date of the next
general meeting or for a period of three months from the date of appointment,
whichever is earlier. The Clause further seeks to provide that a person whose
appointment as a director could not be considered or was not approved by the
members in a general meeting shall not thereafter be appointed by the Board
as an additional director, alternate director or director against a casual
vacancy without the prior approval of the members.

The Committee observe that the proposed amendment seeks to strengthen
shareholder oversight by ensuring that appointments made by the Board are
placed before the members for approval within a specified and reasonable
timeframe. The Committee also note the concerns expressed by stakeholders
that the requirement of convening a general meeting within three months may
impose additional procedural and financial burdens, particularly on small and
unlisted companies, and the suggestion that the period may be extended to six

                                                      462
months or that such directors may be permitted to continue until the next
Annual General Meeting. However, the Committee further note the Ministry's
submission that permitting such directors to continue until the next Annual
General Meeting may dilute the objective of timely shareholder approval and
may enable prolonged continuation of appointments without effective
shareholder oversight. The Committee also note the Ministry's clarification
that the proposed period of three months is considered sufficient for obtaining
the approval of members and that the availability of virtual general meetings
would mitigate the concerns relating to additional cost and logistical burden.

The Committee are of the view that timely approval of appointments by
shareholders is an important corporate governance safeguard and that the
proposed three-month period seeks to ensure that directors appointed by the
Board do not continue in office for an extended period without shareholder
approval. The Committee further observe that the proposed provision under
sub-section (5), which prevents the Board from reappointing a person whose
appointment as a director has not been approved by the members without
their prior approval, appropriately reinforces shareholder primacy and
prevents the circumvention of an adverse decision of the members.

Accordingly, taking into account the justifications and clarifications furnished
by the Ministry, the views and suggestions received from stakeholders and
experts, and the deliberations held by the Committee, the Committee
recommend that Clause 53 be accepted without any amendment.

54.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment seeks to strengthen the disqualification framework for directors by
reducing the threshold for non-filing of financial statements or annual returns from
three consecutive financial years to two. It also expands the scope of disqualification
by including certain professional roles associated with the company and introducing
a "fit and proper person" requirement, and provides for consequential vacation of
office under section 167."

54.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

Some of the important suggestions given by experts and stakeholders are as under:

i) "It has been Suggested against the proposal on the grounds that the "fit and
         proper" criteria is susceptible to abuse, with a recommendation to revise the
         monetary thresholds upward. The proposal relating to the "fit and proper"
         criteria should be omitted, as it may be used to prematurely remove a director
         despite the appointment having been approved by shareholders, thereby
         diminishing the authority of shareholders. Further, the monetary threshold of
         INR 1,000 under Schedule V for disqualification based on fines imposed
                                                      466
         under specified Acts should be revised upward, as it is outdated. For instance,
         the minimum fine under the Companies Act, 2013 is INR 10,000, while the
         minimum fine under the SEBI Act is INR 1 lakh. The proposed "fit and proper"
         criteria also presents a potential risk of misuse, as it may be relied upon to
         facilitate the removal of a director during the course of their tenure.
         Additionally, unlike statutory auditors, a registered valuer is associated with
         the company only for a particular assignment and is not engaged on a
         continuous basis. Accordingly, the proposed three-year cooling-off period is
         disproportionate, considering the assignment-based nature of a registered
         valuer's involvement. "

ii) It was suggested that:

         (i) the amendment to clause (g) be reconsidered, and in any event confined
         to penalties imposed for contraventions of section 188 involving failure to
         obtain requisite approvals, excluding technical defaults; (ii) clause (j) be
         retained as drafted; (iii) clause (k) be reconsidered, and, if retained, recast so
         that the disqualifying criteria are set out in the section itself (conviction for
         specified offences, debarment by a financial-sector regulator, wilful default,
         fugitive status), with assessment by the board recorded by reasoned
         resolution and subject to the aggrieved person's right to be heard; and (iv) the
         change to sub-section (2)(a) be retained as drafted in view of the six month
         cure period introduced by Clause 57. (i) Attaching the civic disability of
         disqualification to a civil penalty inverts the Bill's own decriminalisation logic-
         penalties are being substituted for offences precisely because the underlying
         defaults are technical; (iii) "fit and proper" as an open-ended, rule-prescribed
         disqualification is constitutionally vulnerable for vagueness and excessive
         delegation- disqualification affects the right to carry on occupation and
         demands legislative precision (cf. the structured fit-and-proper tests in the
         SEBI Intermediaries Regulations and the Banking Regulation Act, section
         10A); a board administered test also risks incumbent entrenchment against
         nominee and minority-appointed directors. Clause (j), by contrast, is a well-
         crafted cooling-off that fortifies gatekeeper independence and merits support.

iii) The provisions related to `subjected to penalty for default' and `fit and proper'
         criteria will be omitted Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws
         (Amendment) Bill, 2026 shall be modified accordingly.

          It has further been submitted that attaching the disqualification under clause
         (g) to a mere monetary penalty runs contrary to the decriminalisation logic
         underlying the Bill, since penalties are being substituted for offences precisely
         because the underlying defaults are technical in nature. It has also been
         submitted that the "fit and proper" criterion proposed under clause (k), being
         left to be prescribed by rules, is vague and amounts to excessive delegation
         of a matter that carries serious civil consequences for the individual
         concerned, and that a disqualification test administered by the board itself
         risks being used against nominee or minority-appointed directors. Clause (j),

                                                      467
         providing a cooling-off period for auditors and other professionals, has been
         described as well-drafted and worthy of retention. Accordingly, it has been
         suggested that clause (g) be reconsidered and, in any event, confined to
         failure to obtain requisite approvals under Section 188, excluding technical
         defaults; that clause (j) be retained as drafted; that clause (k), if retained, set
         out the disqualifying criteria in the statute itself, namely conviction for specified
         offences, debarment by a financial sector regulator, wilful default, or fugitive
         status, with the board's assessment recorded by reasoned resolution and
         subject to the aggrieved person's right to be heard; and that the amendment
         to sub-section (2)(a) be retained as drafted, having regard to the six-month
         cure period introduced under Clause 57.

         On clause (g), it has been submitted that the proposed expansion of
         disqualification to cover monetary penalties brings into focus the overlap
         between Section 188 and Regulation 23 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations,
         2015, which differ in their definition of "related party", approval thresholds and
         disclosure requirements, creating a grey area where a transaction compliant
         with one may breach the other. It has been suggested that clarity be provided
         on whether a penalty arising from an otherwise Section 188-compliant
         transaction, or one identified solely through SEBI action, would attract
         disqualification, and that the amendment be calibrated so as not to extend to
         transactions undertaken in compliance with the safeguards under Section
         188, since the real regulatory concern is abuse through inadequate disclosure
         or diversion of funds, and not the existence of related party transactions as
         such.

         On clause (j), it has been submitted that including registered valuers within
         the same disqualification framework as auditors and insolvency professionals
         merits reconsideration, since a valuer's engagement is ordinarily limited to a
         specific assignment and ends on its completion, unlike the continuous
         association of auditors, and that valuers are already subject to stringent
         independence requirements under the Companies (Registered Valuers and
         Valuation) Rules, 2017. It has accordingly been suggested that the
         disqualification for registered valuers be reconsidered, distinguished from
         continuing engagements, or made subject to a shorter cooling-off period.

         On clause (k), it has been submitted that leaving substantive matters such as
         the "fit and proper" criteria, and the scope and quantum of penalties under
         Sections 139(12) and 446B, to be prescribed by rules amounts to excessive
         delegation of essential legislative functions, and it has been suggested that
         the Bill incorporate the essential parameters and guiding principles for such
         criteria in the primary legislation itself.

iv) Section 164(1)(g) may accordingly be amended as follows: A person shall not
         be eligible for appointment as a director of a company, if -- he has been
         convicted of the offence penalties have been imposed upon him for violation
         of the provisions dealing with related party transactions under section 188 at
                                                      468
         any time during the last preceding five years, or penalties have been imposed
         upon him by the Securities and Exchange Board, or he has been convicted
         under the provisions of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
         (15 of 1992), for violation of the provisions dealing with related party
         transactions under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing
         Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, at any time
         during the last preceding five years; or Section 164(1)(g) of the Companies
         Act provides that a person shall not be eligible for appointment as a director of
         a company, if he has been convicted of the offence dealing with related party
         transactions under Section 188 at any time during the last preceding five
         years. The Companies (Amendment) Act, 2020 decriminalised Section 188,
         and the provision dealing with imposition of criminal liability was replaced with
         a provision for imposition of monetary penalties on the company, and any
         officer who is in default. However, no corresponding amendment was made to
         Section 164(1)(g). The Committee Report has now recommended that Section
         164(1)(g) should be amended to provide that the imposition of monetary
         penalties on a director, for non compliance with Section 188 would attract the
         disqualification provided under Section 164(1)(g). Hence, if the amendment is
         incorporated, any director on whom monetary penalties are imposed for non-
         compliance with Section 188 would stand disqualified from holding office as a
         director, for a period of five years from the date on which the penalties have
         been imposed. The Committee Report has not expressed any view relating to
         whether noncompliance with the RPT regime under the SEBI (LODR)
         Regulations, 2015 ("LODR") would also attract the disqualification under
         Section 164(1)(g)

54.5 Examination by the Committee:

54.5.1 Acknowledging the issue relating to the inclusion of registered valuers within
the proposed disqualification framework and the concern that the three-year cooling-
off period is disproportionate given the assignment-based nature of their
engagement, the Ministry, in its written reply, submitted as under:

         "The provisions related to `subjected to penalty for default' and `fit and proper'
         criteria will be omitted. This would address the suggestion from stakeholders
         to rationalize disqualification of directors in cases of conviction in provisions
         related to related parties transactions and assessment of director as "fit and
         proper" by Board and the cooling off period be reduced to two years. Hence,
         the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 shall be modified
         accordingly."

54.5.2. Clarification was sought on the proposed extension of disqualification under
Section 164(1)(g) to cases involving monetary penalties imposed for non-compliance
with Section 188 following its decriminalisation, including whether such
disqualification would also extend to violations of the related party transaction
provisions under the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, the Ministry I its written reply
stated as under:

                                                      469
        "Section 164(1)(g) of the Companies Act, 2013 specifically relates to offences
        and penalties under Section 188 of the Act. Extending such disqualification to
        regulatory violations under other laws may require separate consideration
        under the respective regulatory framework. Hence, the provision in the
        Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
        change."

54.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

54.6.1  The Committee note that Clause 54 seeks to strengthen the

disqualification framework for directors by, inter alia, reducing the threshold

for disqualification on account of continuous non-filing of financial statements

or annual returns from three consecutive financial years to two financial years,

introducing a cooling-off period for certain professionals associated with the

company before their appointment as directors, expanding the scope of

disqualification under Section 164(1)(g), introducing a "fit and proper person"

criterion, and providing for consequential vacation of office under Section 167.

         The Committee further note the concerns expressed by stakeholders
that extending disqualification to cases where a person has merely been
subjected to a monetary penalty under Section 188 would be inconsistent with
the objective of decriminalisation, since technical defaults no longer
constituting criminal offences should not attract the serious civil consequence
of disqualification. The Committee also note the concern that, given the
diverse categories of directors under the Act, it would be difficult to objectively
determine what constitutes a "fit and proper person", and the proposed
criterion may lead to subjective and arbitrary application. The Committee
further note the concerns that the proposed "fit and proper person" criterion,
to be prescribed through subordinate legislation, confers an excessively broad
delegated power in a matter involving significant civil consequences. The
Committee further note the concerns regarding the inclusion of registered
valuers within the proposed cooling-off framework, having regard to the
assignment-based nature of their engagement.

        470
         The Committee are of the view that the proposed amendment under sub-
clause (A) of clause (g) of sub-section (1), seeking to substitute the words
"dealing with related party transactions" with the words "or subjected to
penalty for default", is inconsistent with the objective of decriminalisation, as
technical defaults attracting civil penalties should not automatically result in
the serious consequence of disqualification from holding office as a director.
The Committee are of the view that the Companies Act, 2013 recognises
different categories of directors each performing distinct roles and
responsibilities. In the absence of objective statutory parameters, it would be
difficult to prescribe a uniform standard for determining what constitutes a "fit
and proper person" across such diverse categories of directors. The
Committee are of the view that such a broad and undefined criterion may lead
to subjective interpretation, inconsistent application and the possibility of
arbitrary exercise of power in matters involving significant civil consequences.
The Committee further consider that the proposed "fit and proper person"
criterion under clause (k), being left to be prescribed through subordinate
legislation, involves excessive delegation of essential legislative functions.
The Committee also consider that a cooling-off period of two years for
auditors, secretarial auditors, cost auditors, registered valuers and insolvency
professionals would adequately safeguard the independence of the Board
while avoiding undue restrictions on such professionals.

         The Committee, therefore, recommend that the proposed amendment
under sub-clause (A) of clause (g) of sub-section (1), seeking to substitute the
words "dealing with related party transactions" with the words "or subjected to
penalty for default", be omitted. The Committee further recommend that the
proposed "fit and proper person" criterion under clause (k) be omitted and that
the cooling-off period under clause (j) be reduced to two years. The
Committee, accordingly, recommend that Clause 54 be modified as follows:

In section 164 of the principal Act,--

      (a) in sub-section (1),--
                                                      471
     (i) in clause (g), [***]the word "or" occurring at the end shall be
     omitted;

      (ii) in clause (h), for the word and figures "section 152.", the word and
      figures "section 152;" shall be substituted;

      (iii) after clause (i), the following shall be inserted, namely:--

            "(j) he has been an auditor or a secretarial auditor or a cost
            auditor or a registered valuer or an insolvency professional of the
            company or its holding, subsidiary or associate company
            discharging the functions as such under this Act or under the
            Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 during the immediately
            preceding [***] two financial years or during the current financial
            year.

            Explanation.--For the purposes of this clause, where the audit or
            secretarial audit or cost audit of a company is conducted, or
            valuation services or insolvency professional services are
            provided, by a partnership firm or a limited liability partnership,
            such partner or partners of the partnership firm or a limited
            liability partnership, as the case may be, who conducted the audit
            or provided the valuation services or insolvency professional
            services, as the case may be, shall not be eligible for appointment
            as a director under this sub-section [***];

            [***]

(b) in sub-section (2),--

      (i) in clause (a), for the words "three financial years", the words "two
      financial years" shall be substituted;

(ii) in the longline, after the words "fails to do so", the words, brackets
and figures "and office of director shall become vacant as per the

55. Clause 55 of the Bill proposes to amend Section 165 of the Companies
Act, 2013.

55.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

In section 165 of the principal Act, in sub-section (1),--

(a) after the proviso, the following proviso shall be inserted, namely:--

"Provided further that the Central Government may, by notification,
specify a lower number under this sub-section for a class or classes of
companies or a class or classes of directors.";

(b) in Explanation II, for the words "of twenty companies", the words "under
         this section" shall be substituted.

55.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013):

165. (1) No person, after the commencement of this Act, shall hold office as
         a director, including any alternate directorship, in more than twenty
         companies at the same time:

Provided that the maximum number of public companies in which a
person can be appointed as a director shall not exceed ten.

*  *  *  *  *    *       *  *                               *  *           *

Explanation II.--For reckoning the limit of directorships of twenty
companies, the directorship in a dormant company shall not be
included.

*  *  *  *  *    *       *  *                               *  *           *

55.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
         proposed provision:

            474
         "Amendment in section 165 is proposed to empower the Central Government
         to prescribe a lower number of directorships for such class or classes of
         companies or directors, as may be notified." [MCA justification at Sl.No.71 of the

          Comparative Table]

55.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

Some of the important suggestions given by experts and stakeholders are as under:

55.4.1. "It is recommended that the clause be retained, subject to the proviso that
the number so specified shall not be less than ten in the case of public companies."

55.4.2. "Insert a proviso after the proviso so proposed:

                Provided further that any such notification shall not affect the
                directorships validly held by a director as on the date of the notification,
                and such director shall be allowed a period of one year from the date of
                the notification, or such longer period as may be prescribed, to bring the
                number of their directorships within the revised limit, and no proceedings
                for vacation of office under section 167 shall lie in respect of such
                directorships during the said period."

55.4.3. During the Committee's deliberations, a suggestion was also made to
differentiate between public and listed entities, recommending that while the limit for
public companies be capped at ten directorships, the ceiling for listed companies
could be further reduced to five.

55.5 Examination by the Committee

55.5.1. While acknowledging the suggestion to specify a floor limit of ten
directorships in the case of public companies (referred to in para 55.4.1), the Ministry
of Corporate Affairs in their written reply submitted as under:

                                                      475
"Suggestion shall be dealt with under the subordinate legislation. The further
suggestion will be taken care of at the time of rulemaking. Hence, the provision in the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

55.5.2. Regarding the suggestion to provide transitional protection and immunity
from proceedings under Section 167 for existing directorships (referred to in para
55.4.2), the Ministry in their written reply stated as under:

"Suggestion shall be dealt with under the subordinate legislation. The suggestion
proposes an additional proviso to specify a time limit to comply for directors who may
be in contravention of notifications prescribed by the Central Government. Such
suggestion may be dealt with at the rule making stage. Hence, the provision in the
Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any change."

55.5.3. With respect to the proposal for reducing the directorship ceiling for listed
entities to five (referred to in para 55.4.3), Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs,
during oral evidence held on 17.7.2026, informed the Committee as under:

"SEBI wants to bring it down; that is why we want to make it."

55.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

55.6.1  On scrutinizing Clause 55 of the Bill, which seeks to amend

Section 165 of the Companies Act, the Committee note that it empowers the

Central Government to notify a lower maximum number of directorships for

specific classes of companies or directors.

The Committee acknowledge that calibrating directorship caps is a
progressive measure intended to ensure greater active participation, diligence,
and board oversight by corporate leaders.

The Committee, however, observe that the proposed enabling provision does
not specify a transitional mechanism, which could lead to inadvertent non-
compliance and trigger abrupt vacation of office under Section 167 of the Act
the moment a lower cap is notified.

                                                      476
To prevent administrative hardship and operational disruption, the Committee
expect the Ministry to incorporate a clear compliance window in the rules,
allowing affected directors a reasonable time period to bring their
directorships within the revised ceilings without being exposed to vacation
proceedings under Section 167 during such period.
55.6.2. Regarding the calibration of lower ceilings--including separate limits
for public and listed entities--the Committee emphasize that the power
delegated to the Central Government must be exercised judiciously. The
Committee accordingly desire that the Ministry, while framing statutory rules,
take into account realistic operational requirements, consult key regulators
such as SEBI and other relevant stakeholders, and maintain balanced
standards that do not unduly constrain legitimate corporate group structures.
55.6.3 Subject to the incorporation of these procedural safeguards in the
rules, and upon due consideration of the stakeholder representations
alongside the Ministry's assurances, the Committee concur with the proposed
statutory changes and recommend the adoption of Clause 55 without any
modification.

56. Clause 56 of the Bill proposes to amend Section 166 of the Companies
Act, 2013

56.1 Provision proposed in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

In section 166 of the principal Act,--

(a) in sub-section (7),

(i) for the words "provisions of this section", the words, brackets and figure
"provisions of sub-section (5)," shall be substituted;

(ii) after the words "five lakh rupees", the words, brackets and figure "and the court
may also order such director to pay the amount of undue gains referred to in sub-
section (5) to the company" shall be inserted;

(b) after sub-section (7), the following sub-section shall be inserted, namely:--

"(8) If a director of the company makes default in complying with the provisions of
this section [except sub-section (5)], he shall,--

(i) in case of a listed company, be liable to a penalty of five lakh rupees; and

(ii) in case of any other company, be liable to a penalty of two lakh rupees."

56.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013):

166. Duties of directors.--

(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, a director of a company shall act in
accordance with the articles of the company.

(2) A director of a company shall act in good faith in order to promote the objects of
the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, and in the best interests of
the company, its employees, the shareholders, the community and for the protection
of environment.

                                                      478
(3) A director of a company shall exercise his duties with due and reasonable care,
skill and diligence and shall exercise independent judgment.

(4) A director of a company shall not involve in a situation in which he may have a
direct or indirect interest that conflicts, or possibly may conflict, with the interest of
the company.

(5) A director of a company shall not achieve or attempt to achieve any undue gain
or advantage either to himself or to his relatives, partners, or associates and if such
director is found guilty of making any undue gain, he shall be liable to pay an amount
equal to that gain to the company.

(6) A director of a company shall not assign his office and any assignment so made
shall be void.

(7) If a director of the company contravenes the provisions of this section such
director shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than one lakh rupees
but which may extend to five lakh rupees.

56.3 Reason/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

"The amendment seeks to rationalize the enforcement of directors' duties by
decriminalizing most contraventions under section 166 and shifting them to a civil
penalty regime, while retaining criminal liability for serious breaches involving undue
gain under sub-section (5)."

56.4. Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

56.4.1.  With respect to Clause 56, an important suggestion as received from

the stakeholder is as follows:

"It is recommended that the proposed sub-section (8) be reconsidered. If retained, it
should be confined to contraventions of subsections (6) (assignment of office) and
such other objectively ascertainable defaults, and should expressly exclude
subsections (2) and (3)."

                                479
56.5. Examination by the Committee:

56.5.1.  Regarding the suggestion to restrict penalties under Section 166(8)

strictly to contraventions of sub-section (6)--excluding sub-sections (2) and (3)

(referred to in para 56.4.1)--the Ministry in its written statement submitted that

limiting the penal scope would dilute the provision's overall effectiveness. Asserting

that a comprehensive penalty framework is essential to enforce compliance across

all statutory duties of directors, the Ministry recommended retaining the provision

without modification.

56.5.2.  As such during the Sitting of the Committee held on 17 July, 2026, the

representatives of Ministry of Corporate Affairs, in context of Clause 56, deposed as

under:

"Barring that, we are decriminalizing other procedural aspects. In sub-Section (5)
also, we are making it clear that if someone is making undue gain due to his position,
that undue gain can be calculated by the Court - how much that undue gain was, and
then it has to be taken back from that particular Director. That provision is also
getting added."

56.6. Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

The Committee note that Clause 56 rationalizes the enforcement of directors'
fiduciary duties under Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 by
decriminalizing routine defaults, while preserving criminal liability and
disgorgement mechanisms for grave breaches involving wrongful enrichment
under sub-section (5).

The Committee observe with satisfaction that empowering courts to order the
recovery of undue gains under sub-section (7) and introducing non-criminal
penalties under sub-section (8) fills a critical legislative gap, establishing a
balanced, proportionate, and enforceable compliance framework.

                                     480
Regarding stakeholder concerns over subjecting non-procedural duties--such
as acting in good faith, exercising due care, skill, diligence, and independent
judgment under sub-sections (2) and (3)--to monetary penalties, the
Committee are firmly of the view that excluding these core fiduciary duties
from sub-section (8) would compromise board accountability. The Committee,
therefore, emphasize that all statutory obligations under Section 166 must
remain backed by civil penalties, while expecting adjudicating authorities to
exercise judicious discretion to distinguish between bona fide business
decisions and deliberate breaches of duty.
In view of the overall merit of the proposed statutory changes, the Committee
concur with the provisions and recommend the adoption of Clause 56 without
any modification.

                                               CLAUSE - 57

57.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 :

57.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013) :

                                                      482
167. Vacation of office of director.--(1) The office of a director shall become vacant
in case--

         (a) he incurs any of the disqualifications specified in section 164:

         [Provided that where he incurs disqualification under sub-section (2) of section
164, the office of the director shall become vacant in all the companies, other than
the company which is in default under that sub-section];

         (b) he absents himself from all the meetings of the Board of Directors held
during a period of twelve months with or without seeking leave of absence of the
Board;

         (c) he acts in contravention of the provisions of section 184 relating to entering
into contracts or arrangements in which he is directly or indirectly interested;

         (d) he fails to disclose his interest in any contract or arrangement in which he
is directly or indirectly interested, in contravention of the provisions of section 184;

         (e) he becomes disqualified by an order of a court or the Tribunal;

         (f) he is convicted by a court of any offence, whether involving moral turpitude
or otherwise and sentenced in respect thereof to imprisonment for not less than six
months:

         [Provided that the office shall not be vacated by the director in case of orders
referred to in clauses (e) and (f)--

                (i) for thirty days from the date of conviction or order of disqualification;

                (ii) where an appeal or petition is preferred within thirty days as aforesaid
          against the conviction resulting in sentence or order, until expiry of seven
          days from the date on which such appeal or petition is disposed of; or

                (iii) where any further appeal or petition is preferred against order or
          sentence within seven days, until such further appeal or petition is disposed
          of.]

         (g) he is removed in pursuance of the provisions of this Act;

other employment in the holding, subsidiary or associate company, ceases to hold

   (2) If a person, functions as a director even when he knows that the office of
director held by him has become vacant on account of any of the disqualifications
specified in sub-section (1), he shall be punishable 1*** with fine which shall not be
less than one lakh rupees but which may extend to [five lakh rupees].

   (3) Where all the directors of a company vacate their offices under any of the

   (4) A private company may, by its articles, provide any other ground for the

57.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
proposed provision:

         "This amendment seeks to provide that in cases of disqualification under
section 164(2), the office of director shall be vacated in all companies, including the
defaulting company, after six months or upon expiry of his tenure, whichever is
earlier. Presently, vacation is mandated in such cases in all companies except the
defaulting company. The amendment also replaces the existing fine with a penalty
framework. The amendment is part of the broader decriminalisation exercise under
the Bill."

57.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

Some of the important suggestions given by experts / stakeholders are as follows :

57.4.1.a "Apply disqualification in the defaulting company only to whole-time and

57.4.2 "Retain the existing position -- keep directors responsible in the defaulting
company."

57.4.3 "1. Allow directors to retain their office in other companies if the company's
default is rectified in a specified period.

         2. An exception for Non-executive Directors who are not involved in day-to-

57.4.4 "The existing position may be retained, whereby a director incurring

57.4.7 A suggestion opposed the proposed six-month grace period for a director
before vacation of office takes effect and suggested retaining the provision for

57.5 Examination by the Committee:

57.5.1. Regarding the suggestions to restrict disqualification under Section 164(2) to
whole-time and promoter directors, and to clarify the position of new directors

                                                      485
appointed after a default (referred to in paras 57.4.1.a and 57.4.1.b), the Ministry of
Corporate Affairs in its written reply submitted as under:

"The amendment to Section 167 has been expressly brought up with the goal of
decriminalising offences under the Companies Act, 2013. Clause 57 of the
Amendment Bill must be read with Clause 54 which amends Section 164 of the
Companies Act, 2013 stating that directors must vacate their office upon non-filing of
annual returns for two consecutive years. The contravention of non-filing of financial
statements and annual returns is grave and the Amendment Bill has proportionately
dealt with the same to ensure that all directors, regardless of their designation, are
responsible for the operations of the company. The proposed Section 167 therefore,
acts as a sufficient deterrent to non-compliances regarding filing of annual returns by
companies.

It is also clarified that once the default is made under Section 164(2), no fresh
disqualification for the same default would apply for six months to a new director
appointed after the default.

Hence, the provision for vacation of office of a director in the Corporate Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without change."

57.5.2. While turning down the suggestion for retaining the existing position for
keeping directors responsible in the defaulting company (referred to in para 57.4.2),
the Ministry in its written reply submitted as under:

"The amendment seeks to ensure that directors who incur disqualification under
section 164(2) do not continue on the Board indefinitely. A transition period of six
months has been provided before vacation of office takes effect, enabling the
company to address the default and for orderly transition of the board. Hence, the
provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without
change."

57.5.3. Regarding the proposal to allow directors to retain their office in other
companies provided the default in the primary company is rectified within a specified
period (referred to in Item 1 of para 57.4.3), the Ministry in its written statement
submitted as under:

"The proposed amendment already provides a six-month transition period before the
office of a disqualified director becomes vacant. This provides sufficient time for the
company to address the default. Providing a further exemption based on subsequent

                                                      486
rectification is not considered to be required. Hence, the provision in the Corporate
Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without change."

57.5.4. On the suggestion to create an exception for Non-Executive Directors who
are not involved in day-to-day operations (referred to in Item 2 of para 57.4.3), the
Ministry cited implementation difficulties and stated as under:

"The amendment applies uniformly to directors who incur disqualification under
section 164(2). Introducing a differential framework on the basis of the nature of the
director's role may create ambiguity and weaken the objective of maintaining
collective accountability for directors associated with companies in default. Hence,
the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without
change."

57.5.5. With respect to the suggestion that the existing statutory position be
retained--whereby a disqualified director continues in office in the defaulting
company solely for curing the default while vacating office in other companies
(referred to in para 57.4.4)--the Ministry, while turning down the proposal, submitted
as under:

"The suggestion further proposes to retain directors until the noncompliance is cured.
Accepting this suggestion may be counter-productive to the goal of ensuring that
directors are not held criminally liable but still face serious consequences for
contraventions under the Companies Act, 2013. The Amendment Bill hopes to strike
a balance to deter companies and directors from contravening the provisions of the
Companies Act, 2013 while decriminalising certain contraventions to promote ease of
doing business. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026
may be retained without change."

57.5.6. Regarding the request for administrative relaxations or alternative
authentication mechanisms for foreign directors completing DIR-3 KYC compliance
(referred to in para 57.4.5), the Ministry in its written reply submitted as under:

"The suggestion relates to procedural compliance with DIR-3 KYC and the
deactivation of Director Identification Numbers. The proposed suggestion falls
outside the scope of the statute. Practical difficulties faced by foreign directors in
completing DIR-3 KYC are being examined separately through the relevant Rules. It
is also to be noted that annual Director KYC requirement has been replace with once
in 3 years KYC. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026
may be retained without any change."

                                                      487
57.5.7. With respect to the suggestion proposing explicit references to sub-section

"Provisions under Section 184(1) and 184(2) are very important in nature. Hence, the
provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 may be retained without any
change."

57.5.8. On the suggestion opposing the proposed six-month transition period and

57.4.7), the Ministry in its written statement submitted as under:

"The amendment seeks to strengthen the disqualification framework for directors.
The six-month grace period has therefore been incorporated to provide transitional
stability, allowing companies sufficient time to appoint replacements and maintain
continuity in governance. Hence, the provision in the Corporate Laws (Amendment)
Bill, 2026 may be retained without change."

57.6. Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

57.6.1.  The Committee note that Clause 57 seeks to rationalize the

disqualification and vacation framework under Section 167 of the Companies

Act, 2013 by mandating vacation of office across all companies--including the

defaulting entity--after a uniform six-month transition period. The Committee

consider this transition window vital for ensuring collective board

accountability for fundamental defaults, such as non-filing of financial

statements, while safeguarding operational continuity through an orderly

management transition.

While taking note of the Ministry's clarification that new directors shall not
incur disqualification for past defaults of a company, the Committee express
concern over lingering administrative friction, particularly regarding DIR-3 KYC
compliance for foreign directors. The Committee expect the Ministry to honour
its assurance and resolve these administrative hurdles through suitable rules
without delay.

The Committee, therefore, recommend the Ministry to frame simple, robust,
and accessible rules in a consultative manner, ensuring that statutory
compliance processes do not become operational impediments to
international directorships.

                              489
57.6.2.  The Committee recognize the need to clearly distinguish between

deactivation (temporary suspension) and cancellation (permanent closure) of

DIN. The Ministry clarified that these consequences are comprehensively

addressed under Section 154, making parallel amendments in Sections 152

and 167 redundant. The Committee consider that a unified treatment under

Section 154 avoids duplication, ensures legal clarity, and strengthens

administrative consistency across the Act. Accordingly, to harmonise the

provisions of Sections 152, 154 and 167, the Committee recommend that

Clause 57 be amended in alignment with Section 154, thereby ensuring

statutory consistency and eliminating duplicative references. The amended

Clause 57 may read as under

"In section 167 of the principal Act,--

(b) in sub-section (2), for the words "he shall be punishable with fine which
shall not be less than one lakh rupees but which may extend to five lakh
rupees", the following shall be substituted, namely:

***                          *********        ************

(i) in case of listed company, be liable to a penalty of five lakh rupees; and

(ii) in case of any other company, be liable to a penalty of two lakh rupees."

58. Clause 58 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 173 of the Companies Act
2013 regarding Meetings of Board.

58.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

         In section 173 of the principal Act, in sub-section (5), for the words "each half
of a calendar year and the gap between the two meetings is not less than ninety
days", the words "a calendar year" shall be substituted.

58.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013):

                           MEETINGS OF BOARD AND ITS POWERS

173. (1) * * * * *

(5) A One Person Company, small company and dormant company shall be
deemed to have complied with the provisions of this section if at least one meeting of
the Board of Directors has been conducted in each half of a calendar year and the
gap between the two meetings is not less than ninety days:

         Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section and in section 174 shall
apply to One Person Company in which there is only one director on its Board of
Directors.

                                                 * * * * *

58.3 Reason/Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
          proposed provision:

         "This amendment is to relax the Board meeting requirement for One-Person
Companies, Small companies and dormant companies requiring them to hold only
one Board meeting in a calendar year for ease of doing business."

                                                      491
58.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

58.4.1  Few stakeholders welcomed the amendment to the original Act stating

that this will reduce compliance burden and enhance ease of doing business

especially for MSMEs.

58.4.2  A suggestion regarding promotion of digital governance by recognising

secure digital Board processes, AI-assisted record-keeping with safeguards, and

electronic authentication and retention of Board records was placed before the

Committee wherein it was stated as follows:

         "We recommend that the Committee promote digital governance by
simplifying compliance requirements, prescribing the period for the maintenance and
retention of digital records, and ensuring appropriate Board accountability.

         The Committee may also recommend that the Government of India facilitate
 the development of secure AI-assisted tools to assist in the preparation of Board
 minutes and other Board records, subject to appropriate human oversight and
 approval.

         Further, the Committee may consider recognizing secure digital Board portals
 and the maintenance of electronic attendance registers, and permitting the
 authentication of all Board records through Aadhaar e-Sign or DSC in the case of
 resident directors, while allowing equivalent internationally recognized electronic
 authentication methods or other prescribed alternative proofs for foreign national
 directors".

58.5 Examination by the Committee:

         In response to the suggestion at paragraph 58.4.2 above, the Ministry, in its
written submission, stated that it was unable to incorporate the reform within the
current clause, since the suggestion proposes wider reforms relating to digital
governance. The Ministry noted, however, that this could be considered separately
during the framing of the relevant Rules. (Batch II, Sl. No. 215)

                       492
58.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

58.6.1 The Committee note that Section 173(5) of the Companies Act, 2013
currently requires One Person Companies, small companies, and dormant
companies to hold at least one Board meeting in each half of the calendar year,
with a minimum gap of ninety days between the two meetings. The proviso
exempts One Person Companies with only one director from this requirement.
The Committee further note that the proposed amendment collapses this into a
simpler requirement of at least one Board meeting in a calendar year for these
classes of companies, thereby removing the rigid ninety-day gap stipulation.

58.6.2 The Committee recognize that the earlier requirement imposed
disproportionate procedural burdens on companies with minimal scale and
limited operations. The Committee are of the view that the amendment eases
compliance for very small entities by reducing Board-meeting requirements to
a single annual meeting, thereby aligning governance obligations with
practical realities while still preserving minimum oversight.

58.6.3  The Committee note the Ministry's view that digital governance

reforms suggested are broader in scope and do not require amendment to the

Act, but may be considered separately through Rules. The Committee welcome

this assurance and recommend that, while framing the Rules, the Ministry

incorporate mechanisms for digital record-keeping of Board proceedings to

ensure transparency and accountability even with reduced meeting frequency.

58.6.4  The Committee, therefore, accept Clause 58 as proposed, without

any modification.

         CLAUSE - 59

Clause 59 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 184 of the Companies Act 2013
regarding Disclosure of interest by Director.

59.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

                  In section 184 of the principal Act, in sub-section (1), the words "at the
first meeting of the Board in every financial year or" shall be omitted.

59.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013):

184. (1) Every director shall at the first meeting of the Board in which he participates
as a director and thereafter at the first meeting of the Board in every financial year or
whenever there is any change in the disclosures already made, then at the first
Board meeting held after such change, disclose his concern or interest in any
company or companies or bodies corporate, firms, or other association of individuals
which shall include the shareholding, in such manner as may be prescribed.

59.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
         proposed provision:

"This amendment seeks to make directors' filings in form MBP-1 event based rather
than annual to reduce compliance burden."

59.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

A stakeholder, in its suggestion, appreciated the Bill's attempt towards event-based
digital compliance which in turn reduces repetitive filings.

59.5 Examination by the Committee:

59.5.1   The Ministry of Corporate Affairs, while acknowledging the view of the

stakeholder, reiterated its stand on enhancing ease of compliance for corporate

bodies.

                                    494
59.5.2  Secretary, MCA at the sitting held on 17.7.2026 explained that the

requirement is being changed so that a director discloses his interest at the time of

joining the company, and thereafter discloses only when there is a change, in place

of the earlier requirement of annual disclosure.

59.6. Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

59.6.1  The Committee note that Section 184(1) currently requires every

director to disclose his concern or interest in any company, body corporate,

firm or association of individuals (including shareholding) at the first Board

meeting of every financial year, in addition to disclosing at the first meeting in

which he participates as director and whenever there is a change. The

Committee further note that the proposed amendment in Clause 59 seeks to

remove the recurring annual disclosure obligation, so that disclosures will

now be required only (a) at the first Board meeting attended by a director, and

(b) upon any change in previously declared interests.

59.6.2  The Committee appreciate that this amendment eliminates a

recurring, often perfunctory annual compliance step that added limited

governance value when no change in interest had occurred, making disclosure

event-driven rather than calendar-driven and thereby aligning the obligation

more closely with its substantive purpose. The Committee concur that Clause

59 is consistent with the Bill's broader objective of decriminalisation and

compliance-simplification, easing paperwork while maintaining the substantive

disclosure requirement, and accordingly accept the proposed amendment

without modification.

59.6.3  The Committee, however, observe that with the removal of the

annual catch-all disclosure, companies must adopt diligent mechanisms to

track changes in directors' interests to ensure continued transparency and

accountability, and that robust systems for monitoring directors' interests are

essential to safeguard governance standards and stakeholder confidence in

the absence of an annual disclosure ritual. The Committee recommend that the
                                                      495
Ministry consider instituting a transparent and objective mechanism for
companies to track changes in directors' interests more diligently, such as
through digital registers or authenticated electronic filings, so that governance
integrity is preserved even as compliance is simplified.

                                                      496
                                               CLAUSE - 60

60. Clause 60 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 185 of the Companies Act
2013 regarding Loan to Directors.

60.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

         In section 185 of the principal Act, in sub-section (1), in clause (b), after the
words "any firm", the words "or limited liability partnership" shall be inserted.

60.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013):

185. (1) No company shall, directly or indirectly, advance any loan, including any
loan represented by a book debt to, or give any guarantee or provide any security in
connection with any loan taken by,--

                                                 * * * * *

(b) any firm in which any such director or relative is a partner.

60.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
          proposed provision:

"The amendment seeks to include limited liability partnerships within the scope of the
provision by inserting a reference to LLPs, thereby addressing the existing gap."

60.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

60.4.1     A stakeholder, while seeking to bring in amendments to the provisions

of the Bill, suggested that the amendment proposed vide Clause No. 60 may be

withdrawn as Sub-section (1) deals with individual entities (including firm, which is

also not a corporate entity) and bars a company from advancing any loan, or giving

any Guarantee or providing any security in connection with any loan taken by such

individual entities, if a director of such company is related to any of such individual

entities.

           497
         They further pointed out that Addition of LLP (a corporate entity) in sub-
section (1) may not be in alignment with sub-section (2) wherein such aforesaid
transactions are permitted for corporate entities subject to the Company providing
loan, guarantee or security passing a special resolution in a general meeting.
Therefore, insertion of LLP in sub-section (1)(b) may restrict borrowers, which are
LLPs, from availing finance from Banks / FIs backed by security offered by such a
company and shall not be in keeping with scheme of the section wherein other
corporate entities are permitted to avail such benefit.

60.5 Examination by the Committee:

60.5.1  In response to the suggestion at paragraph 60.4.1 above, the Ministry,

in its written submission, stated as follows:

"Section 185(1) prohibits a company from advancing loans, book debts, guarantees
or security to its directors or entities closely linked to them; prior to this amendment,
the law expressly barred such financial assistance to "any firm" in which a director or
their relative was a partner. By adding LLPs to this clause, the amendment ensures
that any LLP in which a company's director or relative is a partner is now subject to
the same conditions, and the provision may accordingly be retained without any
change."

60.6 Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

60.6.1 The Committee note that Section 185(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013
restricts companies from advancing loans, guarantees or security to directors
or entities closely linked to them. The Committee further note that Clause 60
extends this restriction explicitly to limited liability partnerships in which a
director or his relative is a partner, thereby bringing LLPs within the scope of
related-party lending restrictions that previously applied only to firms.

                                    498
60.6.2 The Committee welcome the amendment, as it closes a structural gap
that could otherwise be used to circumvent related-party lending restrictions
through LLP structures, and ensures parity of treatment between traditional
firms and LLPs. The Committee, therefore, accept Clause 60 as proposed,
without modification.
60.6.3 The Committee, however, are of the view that the Ministry should
mandate a periodic review of existing loan/guarantee arrangements involving
LLPs connected to directors, to ensure continuing compliance, and require
companies to make a declaration of such compliance for the benefit of
stakeholders and the general public.

                                                      499
                                               CLAUSE - 61

61. Clause 61 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 186 of the Companies Act
2013 regarding Loan and investment by company.

61.1 Provision proposed in The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026:

         In section 186 of the principal Act,--

         (a) in sub-section (13), after the words "the provisions of this section", the
brackets, words and figures "[except sub-sections (9) and (10)]" shall be inserted;

         (b) after sub-section (13), the following sub-section shall be inserted, namely:-

         "(14) If a company contravenes the provisions of sub-section (9) or sub-
section (10), the company shall be liable to a penalty of one lakh rupees and in case
of continuing contravention, with a further penalty of five hundred rupees for each
day, after the first during which such contravention continues, subject to a maximum
of five lakh rupees and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable
to a penalty of twenty-five thousand rupees and in case of continuing default, with a
further penalty of two hundred rupees for each day, after the first during which such
default continues, subject to a maximum of one lakh rupees."

61.2 Relevant Provision of the Principal Act (The Companies Act, 2013):

                                              186. (1) * * * * *

         (13) If a company contravenes the provisions of this section, the company
shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand
rupees but which may extend to five lakh rupees and every officer of the company
who is in default shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend
to two years and with fine which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees
but which may extend to one lakh rupees.

         Explanation.--For the purposes of this section,--

                   (a) the expression "investment company" means a company whose
principal business is the acquisition of shares, debentures or other securities and a
company will be deemed to be principally engaged in the business of acquisition of
shares, debentures or other securities, if its assets in the form of investment in
shares, debentures or other securities constitute not less than fifty per cent. of its

                                                      500
total assets, or if its income derived from investment business constitutes not less
than fifty per cent. as a proportion of its gross income;

                   (b) the expression "infrastructure facilities" means the facilities
specified in Schedule VI.

                                                    * * * * *

61.3 Reasons / Justification given by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for the
         proposed provision:

"The amendment carves out contraventions of sub-sections (9) and (10) from the
existing criminal penalty provision and introduces a separate penalty framework for
such defaults under a new sub-section (14). The amendment is part of the broader
decriminalization exercise under the Bill."

61.4 Important Views/Suggestions given by Experts/Stakeholders:

While a stakeholder acknowledged the amendment as a positive step towards
reduction of compliance burden for the medium and small bodies, it suggested
changes as follows:

         "The approach towards decriminalization be extended to cover all minor or
technical contraventions of Section 186, not just the register keeping provisions. It
was suggested that aside from truly egregious cases involving willful or fraudulent
misuse of funds in violation of Section 186, breaches of Section 186 should attract
monetary penalties rather than criminal charges. It has been further suggested that
Section 186(13) be amended to remove imprisonment as a consequence for routine
non-compliance and contraventions of Section 186 would instead be dealt with
through a civil penalty framework (with escalating fines for continuing defaults or
serious breaches as appropriate), reserving criminal liability only for cases involving
fraud, willful misconduct, or harm to public interest."

                                                      501
61.5 Examination by the Committee:

In response to the suggestion at paragraph 61.4.1 above, the Ministry, in its written
submission, stated as follows:

61.5.1  "The proposed amendment decriminalises contraventions relating to

sub-sections (9) and (10) of section 186, which are procedural in nature, by providing

for a civil penalty framework. Other contraventions under section 186 relate to

substantive requirements, and therefore, continue to warrant the existing

enforcement framework. This amendment is a part of the decriminalisation exercise

as recommended by HLC-NFRR and DPIIT.Only procedural contraventions under

Sections 186(9) and (10) are proposed to be decriminalised, while substantive

violations will continue under the existing enforcement framework." .

61.5.2 Secretary, MCA at the sitting held on 17.7.2026 further explained that only two
specific points under section 186 are being decriminalised, and that the suggestion
to decriminalise all provisions under section 186 was not being accepted, since the
remaining sub-sections are serious in nature.

Observations/Recommendations of the Committee:

61.6.1  The Committee note that existing sub-sections (9) and (10) of

Section 186 of the Companies Act 2013 deal with the maintenance of a register

of investments/loans made by a company and the particulars to be entered in

it. Previously, contravention of any provision of section 186, including (9) and

(10), attracted the omnibus penalty under sub-section (13).

61.6.2  The Committee note that Clause 61 of the Bill seeks to carve out

these two sub-sections from the general penalty provision under Sub section

(13). The Committee also note that a new sub-section (14) has been inserted to

create a separate, lower, day-wise capped penalty structure specific to

register-related defaults. Under this framework, contravention by the company

                                    502
attracts a penalty of 1 lakh plus 500 per day for continuing contravention,
capped at 5 lakh. Every defaulting officer is liable to a penalty of 25,000 plus
200 per day for continuing default, capped at 1 lakh.

61.6.3  The Committee find that Clause 61 aligns with the Bill's broader

objective of rationalising penalties by disaggregating them according to the

severity of default, rather than applying a single omnibus penalty across all

violations of a section. The Committee are of the view that the calibrated

penalty framework ensures proportionality between the default and its

consequence, and enhances predictability and compliance certainty. The

Committee, therefore, accept Clause 61 as proposed, without modification.

61.6.4  The Committee also recommend that the Ministry ensure effective

implementation of the new penalty framework, including awareness among

companies and officers regarding the revised register-related obligations, so

that compliance is strengthened while litigation risk is reduced.
